subtopic_detail: adolescent with monthly lower abdominal pain who has never had a period and a bulging bluish membrane
stem:
You are the registrar in a paediatric emergency department seeing a 14-year-old girl brought in by her mother with lower abdominal pain. The pain has come in episodes lasting three or four days roughly every month for the past six months and is worsening; this time she has also found it difficult to pass urine and has not opened her bowels for two days.

She has never had a period. Her mother reports that she developed breasts around the age of eleven and that her growth spurt is finished. On examination she is afebrile and comfortable at rest. Breast development and pubic hair are both Tanner stage 5. There is a smooth, non tender midline suprapubic mass that reaches halfway to the umbilicus. Inspection of the vulva shows normal external genitalia with a tense bluish membrane bulging at the introitus, which becomes more prominent when she coughs. A bladder scan shows a residual volume of 480 mL.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 112/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees
data_table.Examination: Tanner stage 5 breast and pubic hair development, smooth non tender midline suprapubic mass
data_table.Vulval inspection: Normal external genitalia with a tense bluish membrane bulging at the introitus, more prominent on coughing
data_table.Investigations: Post void bladder residual volume 480 mL on bedside scan, urinary pregnancy test negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence a continuous combined oral contraceptive pill to suppress her cyclical symptoms
options.rationale: Menstrual suppression is a legitimate temporising measure when definitive surgery must be delayed, which is why it is tempting here. It does nothing for an existing collection or for the retention it is causing, so it cannot be the primary step. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Request a karyotype with serum testosterone and refer to the adolescent gynaecology clinic
options.rationale: Karyotype and androgen testing investigate complete androgen insensitivity, the near pair that also presents with primary amenorrhoea and normal breast development. That condition gives absent or sparse pubic hair and a blind ending vagina without an obstructed distended collection. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea)

options.text: Aspirate the collection through the membrane in the department with a wide bore needle
options.rationale: Needle aspiration decompresses the collection briefly but leaves the obstruction intact, so it refills, and puncturing a closed space risks converting sterile old blood into a pyocolpos. Formal incision with drainage is the standard. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Imperforate hymen)

options.text: Insert a urinary catheter and refer for surgical incision of the obstructing membrane
options.rationale: Primary amenorrhoea with normal secondary sexual characteristics, cyclical pain and a bulging bluish membrane is an imperforate hymen with haematocolpos, and urinary retention makes it urgent. Catheterisation relieves the retention while definitive surgical hymenotomy under anaesthesia drains the obstruction. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea)

options.text: Arrange an outpatient pelvic ultrasound and gynaecology clinic review within four weeks
options.rationale: Outpatient imaging would be sensible for cyclical pain without retention, and ultrasound does confirm the diagnosis. Waiting a month with a bladder residual of 480 mL risks upper tract dilatation and continued retrograde menstruation. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea)

explanation.summary: Imperforate hymen is the commonest obstructive anomaly of the female genital tract and results from failure of the hymenal membrane to canalise at the junction of the sinovaginal bulb and urogenital sinus. Because ovarian function and the endometrium are normal, girls develop normally through puberty and present only when menstrual blood accumulates, typically at thirteen to fifteen years with cyclical pain and primary amenorrhoea. Accumulated blood distends the vagina and later the uterus, producing a palpable pelvic mass that can compress the bladder neck and cause acute urinary retention, or the rectum and cause constipation. The examination that makes the diagnosis is simple inspection of the vulva, which is why the condition is often missed for months when the abdomen alone is examined. Definitive treatment is surgical hymenotomy under general anaesthesia, and outcomes including future fertility are excellent once the obstruction is relieved.
key_points: Normal secondary sexual characteristics with cyclical pain and no menses is the classic triad.
Vulval inspection shows a tense bulging bluish membrane and makes the diagnosis.
Urinary retention or constipation reflects mass effect from the distended vagina.
Androgen insensitivity is the near pair but gives absent pubic hair and no collection.
Definitive management is surgical hymenotomy, not aspiration.
explanation.pearls: Any adolescent presenting with acute urinary retention and no neurological cause should have the vulva inspected before imaging is ordered, because haematocolpos from an imperforate hymen is the diagnosis that a two minute examination makes and an abdominal examination alone will miss.

subtopic_detail: student with cramping on the first two days of each period since her cycles became regular
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 16-year-old girl who has cramping lower abdominal pain on the first two days of every period. It began about eighteen months after her first period, which was at twelve, and has been present with every cycle since. She describes it as coming in waves low down in the middle, sometimes with an ache into her thighs and some loose bowel motions on the first day.

She has missed three days of school this term. Her cycles are regular at 29 days with four days of bleeding that soaks four pads a day, and there is no bleeding between periods. She is not sexually active. She has been taking paracetamol 1 g as needed on the worst day with partial benefit, starting once the pain is established. Abdominal examination is soft with no masses or tenderness today, and she is systemically well with no weight loss and no urinary or bowel symptoms between periods.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Soft non tender abdomen, no palpable mass, normal secondary sexual characteristics
data_table.Menstrual history: Menarche at twelve, regular 29 day cycles, four days of bleeding, four pads per day, no intermenstrual bleeding
data_table.Current treatment: Paracetamol 1 g as required, started after pain onset, with partial benefit

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Refer for a diagnostic laparoscopy to look for peritoneal deposits and adhesions
options.rationale: Laparoscopy investigates endometriosis, the near pair, which is suggested by pain extending beyond the bleeding days, deep pain with intercourse, cyclical bowel or bladder symptoms, or failure of medical treatment. None of those features is present and no treatment has yet been tried. (Source: RANZCOG: Endometriosis)

options.text: Refer for a transvaginal ultrasound scan of the pelvis before starting any medical treatment
options.rationale: Imaging is reserved for atypical features, an abnormal examination or treatment failure, and transvaginal scanning is inappropriate in a young woman who is not sexually active. A normal scan would not change first line management. (Source: RANZCOG: Dysmenorrhoea)

options.text: Commence a non steroidal anti inflammatory drug started before the pain each cycle
options.rationale: Pain beginning within two years of menarche with regular cycles and no symptoms between periods is primary dysmenorrhoea, driven by endometrial prostaglandin release. Inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis is the mechanism specific treatment and works best when started before or at the onset of bleeding rather than once the pain is established. (Source: RANZCOG: Dysmenorrhoea)

options.text: Increase her paracetamol to 1 g four times daily throughout each day of bleeding
options.rationale: Regular rather than as needed dosing is a genuine improvement on what she is doing and is a reasonable adjunct, so this is the closest wrong answer. Paracetamol does not inhibit peripheral prostaglandin synthesis in the endometrium and is consistently less effective than a non steroidal agent for this indication. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Commence a monophasic combined oral contraceptive taken continuously without a break
options.rationale: Combined hormonal contraception is effective and is the usual second line, or the first choice when contraception is also wanted. It is not the initial step for an adolescent whose simple analgesia has never been optimised and who has not tried a prostaglandin inhibitor. (Source: RANZCOG: Dysmenorrhoea)

explanation.summary: Primary dysmenorrhoea is painful menstruation without identifiable pelvic pathology and affects up to three quarters of adolescents, making it a leading cause of school absence in this age group. Pain arises from prostaglandin F2 alpha released by the shedding endometrium, which causes myometrial contraction and ischaemia, and the same prostaglandins explain the accompanying nausea and diarrhoea. It characteristically begins six to twenty four months after menarche, once ovulatory cycles are established, and is confined to the first day or two of bleeding. Features that should prompt reconsideration include onset with the very first period, pain outside menstruation, deep dyspareunia, and failure to respond to adequate medical treatment, all of which raise endometriosis or an obstructive anomaly. Non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs are first line, combined hormonal contraception is the usual next step, and the two can be used together.
key_points: Onset six to twenty four months after menarche with pain confined to the bleeding days.
Prostaglandin mediated, which is why non steroidal agents outperform paracetamol.
Dosing should begin before or at the onset of bleeding, not after pain is established.
Combined hormonal contraception is second line or first when contraception is wanted.
Pain outside menstruation or treatment failure should prompt evaluation for endometriosis.
explanation.pearls: Mefenamic acid 500 mg three times daily, started one day before the expected period and continued for the first two to three days, is the standard Australian regimen, and taking it pre emptively rather than reactively is what converts a partial response into a complete one.

subtopic_detail: premenopausal woman with spotting between periods and a focal echogenic lesion within the cavity
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 41-year-old woman with eight months of light spotting that occurs about a week before each period. Her periods themselves remain regular at 30 days and are not heavy, and she has no pain. She has two children, is not using hormonal contraception, and her partner has had a vasectomy.

Her cervical screening test six months ago was negative for oncogenic human papillomavirus, and speculum examination at that visit showed a normal cervix. She has no risk factors for endometrial cancer and her body mass index is 24 kg per square metre. A transvaginal ultrasound arranged at her last visit reports a well defined echogenic lesion measuring 14 mm within the endometrial cavity with a single feeding vessel on colour Doppler, surrounded by normal appearing endometrium. Both ovaries are normal and there is no free fluid. A full blood examination shows haemoglobin 128 g/L (115 to 155).

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Normal cervix on speculum, mobile anteverted uterus of normal size, no adnexal mass
data_table.Imaging: Transvaginal ultrasound: well defined 14 mm echogenic intracavity lesion with a single feeding vessel, normal surrounding endometrium and normal ovaries
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 128 g/L (115 to 155), human papillomavirus testing negative six months ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Perform an outpatient endometrial pipelle sampling in the consulting room this afternoon
options.rationale: Blind pipelle sampling reliably detects diffuse endometrial pathology such as hyperplasia or carcinoma, but it samples only a fraction of the cavity and frequently misses a focal lesion entirely. A negative result would falsely reassure. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of abnormal vaginal bleeding)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Investigation of abnormal vaginal bleeding

options.text: Repeat the transvaginal ultrasound in the early follicular phase of her next menstrual cycle
options.rationale: Timing a scan to days five to ten is the right way to reduce false positives when the endometrium looks thickened and non specific, since secretory endometrium can mimic pathology. A discrete lesion with its own feeding vessel is already a definite finding. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of abnormal vaginal bleeding)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Investigation of abnormal vaginal bleeding

options.text: Prescribe tranexamic acid during bleeding days and review her symptoms in three months
options.rationale: Antifibrinolytic therapy reduces menstrual blood loss but has no effect on intermenstrual spotting from a structural lesion, and her blood count is normal so volume is not the problem. This treats the wrong element of her presentation. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Refer for hysteroscopic resection of the lesion with the specimen sent for histology
options.rationale: A well defined echogenic intracavity lesion with a single feeding vessel is an endometrial polyp, and hysteroscopic resection under direct vision both cures the bleeding and provides tissue. It is the definitive investigation and treatment in one procedure. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of abnormal vaginal bleeding)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Investigation of abnormal vaginal bleeding

options.text: Insert a levonorgestrel releasing intrauterine system to control the intermenstrual spotting
options.rationale: The intrauterine system is excellent for heavy menstrual bleeding once the cavity is known to be normal, and it does thin the endometrium. Placing it over an undiagnosed focal lesion leaves the pathology in place and commonly causes further unscheduled bleeding. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)

explanation.summary: Endometrial polyps are focal overgrowths of endometrial glands and stroma with a fibrovascular core, and they are a common structural cause of intermenstrual bleeding in women in their thirties and forties. On transvaginal ultrasound they appear as well defined echogenic intracavity lesions, and the single feeding vessel on colour Doppler, sometimes called the pedicle artery sign, is characteristic. The key management principle is that focal lesions need focal sampling: blind endometrial biopsy is designed for diffuse pathology and has poor sensitivity for a discrete polyp, so hysteroscopy is required. Malignancy within a polyp is uncommon in premenopausal women at well under two per cent, but rises with age, postmenopausal status, tamoxifen use and polyp size, so histology is always obtained. Saline infusion sonohysterography is an alternative way of delineating the cavity where hysteroscopy access is limited.
key_points: Intermenstrual bleeding with a discrete echogenic intracavity lesion suggests a polyp.
A single feeding vessel on colour Doppler supports the diagnosis.
Blind pipelle sampling has poor sensitivity for focal lesions.
Hysteroscopic resection is diagnostic and therapeutic in the same procedure.
Malignancy risk rises with age, postmenopausal status, tamoxifen use and polyp size.
explanation.pearls: Measure the endometrium on days five to ten of the cycle when a scan is being arranged for abnormal bleeding in a premenopausal woman, because a secretory phase endometrium can measure over 14 mm normally and generates unnecessary referrals.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Investigation of abnormal vaginal bleeding

subtopic_detail: woman wanting to conceive with a diffusely enlarged tender uterus and junctional zone thickening
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 36-year-old woman referred with worsening period pain and heavy bleeding over three years. She describes a constant dragging heaviness through the whole of the last week of her cycle rather than pain confined to the bleeding days, and she now takes two days off work each month.

She and her partner have been trying to conceive for eleven months. Her cycles are regular at 27 days and she passes clots, but she has never had bleeding between periods. Examination reveals a symmetrically enlarged globular uterus about the size of a ten week pregnancy, which is tender and boggy on bimanual palpation, with no adnexal masses and no nodularity in the pouch of Douglas. Transvaginal ultrasound reports a globular uterus with asymmetrical myometrial wall thickening, junctional zone thickening of 14 mm, and small myometrial cysts. No discrete fibroid is identified and the endometrium and ovaries appear normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Symmetrically enlarged globular tender uterus of about ten week size, no adnexal mass, no uterosacral nodularity
data_table.Imaging: Transvaginal ultrasound: globular uterus, asymmetrical myometrial wall thickening, junctional zone 14 mm, myometrial cysts, normal endometrium and ovaries
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 108 g/L (115 to 155), ferritin 14 mcg/L (30 to 200)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management to recommend first?

options.text: Insert a levonorgestrel releasing intrauterine system to reduce bleeding and relieve the pain
options.rationale: The intrauterine system is the most effective medical treatment for adenomyosis and would be the right answer for a woman not seeking pregnancy. It is a contraceptive, so recommending it to a woman actively trying to conceive defeats her primary goal. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)

options.text: Commence a gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonist with add back therapy for six months
options.rationale: Agonist therapy shrinks adenomyotic tissue and is sometimes used before surgery, but it induces a hypo oestrogenic anovulatory state and so prevents conception throughout treatment. It also carries bone density consequences over that timeframe. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Commence iron replacement with tranexamic acid during bleeding and refer to fertility services
options.rationale: Junctional zone thickening above 12 mm with a globular tender uterus and myometrial cysts is adenomyosis, and every effective suppressive treatment for it prevents conception. In a woman with an eleven month history of trying, the plan is symptom control that preserves fertility plus timely referral. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)

options.text: Refer for diagnostic laparoscopy with excision of any peritoneal deposits identified
options.rationale: Laparoscopy targets peritoneal endometriosis, the near pair, which produces uterosacral nodularity, a fixed retroverted uterus and deep pain with intercourse rather than a symmetrically enlarged boggy uterus. Adenomyosis lies within the myometrium and is not diagnosed or treated by looking at the peritoneum. (Source: RANZCOG: Endometriosis)

options.text: Refer for uterine artery embolisation to reduce both the bleeding and the uterine bulk
options.rationale: Embolisation does improve adenomyosis symptoms but risks ovarian and endometrial injury and is generally avoided in women with a current pregnancy intention. It is offered mainly to women who have completed their families. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)

explanation.summary: Adenomyosis is the presence of endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium, producing a diffusely enlarged globular uterus with heavy painful periods and a characteristic dragging pelvic heaviness. Ultrasound features include a globular uterus, asymmetrical myometrial thickening, myometrial cysts, linear striations and a thickened or irregular junctional zone, with a junctional zone of 12 mm or more being widely used as a threshold. It is increasingly recognised as a contributor to subfertility and to miscarriage and preterm birth, probably through disrupted junctional zone peristalsis and impaired implantation. The central management tension is that the effective treatments, including the levonorgestrel intrauterine system, gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonists, continuous progestogens and embolisation, are all incompatible with conceiving. For the woman trying to conceive, treatment is therefore limited to fertility sparing symptom control with iron replacement, tranexamic acid and non steroidal analgesia, alongside prompt referral for assisted reproduction where indicated.
key_points: Globular tender uterus with junctional zone thickening above 12 mm suggests adenomyosis.
Endometriosis is distinguished by uterosacral nodularity and a fixed retroverted uterus.
Most effective treatments are contraceptive and therefore unavailable when conception is the goal.
Correct iron deficiency and use tranexamic acid for bleeding while fertility is being pursued.
Adenomyosis is associated with subfertility, miscarriage and preterm birth.
explanation.pearls: Tranexamic acid 1 g three to four times daily for the first three to four days of bleeding reduces menstrual blood loss by roughly 40 per cent without affecting ovulation or conception, which makes it the workhorse for heavy bleeding in a woman actively trying to become pregnant.

subtopic_detail: breastfeeding woman with severe shooting pain and blanching of the nipple starting after the feed ends
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a woman six weeks after the birth of her first baby. She describes severe burning pain in both nipples that comes on a minute or two after the baby comes off the breast and lasts about ten minutes, and she has started dreading feeds. It is much worse when she gets out of the shower or takes the washing off the line on a cold morning.

A lactation consultant reviewed the attachment last week and was satisfied with it, and the baby has regained birth weight and is now gaining 190 g per week. She has completed a course of oral fluconazole and two weeks of topical miconazole prescribed by a colleague, with no improvement. On examination the nipples are intact with no cracks, fissures or discharge, and the areolae and breasts are soft with no erythema, lump or warmth. As you examine her, the tip of the left nipple blanches white, then becomes dusky blue, and then flushes red as the pain she describes builds. She takes no regular medications and has cold hands in winter.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Intact nipples with no fissures, cracks or discharge, soft non erythematous breasts with no palpable lump
data_table.Provoked finding: Triphasic white then blue then red colour change of the nipple tip observed on exposure to room air
data_table.Infant: Regained birth weight, gaining 190 g per week, attachment assessed as satisfactory by a lactation consultant

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer her back for further attachment assessment and a review for tongue tie in the infant
options.rationale: Poor attachment and restrictive tongue tie are the commonest causes of nipple pain overall and would be the first thing to address, which is why this remains tempting. Attachment has already been assessed as satisfactory and the infant is gaining well, and neither explains cold provoked colour change. (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association and Royal Women's Hospital: Nipple vasospasm)
source_refs: Australian Breastfeeding Association and Royal Women's Hospital: Nipple vasospasm

options.text: Prescribe a longer course of oral fluconazole for her with oral nystatin drops for the baby
options.rationale: Extended antifungal therapy for mother and infant is the standard approach to candidal nipple infection, the near pair, which gives a persistent burning pain that is present during as well as after feeds and is usually accompanied by shiny or flaky areolar skin or infant oral thrush. She has already failed adequate antifungal treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Advise warmth immediately after feeds and prescribe oral nifedipine for a two week trial
options.rationale: A triphasic colour change with pain beginning after the feed and provoked by cold is vasospasm of the nipple, a Raynaud phenomenon, not infection. Conservative warming plus a calcium channel blocker is the established treatment and breastfeeding can continue throughout. (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association and Royal Women's Hospital: Nipple vasospasm)
source_refs: Australian Breastfeeding Association and Royal Women's Hospital: Nipple vasospasm

options.text: Advise expressing and cup feeding for two weeks to rest the nipples and allow them to heal
options.rationale: Resting the nipples helps a mechanical or traumatic injury heal, but vasospasm is triggered by the temperature drop when the nipple is exposed to air, which expressing does not avoid. It also risks undermining supply at six weeks. (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association and Royal Women's Hospital: Nipple vasospasm)
source_refs: Australian Breastfeeding Association and Royal Women's Hospital: Nipple vasospasm

options.text: Prescribe oral di flucloxacillin for ten days and advise her to continue feeding from both sides
options.rationale: Antistaphylococcal therapy treats mastitis or an infected nipple fissure, which produces a red tender wedge of breast with systemic symptoms or a visibly broken nipple surface. Her breasts are soft and her nipple skin is intact. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Nipple vasospasm is a Raynaud phenomenon of the nipple in which arteriolar constriction follows the temperature drop as the nipple leaves the warm mouth, and it is a frequently missed cause of severe persistent nipple pain in breastfeeding women. The history that identifies it is pain that starts after rather than during the feed, is described as burning or shooting, and is reliably provoked by cold, together with an observable blanching of the nipple tip. The classic triphasic white to blue to red colour change is not always complete, and blanching alone in the right clinical context is enough. It is very commonly misdiagnosed as candidal infection, and many women arrive having already failed courses of antifungal treatment for both themselves and the infant. Underlying poor attachment and nipple trauma can trigger vasospasm, so attachment must still be assessed, but once optimised the treatment is avoidance of cold, immediate warmth after feeds, and nifedipine where conservative measures fail.
key_points: Pain starting after the feed ends and provoked by cold distinguishes vasospasm.
Blanching of the nipple tip, with or without the full triphasic change, is the sign.
It is routinely misdiagnosed and treated as candidal infection without benefit.
Optimise attachment first, since nipple trauma can trigger the vasospasm.
Nifedipine is compatible with breastfeeding and works within days when it is going to work.
explanation.pearls: Nifedipine 20 mg of the modified release preparation once daily is the usual starting dose for nipple vasospasm, with response expected within about 72 hours, and only trivial amounts pass into breast milk so the infant needs no monitoring.

sources.label: Australian Breastfeeding Association and Royal Women's Hospital: Nipple vasospasm

subtopic_detail: woman unable to tolerate penetration with involuntary tightening and a normal genital examination
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 26-year-old woman who has never been able to have penetrative intercourse. She and her partner of two years have tried many times; she describes a sensation of a wall and involuntary tightening, together with burning at the entrance, and they always stop. She has never been able to insert a tampon and had to abandon an attempted cervical screening test last year.

She is distressed and says she feels she is failing her relationship. She has no history of sexual assault, no dyspareunia beyond the entrance because penetration has never occurred, and no cyclical pelvic pain, bowel or bladder symptoms. On careful inspection with her consent, the vulva looks normal with no fissures, pallor, architectural loss or erythema, and the hymenal ring is patent. Light touch with a cotton bud at the vestibule reproduces her burning and you observe visible contraction of the perineal muscles. She declines any attempt at internal examination and you do not proceed.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Normal vulval architecture with no pallor, fissuring, adhesions or erythema, patent hymenal ring
data_table.Provoked finding: Cotton bud touch at the vestibule reproduces burning with visible involuntary perineal muscle contraction
data_table.History: Lifelong inability to tolerate tampon insertion, cervical screening or penetrative intercourse

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management to recommend?

options.text: Refer to a pelvic floor physiotherapist for graded desensitisation alongside psychosexual therapy
options.rationale: Lifelong inability to tolerate penetration with involuntary pelvic floor contraction and a normal vulva is genito pelvic pain and penetration disorder, in which the muscle response and the anticipatory fear maintain each other. Combined pelvic floor physiotherapy and psychosexual therapy is the treatment with the best evidence. (Source: RANZCOG: Female sexual dysfunction)

options.text: Refer for examination under anaesthesia with division of any obstructing hymenal band
options.rationale: Surgery addresses an anatomical obstruction such as a microperforate hymen or a transverse vaginal septum, the structural near pair. The hymenal ring is patent on inspection here, and operating on a normal introitus reinforces the belief that something is physically wrong. (Source: RANZCOG: Female sexual dysfunction)

options.text: Arrange injection of botulinum toxin into the levator ani muscles under conscious sedation
options.rationale: Botulinum toxin is studied as a third line option for refractory cases and is not first line, since it does not address the cognitive and behavioural components. Offering it before conservative therapy exposes her to an invasive procedure with modest evidence. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Vaginismus)

options.text: Prescribe topical oestrogen cream nightly for six weeks and arrange a further review after that
options.rationale: Vaginal oestrogen treats the thin pale friable epithelium of genitourinary syndrome of menopause or of prolonged lactational hypo oestrogenism. A well oestrogenised vulva in a 26 year old with normal cycles will not respond to it. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Prescribe topical lignocaine gel for use before intercourse and review her again in three months
options.rationale: Topical anaesthetic is a reasonable adjunct that some women use alongside desensitisation work, so it is not a wrong treatment in itself. Used alone it numbs the vestibular pain without addressing the involuntary muscle response that physically prevents penetration. (Source: RANZCOG: Female sexual dysfunction)

explanation.summary: Genito pelvic pain and penetration disorder is the current diagnostic term that unified what were previously called vaginismus and dyspareunia, and it covers difficulty with penetration, vulvovaginal pain on attempted penetration, fear of that pain, and involuntary pelvic floor tightening. Lifelong forms present exactly as this woman does, with tampons, examinations and intercourse all impossible from the outset and a structurally normal genital tract. A pain and fear cycle sustains the condition: anticipation increases pelvic floor tone, the increased tone makes penetration painful, and the pain reinforces the anticipation. Assessment must still exclude organic causes including lichen sclerosus, vulval dermatoses, obstructive anomalies and hypo oestrogenism, which is why unhurried inspection matters even when internal examination is declined. Treatment combines pelvic floor physiotherapy with graded self directed dilator work and psychosexual therapy, ideally with the partner involved, and success rates with this combination are high.
key_points: Involuntary pelvic floor contraction with a structurally normal vulva defines the disorder.
Lifelong forms prevent tampon use and clinical examination as well as intercourse.
Exclude lichen sclerosus, obstructive anomalies and hypo oestrogenism by inspection.
Pelvic floor physiotherapy plus psychosexual therapy is first line and highly effective.
Never force an internal examination; it reinforces the fear that maintains the condition.
explanation.pearls: Offering the woman control of the pace and of the instrument, including letting her place her own hand over yours or insert a dilator herself, changes outcomes measurably, because loss of control during examination is one of the strongest perpetuating factors in this disorder.

subtopic_detail: pregnant childcare worker exposed to a slapped cheek rash outbreak at work in the second trimester
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 31-year-old woman at 16 weeks in her second pregnancy. She works in a childcare centre where three children developed a bright red rash across both cheeks last week, and she has been told to see a doctor. She had face to face contact with all three children in the two days before their rashes appeared.

She feels well and has no rash, fever or joint pains. Her first pregnancy and birth were uncomplicated. Her booking bloods showed her to be rubella immune, varicella immune and negative for syphilis, hepatitis B, hepatitis C and human immunodeficiency virus, and her blood group is O positive. Her 12 week ultrasound was consistent with dates and showed no abnormality. Examination today is unremarkable with a soft non tender abdomen, a symphysis fundal height consistent with dates, and a fetal heart rate of 148 beats per minute on handheld Doppler.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84 beats per minute, blood pressure 108/66 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees, fetal heart rate 148 beats per minute
data_table.Examination: Soft non tender abdomen, symphysis fundal height consistent with dates, no rash or joint swelling
data_table.Booking investigations: Rubella immune, varicella immune, negative syphilis, hepatitis B, hepatitis C and human immunodeficiency virus serology, blood group O positive
data_table.Imaging: Twelve week ultrasound consistent with dates and structurally normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange weekly middle cerebral artery Doppler studies from now until 30 weeks gestation
options.rationale: Serial middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity is exactly the right surveillance once maternal infection is confirmed, and it is what detects fetal anaemia. Starting it before serology commits an already immune woman to fourteen weeks of unnecessary scans. (Source: RANZCOG: Parvovirus B19 in pregnancy)

options.text: Reassure her that maternal infection at this gestation carries no risk to the pregnancy
options.rationale: The risk is real between about 9 and 20 weeks, when the fetal liver is the main site of erythropoiesis and red cell lifespan is short, which is precisely the window she is in. Vertical transmission occurs in around a third of maternal infections. (Source: RANZCOG: Parvovirus B19 in pregnancy)

options.text: Refer for amniocentesis with viral polymerase chain reaction on the amniotic fluid sample
options.rationale: Amniotic fluid testing confirms fetal infection but is invasive and is reserved for cases where fetal anaemia or hydrops is already suspected on ultrasound. It is not a screening test after an exposure. (Source: RANZCOG: Parvovirus B19 in pregnancy)

options.text: Offer intravenous immunoglobulin within 72 hours of the exposure to prevent transmission
options.rationale: Post exposure immunoglobulin is effective for varicella and for measles but there is no established prophylaxis against parvovirus B19 in pregnancy. Offering it implies a protection that does not exist. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Send maternal immunoglobulin M and immunoglobulin G serology and act on the result
options.rationale: Around 60 per cent of Australian women of childbearing age are already immune to parvovirus B19, so serology first establishes whether she is at any risk at all before committing to surveillance. Immunoglobulin G positive with immunoglobulin M negative means past infection and needs nothing further. (Source: RANZCOG: Parvovirus B19 in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Parvovirus B19 causes erythema infectiosum, or fifth disease, and childcare and primary school staff are the classic occupational exposure group. Infected children are contagious in the week before the rash appears and are no longer infectious once it is visible, so exposure has usually already occurred by the time an outbreak is recognised. Maternal infection before 20 weeks carries the highest fetal risk because the virus targets erythroid precursors, and the foetus of that gestation has rapid red cell turnover and limited marrow reserve, producing anaemia, high output cardiac failure and hydrops. Vertical transmission occurs in roughly a third of maternal infections and hydrops develops in a few per cent, typically two to six weeks after maternal infection. Management after a confirmed maternal infection is serial ultrasound with middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity measurement, and intrauterine transfusion where anaemia is detected, which achieves good survival.
key_points: Children are infectious before the rash appears, not after it.
About 60 per cent of women of childbearing age are already immune, so test serology first.
Maternal infection before 20 weeks carries the greatest risk of fetal anaemia and hydrops.
Confirmed infection is followed with serial middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity.
Intrauterine transfusion treats detected fetal anaemia with good survival.
explanation.pearls: A middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity above 1.5 multiples of the median for gestational age is the threshold that triggers referral for fetal blood sampling and intrauterine transfusion, and it detects significant anaemia non invasively with sensitivity above 90 per cent.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Parvovirus B19 infection

subtopic_detail: postmenopausal woman with a glazed red vestibule, lacy white streaks and a narrowing vaginal opening
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 58-year-old woman with two years of vulval soreness, a raw burning feeling and a yellow stained discharge. She has been treated with six separate courses of topical and oral antifungal therapy and one course of topical oestrogen without benefit, and intercourse has become impossible.

She went through menopause at 51 and has no other medical problems. She mentions in passing that the inside of her cheeks has been sore and that her dentist commented on some white lines there. On examination the labia minora have partly fused anteriorly and the vaginal opening admits only one fingertip. The vestibule is a glazed bright red with a sharply demarcated edge, and at the margin of the erythema there is a fine lacy white network. There is no white parchment like change over the labia and perineum and no ecchymosis. A vaginal pH is 6.0 and a vaginal swab is negative for candida, bacterial vaginosis and trichomonas.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Glazed sharply demarcated vestibular erythema with a lacy white reticular border, partial anterior labial fusion, introitus admitting one fingertip
data_table.Oral: Reticular white striae on the buccal mucosa with associated soreness
data_table.Investigations: Vaginal pH 6.0, swab negative for candida, bacterial vaginosis and trichomonas

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe a further eight week course of oral fluconazole taken as a weekly maintenance dose
options.rationale: Suppressive antifungal therapy is used for recurrent candidiasis, which she does not have on repeated swabs and which does not fuse the labia or narrow the introitus. Six failed courses should already have prompted a change of diagnosis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Refer for surgical division of the adhesions with vaginal dilator therapy started afterwards
options.rationale: Surgery has a place once the inflammatory disease is controlled, because operating on actively inflamed tissue leads to rapid re adhesion through the same process that caused the fusion. Medical control comes first, with dilators used as an adjunct. (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval disorders)

options.text: Commence an ultrapotent topical corticosteroid for lichen sclerosus and review in three months
options.rationale: The treatment is right but the diagnosis is the near pair that gets confused: lichen sclerosus gives white parchment like atrophic skin over the labia, perineum and perianal area in a figure of eight, with ecchymosis and fissuring, and it spares the vagina. Erosive lichen planus involves the vestibule and vagina and produces the reticular border seen here. (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval disorders)

options.text: Take a punch biopsy from the affected edge and commence long term topical oestrogen therapy
options.rationale: Vaginal oestrogen treats genitourinary syndrome of menopause, which produces a uniformly pale thin friable epithelium rather than a sharply demarcated erosion with a reticular border. She has already failed a course of it, which argues against that diagnosis. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Take a punch biopsy from the affected edge and commence an ultrapotent topical corticosteroid
options.rationale: Glazed erosive vestibular erythema with a lacy reticular border and matching buccal striae is erosive lichen planus, which is confirmed histologically and treated with an ultrapotent topical corticosteroid. Biopsy also establishes a baseline because the condition carries a malignant potential. (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval disorders)

explanation.summary: Erosive lichen planus is an immune mediated mucocutaneous disease that affects the vulva, vagina and mouth and is the most disabling of the vulval dermatoses. The vulvovaginal gingival syndrome describes the combination of erosive vulval and vaginal disease with desquamative gingivitis, and asking about the mouth often unlocks a diagnosis that has been missed for years. The physical signs that separate it from lichen sclerosus are its involvement of the vestibule and vagina, the glazed erosive surface, the lacy white reticular Wickham striae at the border, and the raised vaginal pH from the associated vaginitis. Untreated disease causes progressive scarring with labial resorption, introital narrowing and vaginal stenosis, and it carries a squamous cell carcinoma risk of the order of one to three per cent. First line treatment is an ultrapotent topical corticosteroid such as clobetasol, with calcineurin inhibitors, vaginal preparations or systemic immunosuppression added for resistant disease, and long term surveillance is required.
key_points: Erosive lichen planus involves the vagina and vestibule; lichen sclerosus spares the vagina.
A lacy white reticular border and oral striae are the discriminating findings.
Repeated failed antifungal courses should prompt reassessment of the diagnosis.
Biopsy from the edge of the lesion confirms the diagnosis and establishes a baseline.
Scarring causes labial fusion and vaginal stenosis, and malignant transformation can occur.
explanation.pearls: A vaginal pH above 4.5 in a woman with vulval symptoms points to vaginal involvement, which occurs in erosive lichen planus and desquamative inflammatory vaginitis but essentially never in lichen sclerosus, so a strip of indicator paper separates the two dermatoses at the bedside.

subtopic_detail: woman who never established milk supply and has had no periods since a delivery needing massive transfusion
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 33-year-old woman nine months after the birth of her second child. She has come about persistent tiredness, feeling cold all the time and dizziness when she stands up quickly. Her periods have not returned and she is using condoms for contraception.

Her delivery was complicated by bleeding requiring eight units of red cells and a return to theatre, and she spent two days in intensive care. She tells you she was never able to produce any milk at all despite considerable support from the lactation service, and that her pubic and axillary hair has thinned. She stopped breastfeeding attempts at three weeks and the baby has thrived on formula. On examination she looks pale with fine dry skin, her blood pressure is 96/58 mmHg lying and 82/50 mmHg standing, her pulse is 64 beats per minute and she is afebrile. Sodium is 128 mmol/L (135 to 145) and a urinary pregnancy test is negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 64 beats per minute, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg lying and 82/50 mmHg standing, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.2 degrees
data_table.Examination: Pale fine dry skin, thinning axillary and pubic hair, no goitre, no hyperpigmentation of palmar creases or buccal mucosa
data_table.Obstetric history: Postpartum haemorrhage requiring eight units of red cells, return to theatre and intensive care admission
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 128 mmol/L (135 to 145), potassium 4.1 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.2), urinary pregnancy test negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Request an early morning cortisol with paired anterior pituitary and thyroid hormone levels
options.rationale: Failure of lactation and amenorrhoea after a haemorrhage needing massive transfusion, with postural hypotension and hyponatraemia, is Sheehan syndrome from pituitary infarction. A combined anterior pituitary panel with a morning cortisol identifies which axes have failed and how urgently replacement is needed. (Source: RANZCOG: Postpartum haemorrhage)

options.text: Request a nine item depression questionnaire with thyroid function and vitamin B12 levels
options.rationale: Screening for postnatal depression is appropriate in any tired new mother and the overlap of symptoms is real. It does not account for absent lactation, postural hypotension, loss of body hair or hyponatraemia, all of which are endocrine findings. (Source: COPE: Perinatal Mental Health Guideline)

options.text: Request a short synacthen test with adrenal antibodies and plasma renin activity
options.rationale: This workup is directed at primary adrenal insufficiency, the near pair, which is distinguished by hyperpigmentation, hyperkalaemia and a raised adrenocorticotrophic hormone because the adrenal itself has failed. Normal potassium and no pigmentation point to a secondary cause. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Request a serum prolactin with a follicle stimulating hormone and a transvaginal ultrasound
options.rationale: This combination investigates secondary amenorrhoea from a prolactinoma or premature ovarian insufficiency and would be reasonable if amenorrhoea were the only problem. It misses the adrenal and thyroid axes, and it is the cortisol deficiency here that is potentially fatal. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea)

options.text: Request thyroid stimulating hormone alone with a full blood count and iron studies
options.rationale: This panel targets postpartum thyroiditis and iron deficiency, which are far commoner causes of postnatal fatigue and are worth having. In pituitary failure the thyroid stimulating hormone is inappropriately normal or low despite a low free thyroxine, so measuring it alone gives false reassurance. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Sheehan syndrome is ischaemic necrosis of the anterior pituitary caused by severe postpartum haemorrhage and hypotension, made possible by the physiological enlargement of the lactotroph rich gland during pregnancy within a fixed bony fossa. Presentation is often delayed by months or years because the deficiencies accumulate gradually, and the two earliest and most specific clues are failure to lactate and failure of menses to return. Anterior pituitary hormones are typically lost in a characteristic order, with growth hormone and gonadotrophins going first, then adrenocorticotrophic hormone and thyroid stimulating hormone, while the posterior pituitary is usually spared. Hyponatraemia is common and reflects cortisol deficiency impairing free water excretion rather than true salt loss. The diagnosis matters because unrecognised secondary adrenal insufficiency can present as adrenal crisis during an intercurrent illness, and glucocorticoid must always be replaced before thyroid hormone to avoid precipitating one.
key_points: Failure of lactation plus failure of menses to return after major haemorrhage is the hallmark.
Presentation is frequently delayed by months to years after the index birth.
In secondary hypothyroidism the thyroid stimulating hormone is normal or low, not raised.
Hyponatraemia with normal potassium suggests a secondary rather than primary adrenal cause.
Replace glucocorticoid before thyroxine to avoid precipitating an adrenal crisis.
explanation.pearls: Starting thyroxine before hydrocortisone in any form of hypopituitarism can precipitate adrenal crisis within days, because thyroid hormone accelerates cortisol clearance, so the order of replacement is not a matter of preference.

subtopic_detail: woman whose device threads cannot be seen and whose uterine cavity is empty on transvaginal scanning
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 34-year-old woman who cannot feel the threads of her copper intrauterine device. It was inserted eight months ago at six weeks postpartum while she was fully breastfeeding, and the threads were checked and documented as visible at her six week review after insertion.

Her periods returned four months ago and have been regular since, with no unusually heavy loss and no episode of severe cramping that she recalls. She has had no pelvic pain and no abnormal discharge. A urinary pregnancy test today is negative. On speculum examination no threads are visible at the external os and the cervix looks normal. Gentle exploration of the cervical canal with a thread retriever finds nothing. A transvaginal ultrasound performed in the practice reports an empty uterine cavity with an endometrial thickness of 6 mm, no intrauterine device identified, and normal ovaries with no free fluid.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: No threads visible at the external os, normal cervix, non tender mobile uterus of normal size
data_table.Imaging: Transvaginal ultrasound: empty uterine cavity, endometrial thickness 6 mm, no device identified, normal ovaries, no free fluid
data_table.Investigations: Urinary pregnancy test negative, insertion at six weeks postpartum during full breastfeeding

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange an outpatient hysteroscopy to inspect the cavity and retrieve the device directly
options.rationale: Hysteroscopy is used when the device is known to be intrauterine but embedded or with retracted threads, which is the near pair here. A cavity already shown to be empty on ultrasound will simply be confirmed as empty, and the device is not inside it. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of abnormal vaginal bleeding)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Investigation of abnormal vaginal bleeding

options.text: Refer directly for a diagnostic laparoscopy to locate and retrieve the migrated device
options.rationale: Laparoscopy is the correct retrieval procedure once an intra abdominal device is confirmed, and it is what she will need if the film is positive. Operating before localising the device commits her to an anaesthetic that is unnecessary if it was simply expelled. (Source: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Intrauterine contraception)
source_refs: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Intrauterine contraception

options.text: Arrange a transabdominal pelvic ultrasound before considering any further imaging modality
options.rationale: Transabdominal scanning widens the field beyond the transvaginal view and is a reasonable adjunct, but a device that has migrated into the upper abdomen or omentum lies outside the pelvic field and is easily missed on ultrasound of any window. Radiography covers the whole cavity in one image. (Source: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Intrauterine contraception)
source_refs: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Intrauterine contraception

options.text: Reassure her that the device has been expelled and reinsert a new device at this visit
options.rationale: Expulsion is the commoner of the two outcomes and she has had regular periods since, which makes this genuinely tempting. Reinserting without excluding an intra abdominal device leaves a perforated device in the peritoneal cavity where it can cause adhesions or bowel injury. (Source: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Intrauterine contraception)
source_refs: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Intrauterine contraception

options.text: Arrange a plain abdominal radiograph covering the diaphragm to the pelvic floor
options.rationale: An empty uterus on ultrasound has two explanations, expulsion and perforation, and they cannot be distinguished clinically because up to a third of perforations are painless. A plain film of the whole abdomen and pelvis is the test that finds or excludes a migrated radio opaque device. (Source: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Intrauterine contraception)
source_refs: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Intrauterine contraception

explanation.summary: Missing intrauterine device threads is a common presentation and the assessment follows a fixed sequence: exclude pregnancy, look in the canal, image the uterus, and if the cavity is empty, image the abdomen. Where ultrasound shows no device in the uterus, the two possibilities are expulsion, which occurs in about one in twenty users and is commonest in the first year, and uterine perforation, which occurs in around one to two per thousand insertions. Perforation risk is increased roughly six fold by insertion while breastfeeding and is also higher when insertion occurs within six months of delivery, because the uterus is soft and involuting. Critically, perforation is silent in a substantial minority, so a painless history and normal subsequent periods do not exclude it, and a plain abdominal radiograph is mandatory before a replacement device is inserted. A confirmed intra abdominal device is retrieved laparoscopically because copper in particular incites an inflammatory reaction with adhesions and occasional bowel or bladder erosion.
key_points: Sequence is pregnancy test, canal inspection, pelvic ultrasound, then abdominal radiograph.
An empty cavity means either expulsion or perforation, which cannot be told apart clinically.
Breastfeeding at insertion and insertion within six months of delivery both raise perforation risk.
Up to a third of perforations are asymptomatic, so a painless history excludes nothing.
Never reinsert a device until the abdominal film has excluded a migrated one.
explanation.pearls: Both copper and levonorgestrel devices are radio opaque, so a single plain abdominal film from diaphragm to pelvic floor answers the question in minutes; the common error is limiting the film to the pelvis, which misses devices that have migrated into the omentum or upper abdomen.

sources.label: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Intrauterine contraception
RANZCOG: Investigation of abnormal vaginal bleeding
Faculty of Sexual and Reproductive Healthcare: Intrauterine contraception

subtopic_detail: treating on the basis of a minimal trauma fracture when the bone density score is in the osteopenic range
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 62 year old woman six weeks after she tripped on a flat footpath outside the shops and broke her wrist. She fell from standing height onto her outstretched hand and the fracture has been managed in a cast, which has now come off.

Her last menstrual period was at 51. She has never smoked, drinks two standard drinks a week and walks most days. She has never taken oral corticosteroids. Her mother broke her hip at 74. Her body mass index is 22 kg/m2. You arranged a bone density scan and screening bloods after the fracture and the results are now available.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: No thoracic kyphosis, height unchanged from her recorded height five years ago, wrist fracture united with good range of movement
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium within normal limits, 25 hydroxyvitamin D within normal limits, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, renal function within normal limits, serum protein electrophoresis shows no paraprotein
data_table.Bone densitometry: Femoral neck T score minus 2.3, lumbar spine T score minus 2.1

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Lifestyle advice with a repeat bone density scan in two years
options.rationale: This is the correct approach for a woman with this T score and no fracture, which is exactly why it is tempting. A fracture from a fall at standing height after the age of 50 establishes the diagnosis independently of the densitometry and identifies her as being at high risk of a further fracture in the next two years. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners Osteoporosis Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners Osteoporosis Guideline

options.text: Commence six monthly denosumab injections as initial therapy
options.rationale: Denosumab is an effective antiresorptive and is used where bisphosphonates are contraindicated, not tolerated or ineffective. It requires strict continuity, because stopping it without transitioning to another agent produces rapid bone loss and a risk of multiple vertebral fractures, so it is not the first choice in an otherwise straightforward case. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Commence menopausal hormone therapy for bone protection alone
options.rationale: Hormone therapy does preserve bone density and reduces fracture, and it is a reasonable choice for a woman in her early fifties who also has vasomotor symptoms. At 62 and eleven years past her final period it is not started for bone protection alone, because the balance of cardiovascular and thrombotic risk shifts with time since menopause. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society)

options.text: Commence an oral bisphosphonate with calcium and vitamin D advice
options.rationale: A minimal trauma fracture after 50 defines osteoporosis clinically whatever the T score shows, and it is also the criterion under which antiresorptive therapy is subsidised in Australia. Oral bisphosphonate is the first line agent, with adequate calcium intake and vitamin D as supportive measures rather than as treatment in themselves. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners Osteoporosis Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners Osteoporosis Guideline

options.text: Commence calcium and vitamin D supplements without other therapy
options.rationale: Calcium and vitamin D support the action of antiresorptive therapy but do not meaningfully reduce fracture risk on their own in someone who has already sustained a minimal trauma fracture. Her vitamin D is already within normal limits. (Source: Healthy Bones Australia)

explanation.summary: A minimal trauma fracture is one sustained from a fall at standing height or less, and after the age of 50 it establishes a clinical diagnosis of osteoporosis regardless of the bone density result, which matters because around half of all fragility fractures occur in people whose T score falls in the osteopenic range rather than below minus 2.5. The single strongest predictor of a future fracture is a past fracture, and the risk is highest in the first two years afterwards, a window often described as the imminent fracture risk period. This is the rationale for fracture liaison services and for starting treatment promptly rather than waiting for a densitometry threshold to be crossed. Secondary causes should be screened for before treatment, covering calcium, vitamin D, renal and thyroid function, and a paraprotein, with coeliac serology and testosterone considered in selected patients. Oral bisphosphonates are first line in Australia, with adherence being the main practical limitation, and denosumab or an anabolic agent reserved for intolerance, contraindication or very high risk.
key_points: A fall from standing height causing fracture after 50 defines osteoporosis clinically
Around half of fragility fractures occur in people with osteopenic rather than osteoporotic scores
Risk of a further fracture is highest in the first two years
Screen for secondary causes before starting treatment
Denosumab requires strict continuity because cessation causes rapid bone loss
explanation.pearls: Never stop denosumab without transitioning to a bisphosphonate, because the rebound increase in bone turnover after a missed six monthly dose can cause multiple vertebral fractures within a year, a risk that does not follow cessation of bisphosphonate therapy.

sources.label: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners Osteoporosis Guideline

subtopic_detail: first line medical treatment for heavy painful bleeding with diffuse myometrial changes on ultrasound
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar in the outpatient clinic seeing a 42 year old woman with three years of periods that have become progressively heavier and more painful. She now floods through a pad hourly on her worst two days and the cramping starts two days before any bleeding appears.

She has had two vaginal births and has not been pregnant for nine years. She has taken over the counter ibuprofen with limited benefit. On bimanual examination the uterus is bulky and globular, about the size of a ten week pregnancy, tender to palpation and mobile, with no separate adnexal mass. Her transvaginal ultrasound and bloods are available.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Uterus bulky and globular at approximately ten week size, tender on bimanual palpation, mobile with no adnexal mass, cervix appears normal
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 104 g/L (115 to 165), ferritin 9 micrograms/L (15 to 200), thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, cervical screening test up to date and negative
data_table.Imaging: Transvaginal ultrasound shows a globally enlarged uterus with asymmetrical myometrial thickening, small myometrial cysts and an indistinct junctional zone; no discrete fibroid identified; endometrial thickness 6 mm; ovaries normal

lead_in: What would you first recommend as treatment?

options.text: A gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonist with add back therapy
options.rationale: Induced hypo-oestrogenism does shrink the uterus and reduce bleeding, but it is used for short term control before surgery rather than as ongoing treatment because of bone loss and vasomotor effects. Symptoms return once it is stopped. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Referral for total hysterectomy at the next available list
options.rationale: Hysterectomy is definitive and is appropriate where medical treatment fails or is declined, but proceeding to major surgery before any hormonal treatment has been tried is a substantial escalation. Most women in this situation obtain adequate control medically. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: A continuous combined oral contraceptive pill regimen
options.rationale: Continuous combined oral contraception is a reasonable second line option that reduces bleeding and dysmenorrhoea, and it suits women who prefer an oral method. It is less effective than the intrauterine route for heavy bleeding and carries a thrombotic risk that the local method does not. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Tranexamic acid taken during the days of heavy bleeding
options.rationale: Antifibrinolytic therapy reduces bleeding volume by around a third and is useful as an adjunct or for women wanting non hormonal treatment. It does nothing for the dysmenorrhoea, which is half of her problem here. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Insertion of a levonorgestrel releasing intrauterine system
options.rationale: Local progestogen delivery thins the endometrium and acts directly on the myometrium, reducing both bleeding volume and the associated pain, and it is the recommended first line treatment for this condition. It also treats the iron deficiency driver by reducing ongoing loss. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

explanation.summary: Adenomyosis is the presence of endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium with surrounding smooth muscle hypertrophy, and it classically presents in the fourth and fifth decades with the combination of heavy menstrual bleeding and progressive secondary dysmenorrhoea that begins before the bleeding starts. Examination typically finds a diffusely bulky, globular and tender uterus, in contrast to the irregular firm non tender uterus of fibroid disease, and this distinction carries through to imaging. The ultrasound features are asymmetrical myometrial thickening, myometrial cysts, subendometrial echogenic lines and buds, and an indistinct or thickened junctional zone, with magnetic resonance imaging reserved for cases where ultrasound is equivocal or surgical planning is needed. Because the process is diffuse rather than focal, treatments directed at discrete lesions such as myomectomy or uterine artery embolisation are less reliable than they are for fibroids. The levonorgestrel releasing intrauterine system is first line, combined hormonal or continuous progestogen therapy is second line, and hysterectomy remains definitive for women who have completed their family and in whom medical management has failed.
key_points: Heavy bleeding with dysmenorrhoea starting before the bleeding is the characteristic pattern
A globular tender bulky uterus contrasts with the irregular firm uterus of fibroids
Ultrasound shows myometrial cysts and an indistinct junctional zone without a discrete lesion
The levonorgestrel releasing intrauterine system is first line treatment
Check ferritin, because iron deficiency is usually present before anaemia appears
explanation.pearls: Check ferritin as well as haemoglobin in every woman with heavy menstrual bleeding, because iron stores are exhausted long before the haemoglobin falls and treating the deficiency resolves the fatigue that patients often attribute to the bleeding itself.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

subtopic_detail: initial conservative management of urinary urgency when stress leakage and infection have been excluded
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 58 year old woman with eight months of a sudden compelling need to pass urine that she struggles to defer. She gets up four times most nights and has twice not made it to the toilet in time.

She tells you she does not leak when she coughs, laughs or lifts her grandchildren, and that the problem is entirely about the urgency. She drinks six cups of coffee across the day and a glass of wine most evenings. She has had two vaginal births and her last period was at 52. She has no haematuria, no dysuria and no pelvic pain. Her examination and investigations are complete.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Mild vaginal atrophy, no prolapse beyond the hymen on Valsalva, no leakage demonstrated on cough stress testing, abdomen soft with no palpable bladder
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis negative for nitrites and leucocytes, midstream urine culture no growth, post void residual volume 30 mL on bladder scan, fasting glucose within normal limits, bladder diary shows nine voids by day and four by night with small volumes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Bladder training with caffeine reduction and pelvic floor exercises
options.rationale: Behavioural treatment is first line for urinary urgency and produces improvement rates comparable to drug therapy without adverse effects. Bladder training progressively extends the interval between voids, and her six cups of coffee daily represent a substantial and readily modifiable bladder irritant. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Oral oxybutynin with review of the symptoms in six weeks time
options.rationale: Antimuscarinic therapy is second line after behavioural measures have been tried, and oxybutynin specifically has the highest anticholinergic burden of the available agents, with cumulative exposure linked to cognitive decline in older women. If a drug were indicated, a more selective agent would be preferred. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Oral mirabegron with review of the blood pressure in six weeks
options.rationale: A beta 3 agonist avoids the anticholinergic burden and is a sound pharmacological choice for this condition, so the drug itself is not the error. It still belongs after a trial of behavioural treatment rather than instead of one. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Referral for urodynamic studies before any treatment is started
options.rationale: Urodynamic testing is reserved for diagnostic uncertainty, mixed or complicated symptoms, or failure of initial treatment, and it is invasive and uncomfortable. Her history, bladder diary, negative cough stress test and normal residual volume already identify the pattern. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Referral for insertion of a midurethral sling within three months
options.rationale: A sling supports the urethra and treats leakage provoked by a rise in abdominal pressure, which is the opposite mechanism to hers and which her negative cough stress test excludes. Placing a sling for urgency can worsen symptoms and cause voiding dysfunction. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

explanation.summary: Overactive bladder is a symptom syndrome of urinary urgency, usually with frequency and nocturia and with or without urgency incontinence, in the absence of infection or other identifiable pathology. Separating it from stress incontinence matters because the treatments differ entirely, and the history plus a cough stress test usually achieves this, with mixed patterns being common and managed by treating the more bothersome component first. The initial assessment excludes the conditions that mimic it, principally urinary infection, diabetes, a pelvic mass, incomplete emptying and haematuria requiring investigation, and a three day bladder diary is the single most informative tool because it quantifies volumes, frequency and fluid intake. First line management is behavioural: bladder training to extend voiding intervals, reduction of caffeine and alcohol, sensible fluid intake and supervised pelvic floor muscle training, which together produce meaningful improvement in a majority. Pharmacotherapy follows, with selective antimuscarinics or a beta 3 agonist preferred over oxybutynin because of anticholinergic burden, and intravesical botulinum toxin or neuromodulation reserved for refractory cases.
key_points: Urgency without leakage on coughing distinguishes this from stress incontinence
Exclude infection, diabetes, incomplete emptying and haematuria first
A three day bladder diary is the most informative single assessment tool
Behavioural treatment is first line and matches drug therapy for effectiveness
Avoid oxybutynin in older women because of anticholinergic cognitive burden
explanation.pearls: Cumulative anticholinergic exposure, including from oxybutynin prescribed for bladder symptoms, is associated with an increased risk of dementia in older women, which is why a beta 3 agonist or a more selective antimuscarinic is preferred once behavioural treatment has been tried.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

subtopic_detail: choosing a drainage technique that reduces recurrence for an acute vulval gland abscess
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar in the emergency department seeing a 27 year old woman with four days of increasing pain and swelling at the right side of the vaginal opening. The pain has become severe enough that she cannot sit down properly or walk without discomfort and she did not sleep last night.

She has had no fever or rigors and is not pregnant. She has no history of a similar problem. On examination there is a tense tender swelling at the posterior aspect of the right side of the vaginal opening, about 4 cm across, which is fluctuant with thinning of the overlying skin. There is no surrounding spreading redness and no inguinal lymphadenopathy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 per cent in air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Tense fluctuant 4 cm swelling at the posterior right introitus with thinned overlying skin, exquisitely tender, no surrounding cellulitis, no inguinal lymphadenopathy, speculum examination deferred because of pain
data_table.Investigations: Urinary beta human chorionic gonadotrophin negative, white cell count within normal limits, C reactive protein mildly raised, sexually transmitted infection screening collected

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Oral antibiotics alone with review in the clinic in three days
options.rationale: Antibiotics do not penetrate an established collection adequately and leave the pain untreated. They are added to drainage where there is surrounding cellulitis, systemic features, pregnancy or immunosuppression, none of which applies here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Incision and drainage with insertion of a Word catheter
options.rationale: Drainage relieves the pain immediately, and leaving a small balloon catheter in the cavity for several weeks allows an epithelialised tract to form so that the gland can continue to drain. This reduces recurrence substantially compared with drainage alone and can be done under local anaesthetic. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Simple incision and drainage without any further drainage device
options.rationale: Simple drainage relieves the acute pain effectively, which is why it remains common practice, but the incision seals within days and the gland duct remains obstructed, giving recurrence rates of around a third. The catheter is what converts a temporary measure into a durable one. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Marsupialisation of the cyst in theatre at the next available list
options.rationale: Marsupialisation creates a permanent drainage opening and is an effective alternative, generally reserved for recurrent disease or for failure of catheter treatment. It requires theatre and anaesthesia for a problem that can be managed today under local anaesthetic. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Needle aspiration of the contents under local anaesthetic today
options.rationale: Aspiration alone gives short lived relief because the cavity refills rapidly once the needle is withdrawn, and recurrence rates approach 100 per cent. It does not create a tract for ongoing drainage. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

explanation.summary: The Bartholin glands sit at the four and eight o'clock positions of the vaginal introitus and drain through short ducts into the vestibule, where obstruction produces a cyst that may be asymptomatic and require no treatment, while secondary infection produces an abscess with rapidly increasing pain over a few days. The organisms are usually mixed vaginal and enteric flora rather than a single sexually transmitted pathogen, although screening for chlamydia and gonorrhoea is appropriate because both occur. Definitive treatment is drainage combined with a technique that keeps the tract open, since the underlying problem is duct obstruction rather than infection alone, and a Word catheter left in place for two to four weeks allows epithelialisation of a new drainage tract with recurrence rates well below those of simple incision. Antibiotics are added only for surrounding cellulitis, systemic features, pregnancy, immunosuppression or a confirmed sexually transmitted pathogen. In a woman over 40, particularly with a firm or irregular mass, biopsy should be considered because carcinoma of the gland, although rare, presents in this way.
key_points: The underlying problem is duct obstruction, so drainage must keep a tract open
A Word catheter left for two to four weeks allows a new tract to epithelialise
Simple incision alone recurs in around a third of cases
Antibiotics are reserved for cellulitis, systemic features, pregnancy or immunosuppression
Consider biopsy in a woman over 40 with a firm or irregular vulval mass
