subtopic_detail: how body weight and proximity to ovulation change the choice of emergency contraception thirty eight hours after a condom failure
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 24 year old woman who tells you a condom broke during sex thirty eight hours ago. She is on day thirteen of a regular twenty eight day cycle.

She weighs 92 kg and her body mass index is 32 kg/m2. She has used condoms alone until now and says she would like something ongoing that she does not have to think about. She has no dysmenorrhoea, no abnormal bleeding and no pelvic pain, and a sexual health screen taken today is pending with no symptoms of infection. She has no history of pelvic inflammatory disease and has never been pregnant. A urine pregnancy test in the clinic is negative and she has had no other unprotected sex this cycle.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non tender, no cervical excitation, uterus anteverted and normal size, no adnexal mass
data_table.Investigations: Urine beta human chorionic gonadotropin negative, chlamydia and gonorrhoea nucleic acid testing pending

lead_in: What would you first recommend for emergency contraception?

options.text: Insertion of a copper intrauterine device within the next few days
options.rationale: The copper device is the most effective emergency contraceptive, with a failure rate under one per cent, and unlike the oral options its efficacy is unaffected by body weight or by how close ovulation is, because it prevents implantation as well as fertilisation. It also answers her request for ongoing contraception in the same procedure. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg orally taken as a single dose as soon as possible today
options.rationale: Levonorgestrel works only by delaying ovulation, so it is least effective at exactly the point in the cycle when the risk is highest, and its efficacy declines above about seventy kilograms. Both of the factors that reduce its effectiveness are present in her case. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health

options.text: Ulipristal acetate 30 mg orally taken as a single dose as soon as possible today
options.rationale: Ulipristal delays ovulation later in the follicular phase than levonorgestrel does and is the better oral choice here, but its efficacy also falls with increasing body weight above about eighty five kilograms and it still cannot act once the luteinising hormone surge has peaked. It is the correct oral option and remains less effective than the device. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health

options.text: Levonorgestrel 3 mg orally as a double dose to allow for her higher body weight
options.rationale: Doubling the dose is sometimes offered where no better option exists, but the evidence that it restores efficacy at higher body weight is weak and no pregnancy outcome benefit has been demonstrated. It is a workaround rather than a solution when a device is available. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health

options.text: Start a combined oral contraceptive today and use condoms for the next seven days
options.rationale: Starting ongoing contraception is appropriate but a combined pill begun after the exposure provides no emergency cover for intercourse that has already occurred. It also cannot be started immediately after ulipristal without reducing that drug's effect. (Source: Family Planning Australia)

explanation.summary: Emergency contraception in Australia comprises two oral options and the copper intrauterine device, and choosing between them depends on time since intercourse, position in the cycle, body weight, current hormonal contraception and what ongoing method the woman wants. Levonorgestrel is licensed up to 72 hours and ulipristal up to 120 hours, while the copper device may be inserted up to five days after intercourse or up to five days after the earliest estimated ovulation, whichever is later. Both oral agents act by delaying or preventing ovulation and therefore fail if the luteinising hormone surge has already begun, which means effectiveness falls precisely in the fertile window where risk is greatest. The copper device has an additional post fertilisation mechanism, which is why its failure rate is under one per cent regardless of cycle timing or body weight. Ulipristal is a progesterone receptor modulator, so hormonal contraception is delayed for five days after taking it and additional precautions are needed until the new method is reliable.
key_points: The copper device is the most effective option and is unaffected by weight or cycle timing
Oral agents act by delaying ovulation and fail once the surge has started
Levonorgestrel efficacy declines above about seventy kilograms
Ulipristal extends the window to 120 hours but is also weight sensitive
Hormonal contraception is delayed for five days after ulipristal
explanation.pearls: Screen for chlamydia and gonorrhoea at the time of emergency device insertion but do not delay the insertion waiting for results, because the pregnancy risk is immediate while any detected infection can be treated with the device left in place.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists
Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health

subtopic_detail: ripening an unfavourable cervix at term in a woman with one previous caesarean who wants a vaginal birth
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in the antenatal day unit seeing a 32 year old woman at 41 weeks and 0 days in her second pregnancy. Her first baby was born by lower segment caesarean section for a breech presentation at term, with no infection and an uncomplicated recovery.

This pregnancy has been uncomplicated, the foetus is cephalic with an estimated weight on the fiftieth centile, and the placenta is fundal and well clear of the previous scar. She has had no contractions and her membranes are intact. She is clear that she would like to give birth vaginally and has attended two counselling appointments about her options. On vaginal examination the cervix is 1 cm dilated, 1 cm long, firm, posterior and the station is minus three, giving a Bishop score of 3. The cardiotocograph is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, blood pressure 116/72, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 per cent in air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 138
data_table.Examination: Cephalic presentation, Bishop score 3, membranes intact, no uterine tenderness or scar tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Cardiotocograph normal with baseline 138, good variability and accelerations, amniotic fluid index within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate method of induction of labour?

options.text: Transcervical balloon catheter for ripening, then amniotomy and oxytocin
options.rationale: Mechanical ripening with a balloon catheter avoids the excess uterine rupture risk associated with prostaglandin ripening in a scarred uterus while still converting an unfavourable cervix, and it is the preferred method in Australian practice for this situation. Continuous electronic fetal monitoring follows once labour is established because an abnormal fetal heart rate pattern is the earliest sign of scar dehiscence. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Vaginal prostaglandin E2 gel repeated after six hours, then amniotomy and oxytocin
options.rationale: Prostaglandin ripening roughly doubles the risk of uterine rupture compared with spontaneous labour in a woman with a previous caesarean, and that risk is the reason mechanical methods are preferred. The two approaches achieve similar cervical change, so the difference is entirely one of scar safety. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Vaginal misoprostol in low dose repeated six hourly, then amniotomy and oxytocin
options.rationale: Misoprostol carries the highest rupture risk of all ripening agents in a scarred uterus and is contraindicated for induction at term after a previous caesarean. Its use in obstetrics at term is confined to women with no uterine scar. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Obstetrics)

options.text: Amniotomy today followed by an oxytocin infusion titrated to contraction frequency
options.rationale: Artificial rupture of membranes is not feasible with a closed, firm, posterior cervix at station minus three, and oxytocin without cervical ripening in this setting produces a prolonged induction with a high failure rate. The unfavourable Bishop score is what makes a ripening step necessary first. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Elective repeat caesarean section arranged for tomorrow given her unfavourable cervix
options.rationale: A repeat caesarean is a legitimate choice and must remain available to her, but an unfavourable cervix alone is not a contraindication to induction, and abandoning her stated preference without offering a safe ripening method is not supported. This would be the answer if she changed her mind or if a contraindication to labour emerged. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

explanation.summary: Around three quarters of women who labour after one previous lower segment caesarean achieve a vaginal birth, and the background risk of uterine rupture in spontaneous labour is roughly one in two hundred. That risk rises with induction and augmentation, and the rise is steepest with prostaglandin agents, which is why mechanical ripening has become the preferred approach when the cervix is unfavourable. Contraindications to attempting vaginal birth include a previous classical or inverted T incision, previous uterine rupture, a placenta praevia or accreta, and any other standard indication for caesarean. The practical requirements for a trial of labour are a hospital with immediate access to theatre and blood, continuous electronic fetal monitoring in established labour, and intravenous access. An abnormal cardiotocograph is the commonest and earliest sign of scar rupture and precedes scar pain, loss of contractions, vaginal bleeding and maternal haemodynamic change.
key_points: Uterine rupture risk in spontaneous labour after one caesarean is about one in two hundred
Prostaglandin ripening approximately doubles that risk and misoprostol is contraindicated
Mechanical balloon ripening is preferred for an unfavourable cervix
Continuous electronic fetal monitoring is required in established labour
An abnormal fetal heart rate pattern is the earliest sign of scar rupture
explanation.pearls: Two or more previous caesareans, a short interdelivery interval of under eighteen months, and induction of labour each independently raise rupture risk, and it is the combination rather than any single factor that most often tips counselling toward a repeat caesarean.

subtopic_detail: what to do with a treated hypothyroid woman's replacement dose on the day she reports a positive pregnancy test
stem:
You are the general practitioner taking a telephone call from a 30 year old woman who has just had a positive home pregnancy test. Her last menstrual period was five weeks ago and the pregnancy was planned.

She has autoimmune hypothyroidism diagnosed six years ago with positive thyroid peroxidase antibodies, and has taken levothyroxine 100 micrograms daily without missing doses. Her thyroid function was checked three months ago as part of her preconception care and her thyroid stimulating hormone was 2.0 mIU/L with a normal free thyroxine. She takes no other medication, no iron and no calcium supplement, and takes her tablet on an empty stomach each morning. She has no goitre, no palpitations and no heat intolerance. She asks whether she should change anything now or wait until her first antenatal appointment in three weeks.

data_table.Examination: Not examined; telephone consultation
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 2.0 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0) and free thyroxine within normal limits three months ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice to give her today?

options.text: Continue the same daily dose and have thyroid function checked at twelve weeks
options.rationale: Thyroid hormone requirement rises from very early in the first trimester, so holding the dose steady for seven weeks leaves her underdosed during the period when fetal brain development depends entirely on maternal hormone. A pre pregnancy level of 2.0 does not provide a margin large enough to absorb that rise. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Take two extra tablets each week from today and check thyroid function in four weeks
options.rationale: Requirement increases by roughly a quarter to a third within the first weeks, and adding two extra tablets each week delivers about that increase immediately using the tablets she already has. Rechecking in four weeks then confirms the first trimester target has been reached rather than assumed. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Arrange thyroid function testing today and adjust the dose once the result arrives
options.rationale: Testing is certainly needed, but waiting several days for the result before acting delays an increase that is predictable in every treated hypothyroid pregnancy, so the dose is raised at the same time the test is ordered. This is one of the few situations where empirical dose adjustment precedes the result. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Reduce the daily dose slightly to allow for the pregnancy related rise in hormone
options.rationale: The transient fall in thyroid stimulating hormone seen in early pregnancy reflects stimulation of the thyroid by human chorionic gonadotropin in women with a functioning gland, which she does not have. In treated hypothyroidism the requirement rises rather than falls. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Add liothyronine to her current regimen and check thyroid function in four weeks
options.rationale: Combination therapy with triiodothyronine is avoided in pregnancy because it crosses the placenta poorly and suppresses maternal thyroid stimulating hormone without supplying the thyroxine the foetus needs. Levothyroxine alone is the only appropriate replacement in pregnancy. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Maternal thyroxine requirement rises early in pregnancy because oestrogen driven thyroxine binding globulin increases, human chorionic gonadotropin stimulates the gland, placental deiodinase increases hormone degradation, and the plasma volume expands. Women with an intact gland accommodate this automatically, whereas women on replacement cannot and need their dose increased. The fetal thyroid does not begin producing hormone until around twelve weeks, so the whole of early neurodevelopment depends on transplacental maternal thyroxine, which is why the increase is made immediately rather than at the first antenatal visit. The recommended first trimester target is a thyroid stimulating hormone below 2.5 mIU/L, and levels are rechecked every four to six weeks until mid pregnancy and at least once thereafter. Iron, calcium and antacids, all common in pregnancy, bind levothyroxine in the gut and must be separated from it by at least four hours, which is a frequent and easily missed cause of apparent dose failure.
key_points: Requirement rises by roughly 25 to 30 per cent in the first trimester
Two extra tablets per week delivers approximately that increase without a new prescription
First trimester target is a thyroid stimulating hormone below 2.5 mIU/L
The fetal thyroid does not function until about twelve weeks
Iron and calcium must be taken at least four hours apart from levothyroxine
explanation.pearls: Recheck thyroid function four weeks after any dose change and then every four to six weeks until mid pregnancy, and return to the pre pregnancy dose immediately after birth with a further check six weeks postpartum.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

subtopic_detail: a seizure free woman on valproate who wants to conceive within the year, and whether folate supplementation is sufficient mitigation
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 27 year old teacher who tells you she and her partner would like to start trying for a baby in the next few months. She has generalised tonic clonic seizures that began at fourteen.

She has taken sodium valproate 1000 mg daily for six years and has been free of seizures for the past three. She holds an unrestricted driver licence. She currently uses a copper intrauterine device for contraception. She has not seen her neurologist for two years because she has been well. She has no other medical conditions, takes no other medication, and there is no family history of neural tube defect. She asks whether she should simply start folic acid and continue as she is.

data_table.Examination: Neurological examination normal, blood pressure 112/70, body mass index 24 kg/m2
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, urea electrolytes and creatinine and liver function tests all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue valproate at the current dose and add folic acid 5 mg daily now
options.rationale: High dose folate is recommended for any woman with epilepsy planning pregnancy, but it does not offset the dose dependent risk of neural tube defects, other major malformations and impaired childhood neurodevelopment that valproate carries. Adding folate without changing the drug gives the appearance of mitigation without the substance of it. (Source: Therapeutic Goods Administration Valproate Safety Advisory)
source_refs: Therapeutic Goods Administration Valproate Safety Advisory

options.text: Continue valproate and arrange an early detailed morphology scan once she conceives
options.rationale: Detailed anomaly imaging will detect structural defects but cannot detect the neurodevelopmental and autism spectrum outcomes that constitute the largest part of the harm, and by then the exposure has already occurred. Surveillance is not a substitute for avoiding the exposure. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Refer urgently to neurology to plan a change of medication before she conceives
options.rationale: A supervised switch to an agent such as lamotrigine or levetiracetam must be completed and stability confirmed before conception, because changing during an established pregnancy exposes the foetus to both drugs and risks breakthrough seizures. Referring now, while she still has effective contraception in place, is what creates the time the switch requires. (Source: Therapeutic Goods Administration Valproate Safety Advisory)
source_refs: Therapeutic Goods Administration Valproate Safety Advisory

options.text: Stop the valproate now and review her seizure control again in three months
options.rationale: Abrupt withdrawal in a woman with generalised tonic clonic seizures risks status epilepticus, loss of her driver licence and injury, and maternal seizures in pregnancy carry their own fetal risks including hypoxia and trauma. Any change is a supervised cross titration rather than a cessation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Change her today to carbamazepine at an equivalent dose and review in one month
options.rationale: Switching an antiseizure medication in a woman with generalised epilepsy is specialist work, and carbamazepine can aggravate generalised seizure types including absence and myoclonic seizures as well as carrying its own teratogenic risk. The specific hazard here is choosing an agent that is wrong for her seizure syndrome. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Valproate carries the highest teratogenic risk of the commonly used antiseizure medications, with major congenital malformations in roughly one in ten exposed pregnancies and impaired neurodevelopment, reduced cognitive scores and increased autism spectrum diagnoses in a substantially larger proportion. Both risks are dose dependent, and there is no dose that has been shown to be free of neurodevelopmental effect. Australian regulatory advice requires that valproate is not used in women of childbearing potential unless other treatments are ineffective or not tolerated, that effective contraception is in place, and that the risks are discussed and documented at least annually. Preconception is the only safe point at which to change treatment, because a switch made after a positive pregnancy test exposes the foetus during organogenesis to both the old and the new drug. Where valproate genuinely cannot be replaced, the dose is minimised, the daily dose is divided, high dose folate is given, and the pregnancy is managed jointly by neurology and obstetrics.
key_points: Valproate causes major malformations in about ten per cent and neurodevelopmental harm in more
Both effects are dose dependent and folate does not offset them
Any switch is completed and stability confirmed before conception
Contraception is maintained until the new regimen is established
Abrupt withdrawal risks status epilepticus and loss of driving privileges
explanation.pearls: Lamotrigine clearance rises substantially through pregnancy because of oestrogen induced glucuronidation, so levels fall and doses often need increasing, then must be reduced promptly within days of birth to avoid toxicity.

sources.label: Therapeutic Goods Administration Valproate Safety Advisory
Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

subtopic_detail: epigastric pain with falling platelets and rising transaminases at thirty four weeks when the blood pressure is only mildly raised
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar assessing a 34 year old woman at 34 weeks and 3 days in her first pregnancy who came in overnight with twelve hours of pain under her ribs on the right and persistent nausea. She thought she had eaten something that disagreed with her.

She has no headache, no visual disturbance and no ankle swelling that she has noticed. Her blood pressure at her last antenatal visit a week ago was 118 over 72 with no proteinuria. She has vomited twice. Her blood glucose is normal and she is not confused or drowsy. Fetal movements have been normal and the cardiotocograph is reassuring. She takes no regular medication and has had no previous liver or gallbladder problems.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, blood pressure 148/94, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 98 per cent in air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 145
data_table.Examination: Tender in the right upper quadrant and epigastrium, no guarding, reflexes normal with no clonus, uterus soft and non tender
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 78 x10^9/L (150 to 400), alanine aminotransferase 210 U/L (less than 35), lactate dehydrogenase 720 U/L (120 to 250), haptoglobin low, blood film shows fragmented red cells, creatinine 62 micromol/L (45 to 90), international normalised ratio 1.0, glucose 5.1 mmol/L, urine protein creatinine ratio 38 mg/mmol (less than 30)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Transfuse platelets and repeat the full blood count before deciding on delivery
options.rationale: Platelets are consumed rapidly in this process so a transfusion given without delivering produces only a transient rise, and it is reserved for active bleeding or for cover immediately before an operative procedure. Transfusing to defer the decision treats the number rather than the disease. (Source: National Blood Authority Australia)

options.text: Manage expectantly with twice weekly bloods and birth planned at 37 weeks
options.rationale: Expectant management is considered only before 34 weeks and only where maternal and fetal parameters are stable, whereas she is past 34 weeks with an actively deteriorating haematological and hepatic picture. The syndrome characteristically progresses over hours rather than days. (Source: Society of Obstetric Medicine of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Society of Obstetric Medicine of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Give dexamethasone to raise the platelet count and continue the pregnancy further
options.rationale: Corticosteroids do produce a transient improvement in platelet count but have not been shown to improve maternal or perinatal outcome, and using them to justify prolonging the pregnancy is the error rather than the drug itself. Antenatal corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity are a separate and legitimate indication. (Source: Society of Obstetric Medicine of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Society of Obstetric Medicine of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Commence magnesium sulfate and antihypertensive therapy, and plan birth today
options.rationale: Haemolysis with fragmented cells, transaminases above twice the upper limit and platelets below 100 x10^9/L at 34 weeks establishes a severe manifestation of the hypertensive disorders of pregnancy in which the only definitive treatment is birth. Magnesium sulfate is given for seizure prophylaxis and the blood pressure treated while delivery is organised. (Source: Society of Obstetric Medicine of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Society of Obstetric Medicine of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Start oral labetalol and arrange outpatient review with repeat bloods in two days
options.rationale: Lowering the blood pressure prevents maternal stroke but does nothing to halt the underlying endothelial and hepatic process, so treating the pressure alone and sending her home would allow the syndrome to progress unobserved. Her pressure is also not in the severe range, which is precisely why it cannot be used to gauge severity here. (Source: Society of Obstetric Medicine of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Society of Obstetric Medicine of Australia and New Zealand

explanation.summary: Haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes and low platelets constitute a severe variant of pre-eclampsia that can present with only modest hypertension and minimal proteinuria, so severity is judged on the end organ picture rather than on the blood pressure reading. Right upper quadrant or epigastric pain from hepatic capsular distension is the characteristic symptom and is often misattributed to reflux, gallbladder disease or gastroenteritis, which delays diagnosis. The main differential is acute fatty liver of pregnancy, which is distinguished by hypoglycaemia, coagulopathy with a prolonged international normalised ratio, a rising creatinine and often encephalopathy, none of which is present here. Complications include eclampsia, placental abruption, disseminated intravascular coagulation, acute kidney injury and hepatic haematoma or rupture, and the disease may worsen for the first twenty four to forty eight hours after birth, so postnatal surveillance continues. Birth is the only definitive treatment, and the decision to deliver is made on the maternal condition rather than on the gestation once past thirty four weeks.
key_points: Blood pressure may be only mildly raised and proteinuria minimal
Epigastric or right upper quadrant pain reflects hepatic capsular stretch
Hypoglycaemia, coagulopathy and rising creatinine suggest acute fatty liver instead
Birth is the only definitive treatment and is not deferred past 34 weeks
The disease can worsen in the first two days after birth
explanation.pearls: Magnesium sulfate is given for seizure prophylaxis and continued for twenty four hours after birth, with monitoring of deep tendon reflexes, respiratory rate and urine output, and calcium gluconate kept immediately available as the antidote for toxicity.

sources.label: Society of Obstetric Medicine of Australia and New Zealand
Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

subtopic_detail: first trimester anticoagulation for a mechanical mitral prosthesis where the daily warfarin requirement sits at the embryopathy dose threshold
stem:
You are the obstetric medicine registrar seeing a 31 year old woman who had a bileaflet mechanical mitral valve replacement at twenty four for rheumatic heart disease. She had a positive pregnancy test three days ago and is now six weeks by her dates.

She takes warfarin 4 mg daily with a target international normalised ratio of 2.5 to 3.5 and her results have been within range at every check for two years. She has had no thromboembolic event and no bleeding. Her echocardiogram four months ago showed a normally functioning prosthesis with no pannus, no regurgitation and a normal left atrial size, and she is in sinus rhythm. She has no other medical conditions and takes no other medication. She has read online that warfarin harms babies and has already missed two doses because she was frightened to take it.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76 and regular, blood pressure 110/68, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99 per cent in air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Crisp mechanical first heart sound, no murmur of prosthetic dysfunction, chest clear, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: International normalised ratio 1.6 today, full blood count and creatinine within normal limits, transthoracic echocardiogram four months ago showed normal prosthetic function

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anticoagulation plan for the first trimester?

options.text: Switch to a direct oral anticoagulant for the first trimester, then resume warfarin
options.rationale: Direct oral anticoagulants are contraindicated with mechanical valves at any time because a randomised trial in non pregnant patients was stopped early for excess valve thrombosis and stroke, and they are separately contraindicated in pregnancy. This is the one option that is wrong on both counts simultaneously. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Withhold anticoagulation until twelve weeks, then restart warfarin at her usual dose
options.rationale: Pregnancy is a strongly prothrombotic state and a mechanical mitral prosthesis left unanticoagulated for six weeks carries a high risk of valve thrombosis, which is frequently fatal to both mother and foetus. Her missed doses and an international normalised ratio already down at 1.6 make this the immediate danger rather than a theoretical one. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Switch to twice daily therapeutic enoxaparin with dosing guided by her weight alone
options.rationale: Low molecular weight heparin is a legitimate first trimester strategy and the one chosen when the warfarin requirement is high, but it must be given twice daily with peak anti factor Xa monitoring and dose adjustment, because valve thrombosis has occurred in pregnant women dosed on weight without monitoring. The flaw is the omission of monitoring rather than the choice of drug. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Switch to a continuous unfractionated heparin infusion for the whole first trimester
options.rationale: Unfractionated heparin carries the highest rate of valve thrombosis of all the regimens used in this setting and commits her to hospital or to an indwelling line for six weeks with attendant infection and osteoporosis risk. Its proper place is the immediate peripartum window, not the first trimester. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Restore warfarin at her usual dose now with close monitoring after documented counselling
options.rationale: Embryopathy risk is dose dependent and is low when the daily requirement is 5 mg or less, so continuing warfarin through the first trimester carries the lowest maternal risk of valve thrombosis and an acceptable fetal risk at her dose of 4 mg. Her subtherapeutic ratio of 1.6 makes restoration urgent, and the decision is made with her after explicit counselling because both branches carry real risk. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand

explanation.summary: Pregnancy with a mechanical heart valve is one of the highest risk cardiac situations in obstetrics, and no anticoagulation strategy is free of harm, so the task is to choose the least bad option for the individual woman and to document the discussion. Warfarin gives the most reliable protection against valve thrombosis but crosses the placenta and causes embryopathy with nasal hypoplasia and stippled epiphyses when taken between six and twelve weeks, together with fetal intracranial haemorrhage later in pregnancy. That embryopathy risk is dose dependent, and the widely used threshold is a daily requirement of 5 mg or less, below which continuation through the first trimester is considered reasonable and above which a switch to low molecular weight heparin between six and twelve weeks is preferred. Heparins do not cross the placenta and so carry no fetal risk, but they protect the valve less reliably and demand twice daily dosing with peak anti factor Xa monitoring and dose adjustment. Mitral position, older generation prostheses, atrial fibrillation and a previous thromboembolic event all raise thrombotic risk and push the balance back toward warfarin.
key_points: No regimen is risk free; the choice is documented shared decision making
Warfarin embryopathy risk is dose dependent, with 5 mg daily as the usual threshold
The vulnerable window for embryopathy is six to twelve weeks
Low molecular weight heparin requires twice daily dosing with peak anti factor Xa monitoring
Direct oral anticoagulants are contraindicated with any mechanical valve
explanation.pearls: Warfarin is converted to intravenous unfractionated heparin at around thirty six weeks and the heparin stopped four to six hours before birth, because a warfarinised foetus has an anticoagulated brain and vaginal birth then carries an unacceptable risk of intracranial haemorrhage.

sources.label: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand
Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

subtopic_detail: advising about feeding and antibiotics for a painful red breast segment with fever in the third postnatal week
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 29 year old woman who is 18 days postnatal after an uncomplicated vaginal birth of her first baby, and who has been exclusively breastfeeding.

She has had 36 hours of aching and shivering and feels as though she has influenza. A wedge shaped area of her left breast is red, hot and painful, and feeding from that side is uncomfortable. She has had cracked nipples since the first week and has been feeding the baby mostly on the right because the left hurts. There is no discrete lump that moves under your fingers, no fluctuance and no overlying skin breakdown. The baby is feeding well, has plenty of wet nappies and is back above birth weight. She asks whether she should stop feeding from that breast.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 102/min, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 38.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Wedge shaped erythema over the upper outer quadrant of the left breast with warmth and tenderness, generalised firmness of that segment, no fluctuant mass, no axillary abscess, fissured left nipple, right breast normal
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Stop feeding from the affected breast and suppress lactation on that side
options.rationale: Stopping removal of milk from an inflamed segment worsens stasis, which is the mechanism driving the inflammation, and markedly increases the likelihood of progression to abscess. Suppression also ends breastfeeding for a problem that resolves with treatment. (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association and Therapeutic Guidelines)
source_refs: Australian Breastfeeding Association and Therapeutic Guidelines

options.text: Arrange urgent breast ultrasound and surgical referral for drainage of an abscess
options.rationale: Ultrasound with drainage is the pathway once an abscess has formed, indicated by a fluctuant or discrete tender mass or by failure to improve after 48 hours of appropriate antibiotics. She has diffuse segmental firmness without a discrete or fluctuant mass, so she has not reached that point. (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association and Therapeutic Guidelines)
source_refs: Australian Breastfeeding Association and Therapeutic Guidelines

options.text: Advise cold packs and simple analgesia alone with review only if she worsens
options.rationale: Conservative management with improved milk removal is appropriate for blocked ducts and for inflammation of under 24 hours without systemic features. Thirty six hours of fever at 38.6 degrees C with tachycardia and a fissured nipple providing a portal of entry indicates infection that needs antibiotic treatment. (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association and Therapeutic Guidelines)
source_refs: Australian Breastfeeding Association and Therapeutic Guidelines

options.text: Prescribe oral metronidazole and advise expressing and discarding the milk
options.rationale: Metronidazole targets anaerobes and does not cover Staphylococcus aureus, which is the usual pathogen entering through a nipple fissure. Discarding expressed milk is also unnecessary, since the milk is safe for the baby and continued feeding is part of the treatment. (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association and Therapeutic Guidelines)
source_refs: Australian Breastfeeding Association and Therapeutic Guidelines

options.text: Continue feeding from both breasts with oral flucloxacillin and feeding review
options.rationale: Effective and frequent milk removal from the affected side is the central treatment because stasis drives the inflammation, and continued feeding poses no risk to the baby. Flucloxacillin covers Staphylococcus aureus, which enters through the nipple fissure, and referral for attachment review addresses the cracked nipple and the underfeeding of that breast that together caused the problem. (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association and Therapeutic Guidelines)
source_refs: Australian Breastfeeding Association and Therapeutic Guidelines

explanation.summary: Lactational mastitis arises from milk stasis with or without bacterial infection, and in this woman both elements are present: she has been feeding predominantly on the right because of pain, and a nipple fissure has given Staphylococcus aureus a portal of entry. The counterintuitive but essential instruction is to keep feeding from the affected breast, because continued milk removal resolves the stasis that sustains the inflammation, and the milk is safe for the baby. Antibiotics are indicated when systemic features persist beyond about 24 hours, when there is a nipple fissure, or when conservative measures fail, and flucloxacillin is the appropriate choice. Failure to improve within 48 hours, or a discrete fluctuant mass, suggests abscess and requires ultrasound with aspiration or drainage. Addressing attachment is what prevents recurrence.
key_points: Milk stasis is the underlying mechanism, so continued effective milk removal is central to treatment.
Breastfeeding from the affected side is safe for the baby and should continue.
Flucloxacillin covers Staphylococcus aureus, the usual organism entering through a nipple fissure.
Failure to improve within 48 hours or a fluctuant mass suggests abscess requiring ultrasound and drainage.
Review of attachment and positioning addresses the cause and prevents recurrence.
explanation.pearls: Tell a woman with mastitis to feed more often from the affected breast rather than less, because stopping feeds on that side is the commonest reason simple mastitis progresses to an abscess, and review her attachment to fix the fissure that let the organism in.

sources.label: Australian Breastfeeding Association and Therapeutic Guidelines

subtopic_detail: deciding whether an incidental late pregnancy platelet fall needs treatment or only observation
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 27 year old woman at 34 weeks in her first pregnancy whose routine full blood count shows a platelet count of 98 x10^9/L.

She feels entirely well. She has had no bruising, no bleeding from her gums, no nosebleeds and no petechiae. Her platelet count was 243 x10^9/L at booking and 176 x10^9/L at 28 weeks. She has no history of autoimmune disease, takes no medication and has never had a low platelet count outside pregnancy. Her blood pressure has been normal at every visit and her urinalysis today shows no protein. Her liver enzymes, creatinine and urate are all within normal limits, and her blood film shows no fragments, no clumping and no atypical cells. She is anxious about whether she can have an epidural.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 82/min, blood pressure 114/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C, fetal heart rate 142/min
data_table.Examination: No bruising, petechiae or mucosal bleeding, no hepatosplenomegaly, no oedema, no epigastric or right upper quadrant tenderness, symphysiofundal height 34 cm
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 98 x10^9/L (150-400), haemoglobin 118 g/L (110-140), alanine aminotransferase and bilirubin within normal limits, creatinine 58 micromol/L (45-90), urate within normal limits for gestation, blood film shows no fragments or platelet clumping, urinalysis negative for protein

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone to raise the count before she reaches term
options.rationale: Corticosteroid is the first line treatment for immune thrombocytopenia in pregnancy, which is suggested by a count that was already low before pregnancy or in the first trimester, or by a fall below about 75 x10^9/L. Her count was normal at booking and has fallen gradually in the third trimester, which is the opposite pattern. (Source: RANZCOG: Thrombocytopenia in pregnancy)

options.text: Give intravenous immunoglobulin now and repeat the count in 48 hours
options.rationale: Immunoglobulin raises the count rapidly and is reserved for immune thrombocytopenia with bleeding or with very low counts close to delivery, where a fast response is needed. Using it for a physiological process in an asymptomatic woman exposes her to a blood product without any indication. (Source: RANZCOG: Thrombocytopenia in pregnancy)

options.text: Repeat the count at intervals through to delivery with no specific treatment
options.rationale: A count that was normal at booking and has drifted down only in the third trimester, in a well woman with no bleeding, normal blood pressure, normal liver enzymes and a normal film, is gestational thrombocytopenia, which accounts for the great majority of low platelet counts in pregnancy and requires no treatment. Serial monitoring is all that is needed, and a count above 70 to 80 x10^9/L generally permits neuraxial anaesthesia, which is the question she is actually asking. (Source: RANZCOG: Thrombocytopenia in pregnancy)

options.text: Deliver her within 24 hours after administering antenatal corticosteroids
options.rationale: Delivery is the treatment for the HELLP syndrome, in which thrombocytopenia occurs alongside haemolysis and raised transaminases, usually with hypertension and epigastric pain. Her liver enzymes are normal, her blood pressure is normal, her film shows no fragments and she has no symptoms, which excludes it. (Source: RANZCOG: Thrombocytopenia in pregnancy)

options.text: Transfuse platelets before labour to ensure a safe count for regional anaesthesia
options.rationale: Platelet transfusion is reserved for active bleeding or for counts well below the threshold for neuraxial anaesthesia at the time of delivery. Transfusing prophylactically at 98 x10^9/L would give a short lived rise, risk alloimmunisation and treat a number rather than a problem. (Source: RANZCOG: Thrombocytopenia in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Thrombocytopenia complicates around one in ten pregnancies and gestational thrombocytopenia accounts for the large majority of cases. Its defining features are a normal count in early pregnancy with a gradual third trimester fall, an asymptomatic woman, a count that rarely drops below 70 x10^9/L, and resolution within weeks of delivery. The differential is separated on the history and the accompanying results rather than on the platelet count alone: immune thrombocytopenia typically predates the pregnancy or presents earlier and falls further, while pre-eclampsia and the HELLP syndrome bring hypertension, proteinuria, raised transaminases and red cell fragments. No treatment is required and the count should simply be monitored to delivery. Most anaesthetists will site a neuraxial block above about 70 to 80 x10^9/L provided the count is stable and there is no coagulopathy.
key_points: Gestational thrombocytopenia causes a gradual third trimester fall in a previously normal count.
It is asymptomatic, rarely falls below 70 x10^9/L, and resolves within weeks of delivery.
Immune thrombocytopenia usually predates pregnancy or appears earlier and falls further.
Hypertension, proteinuria, raised transaminases or red cell fragments point to pre-eclampsia or the HELLP syndrome.
Neuraxial anaesthesia is generally acceptable above a stable count of about 70 to 80 x10^9/L.
explanation.pearls: Look at the booking platelet count before working up thrombocytopenia in late pregnancy, because a normal count in the first trimester that drifts down in the third is gestational and needs nothing, whereas a count that was already low points to immune thrombocytopenia and changes the management entirely.

sources.label: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand

subtopic_detail: adjusting thyroid hormone replacement at the moment a treated hypothyroid woman confirms she is pregnant
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 30 year old woman who has just had a positive home pregnancy test. Her last menstrual period was six weeks ago and a serum test today confirms the pregnancy.

She has had Hashimoto thyroiditis for eight years and takes levothyroxine 100 micrograms daily. Her thyroid stimulating hormone three months ago was 2.9 mIU/L, which her previous doctor described as satisfactory. She feels well, has no goitre symptoms and has had no change in weight, bowel habit or heat tolerance. She takes an over the counter pregnancy multivitamin containing iron and calcium with her breakfast, at the same time as her levothyroxine tablet. She asks whether she needs to change anything.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 76/min, blood pressure 106/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: No goitre palpable, no tremor, no lid lag, reflexes normal with a normal relaxation phase, no pretibial change
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 2.9 mIU/L three months ago on current dose, thyroid peroxidase antibodies strongly positive at diagnosis, beta human chorionic gonadotrophin consistent with six weeks gestation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management today?

options.text: Continue the current dose and recheck thyroid function at 20 weeks gestation
options.rationale: Continuing unchanged would be right if thyroid requirements were stable in pregnancy, and they rise by roughly a quarter to a half from very early gestation as binding globulin increases and the placenta deiodinates hormone. Deferring the first check to 20 weeks misses the first trimester, when fetal brain development depends entirely on maternal supply. (Source: RANZCOG: Thyroid disease in pregnancy)

options.text: Stop levothyroxine now and retest thyroid function in four weeks time
options.rationale: Withdrawal would be considered where replacement had been started without a confirmed diagnosis, and this woman has antibody positive autoimmune hypothyroidism requiring lifelong treatment. Stopping would produce overt maternal hypothyroidism during organogenesis, which is associated with pregnancy loss and impaired neurodevelopment. (Source: RANZCOG: Thyroid disease in pregnancy)

options.text: Add liothyronine to the current levothyroxine and test again in six weeks
options.rationale: Combination therapy with triiodothyronine is occasionally trialled in non pregnant patients with persistent symptoms despite normal biochemistry, and it is specifically avoided in pregnancy. Triiodothyronine crosses the placenta poorly and suppresses maternal thyroid stimulating hormone without supplying the foetus with the thyroxine it needs. (Source: RANZCOG: Thyroid disease in pregnancy)

options.text: Increase the levothyroxine dose now and separate it from the multivitamin
options.rationale: Requirements rise from early in the first trimester, so the accepted practice is to increase the dose as soon as pregnancy is confirmed rather than waiting for a result, commonly by taking two additional tablets each week, with thyroid function checked within four weeks and then four to six weekly against a first trimester target below 2.5 mIU/L. Taking levothyroxine with iron and calcium markedly reduces its absorption, so separating them by at least four hours is part of the same correction. (Source: RANZCOG: Thyroid disease in pregnancy)

options.text: Measure free triiodothyronine and adjust the dose according to that result
options.rationale: Free triiodothyronine is useful in assessing thyrotoxicosis, particularly the triiodothyronine predominant form, and it is not used to titrate replacement. Thyroid stimulating hormone with free thyroxine against trimester specific ranges is the correct monitoring pair in pregnancy. (Source: RANZCOG: Thyroid disease in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Thyroxine requirements increase from the earliest weeks of pregnancy because oestrogen raises thyroxine binding globulin, the placenta degrades maternal hormone, and human chorionic gonadotrophin alters the set point. The fetal thyroid does not produce hormone until around 12 weeks, so first trimester brain development depends entirely on maternal thyroxine. A thyroid stimulating hormone of 2.9 mIU/L that was acceptable outside pregnancy sits above the first trimester target of 2.5 mIU/L. The correct action is therefore to increase the dose immediately on confirmation of pregnancy rather than waiting for a new result, then monitor four to six weekly. The multivitamin is a second correctable problem, because iron and calcium chelate levothyroxine and substantially reduce absorption.
key_points: Levothyroxine requirements rise by roughly 25 to 50 percent from the first trimester of pregnancy.
Dose is increased as soon as pregnancy is confirmed rather than waiting for a new thyroid result.
The first trimester thyroid stimulating hormone target is below 2.5 mIU/L in treated hypothyroidism.
Iron and calcium reduce levothyroxine absorption and must be separated by at least four hours.
Liothyronine is avoided in pregnancy because it crosses the placenta poorly while suppressing maternal thyroid stimulating hormone.
explanation.pearls: Tell every woman on levothyroxine who is planning pregnancy to take two extra tablets each week from the day her test is positive and to telephone for a thyroid function test, because waiting for the appointment costs several weeks of the period when fetal brain development depends wholly on maternal supply.

subtopic_detail: planning surveillance after evacuation of a complete molar pregnancy in a woman who wants to conceive again soon
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 31 year old woman two weeks after suction evacuation of the uterus. She had presented at 11 weeks with vaginal bleeding and a uterus larger than expected for dates, with hyperemesis requiring admission.

Her pre-evacuation human chorionic gonadotrophin was 268 000 IU/L and her ultrasound had shown a heterogeneous intrauterine mass with multiple small cystic spaces and no fetal parts. Histopathology reports diffuse trophoblastic hyperplasia with hydropic villi and absent fetal tissue. Her bleeding has settled and she feels well. Her human chorionic gonadotrophin today is 4 100 IU/L. She and her partner are keen to try for another pregnancy as soon as possible and she asks whether she should stop using contraception now.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 15/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non tender, uterus no longer palpable abdominally, minimal vaginal bleeding, no adnexal mass, chest clear
data_table.Investigations: Human chorionic gonadotrophin 268 000 IU/L before evacuation and 4 100 IU/L today, histopathology confirms diffuse trophoblastic hyperplasia with hydropic villi and no fetal tissue, haemoglobin 116 g/L (115-155), thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice about follow up and future pregnancy?

options.text: Begin methotrexate now because the hormone level remains substantially raised
options.rationale: Chemotherapy is given for gestational trophoblastic neoplasia, which is diagnosed when the hormone plateaus or rises across defined measurements, when it remains detectable beyond six months, or when metastases or choriocarcinoma histology are present. A level falling from 268 000 to 4 100 IU/L over two weeks is the expected decline after successful evacuation. (Source: RANZCOG: Gestational trophoblastic disease)

options.text: Repeat the evacuation to ensure that no residual molar tissue has been retained
options.rationale: A second evacuation is considered for persistent heavy bleeding or ultrasound evidence of substantial retained tissue, and it carries risks of perforation and intrauterine adhesions. Her bleeding has settled and her hormone level is falling appropriately, so there is nothing to suggest retained tissue. (Source: RANZCOG: Gestational trophoblastic disease)

options.text: Serial hormone surveillance with reliable contraception until follow up completes
options.rationale: Surveillance exists because around one in six complete moles progresses to gestational trophoblastic neoplasia, and that progression is detected only by a hormone level that plateaus or rises, so the measurement must not be confounded. Pregnancy would raise the hormone and make the result uninterpretable, which is why effective contraception is essential throughout follow up, and the combined oral contraceptive pill is acceptable once the level has normalised. (Source: RANZCOG: Gestational trophoblastic disease)

options.text: Advise that no follow up is required now that the uterus has been emptied
options.rationale: Discharging her would forfeit the entire purpose of managing molar pregnancy, since the risk that matters arises after the evacuation rather than before it. Progression to neoplasia is curable when detected by surveillance and considerably more dangerous when it presents late with metastatic disease. (Source: RANZCOG: Gestational trophoblastic disease)

options.text: Recommend hysterectomy given the very high pre-evacuation hormone concentration
options.rationale: Hysterectomy is an option for women who have completed their family, particularly those over 40 or with heavy bleeding, and it reduces but does not eliminate the risk of neoplasia because metastatic disease can still occur. Recommending it to a 31 year old who wants another pregnancy would be disproportionate. (Source: RANZCOG: Gestational trophoblastic disease)

explanation.summary: A complete hydatidiform mole arises from fertilisation of an ovum lacking maternal genetic material, giving a diploid conceptus of entirely paternal origin with no fetal tissue, which matches the histology and the ultrasound appearance here. Presentation with bleeding, a uterus large for dates, hyperemesis and a very high human chorionic gonadotrophin is characteristic, and thyrotoxicosis can occur because the hormone cross reacts with the thyroid stimulating hormone receptor. After suction evacuation the central task is surveillance, because approximately one in six complete moles progresses to gestational trophoblastic neoplasia, which is detected by a hormone level that plateaus or rises rather than falling to normal. Reliable contraception throughout follow up is essential, since a new pregnancy would make the hormone uninterpretable and mask progression. Registration with a trophoblast centre and adherence to the surveillance schedule are what make this a highly curable condition.
key_points: A complete mole is diploid and entirely paternal in origin, with no fetal tissue present.
A uterus large for dates, hyperemesis and a very high hormone level are characteristic features.
Around one in six complete moles progresses to gestational trophoblastic neoplasia.
Progression is detected by a hormone level that plateaus or rises rather than normalising.
Reliable contraception is essential throughout follow up so that the hormone remains interpretable.
explanation.pearls: Stress that contraception is part of the treatment rather than an optional extra after a molar pregnancy, because a new pregnancy raises human chorionic gonadotrophin and makes it impossible to distinguish a healthy conception from the trophoblastic neoplasia that follows about one in six complete moles.

sources.label: Cancer Council Australia: Gestational trophoblastic disease

subtopic_detail: planning mode of birth after a first episode of genital ulceration acquired close to term
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar seeing a 26 year old woman at 36 weeks in her first pregnancy who presents with three days of painful vulval ulceration, dysuria and feeling generally unwell.

She describes a cluster of small blisters that broke down into shallow painful ulcers, and she has tender swollen glands in both groins. She has never had anything like this before and has had no previous genital or oral ulceration of any kind. Her partner has recently disclosed a past episode of genital blistering. A swab from the ulcer base has returned positive for herpes simplex virus type 2 by polymerase chain reaction, and type specific serology taken the same day shows no herpes simplex virus type 1 or type 2 antibodies. She has had no contractions and no ruptured membranes.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92/min, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 17/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 37.8 degrees C, fetal heart rate 148/min
data_table.Examination: Multiple shallow tender vulval ulcers with surrounding erythema, bilateral tender inguinal lymphadenopathy, cervix closed on speculum with no ruptured membranes, symphysiofundal height 36 cm
data_table.Investigations: Ulcer swab positive for herpes simplex virus type 2 by polymerase chain reaction, type specific serology negative for both type 1 and type 2 antibodies, syphilis and human immunodeficiency virus serology negative, full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Plan vaginal birth with intrapartum aciclovir given to the mother in labour
options.rationale: Vaginal birth with maternal antiviral cover is reasonable for recurrent disease, where transplacental antibody protects the neonate and transmission risk is low. Intrapartum aciclovir does not reduce neonatal transmission in a woman who has no antibodies to pass on. (Source: RANZCOG: Genital herpes in pregnancy)

options.text: Treat the episode topically and reassess the need for caesarean only in labour
options.rationale: Topical antiviral treatment is ineffective for genital herpes and systemic treatment is required. Deferring the decision to labour also removes the opportunity to plan a birth that avoids contact with the infected genital tract at the time transmission occurs. (Source: RANZCOG: Genital herpes in pregnancy)

options.text: Perform serial viral swabs from 38 weeks and allow vaginal birth if they are negative
options.rationale: Serial antenatal cultures were used historically and were abandoned because they predict shedding at delivery poorly, with negative swabs frequently followed by shedding in labour. Basing the mode of birth on them would give false reassurance. (Source: RANZCOG: Genital herpes in pregnancy)

options.text: Start oral aciclovir now and offer caesarean section at term for this birth
options.rationale: Negative type specific serology alongside a positive swab confirms a genuine primary infection, meaning she has not yet developed antibodies to transfer across the placenta, and neonatal transmission risk during vaginal birth approaches forty percent when primary infection occurs within six weeks of delivery. Aciclovir treats the episode and is continued as suppression until birth, while caesarean section performed before membrane rupture avoids the exposure that causes neonatal herpes, a condition with high mortality and neurological morbidity. (Source: RANZCOG: Genital herpes in pregnancy)

options.text: Give the neonate prophylactic aciclovir after a planned vaginal birth at term
options.rationale: Neonatal aciclovir is treatment for established or strongly suspected neonatal infection rather than a substitute for avoiding exposure. Neonatal herpes carries substantial mortality and neurological morbidity even when treated, so prevention at the time of birth is far preferable. (Source: RANZCOG: Genital herpes in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: The distinction that determines management in genital herpes in pregnancy is whether the episode is a primary infection or a recurrence, and clinical appearance alone cannot make it because a first clinical episode may be the first recognised recurrence of a long standing infection. Type specific serology resolves this: antibodies absent alongside a positive swab confirms true primary infection. That matters because maternal antibodies cross the placenta and protect the neonate, so a woman with recurrent disease transmits in fewer than three percent of vaginal births, whereas primary infection within six weeks of delivery carries a transmission risk approaching forty percent. Primary infection in the third trimester is therefore treated with aciclovir continued as suppression, and caesarean section is offered, ideally before membranes rupture. Serial antenatal viral cultures were abandoned because they predict shedding at delivery poorly.
key_points: Type specific serology distinguishes true primary infection from a first recognised recurrence.
Maternal antibodies cross the placenta and protect the neonate, which recurrent disease provides and primary does not.
Primary infection within six weeks of delivery carries transmission risk approaching forty percent.
Recurrent disease carries a transmission risk below three percent and permits vaginal birth.
Serial antenatal viral cultures predict shedding at delivery poorly and are no longer performed.
explanation.pearls: Send type specific serology alongside the swab in any first episode of genital herpes in pregnancy, because absent antibodies confirm primary infection and change the plan from vaginal birth to caesarean section, while a positive antibody result means this is a recurrence and vaginal birth remains appropriate.

sources.label: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine

subtopic_detail: responding to a woman who has halved her preventer dose in early pregnancy because she is worried about the baby
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 26 year old woman at 14 weeks in her first pregnancy for a routine antenatal visit. She has had asthma since childhood and was well controlled before pregnancy on budesonide with formoterol as a combination preventer taken twice daily.

She tells you that when she found out she was pregnant she halved her preventer because she did not want the baby exposed to a steroid. Since then she has needed her salbutamol most days, has woken breathless twice in the past week and has stopped walking the dog up the hill near her house. She has had no fever, no coloured sputum and no chest pain. She has not smoked and there is no hay fever flare. Her peak expiratory flow today is 300 L/min against a personal best of 450 L/min.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88/min, blood pressure 104/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C, fetal heart rate 150/min
data_table.Examination: Speaking in full sentences, mild expiratory wheeze throughout both lung fields, no accessory muscle use, no focal crackles
data_table.Investigations: Peak expiratory flow 300 L/min against a personal best of 450 L/min, no other investigations performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Restore the preventer to her pre pregnancy dose and review in two weeks
options.rationale: Inhaled corticosteroids have a long record of safe use in pregnancy and the risk to the foetus comes from uncontrolled asthma rather than from the medication, because maternal hypoxaemia causes growth restriction, preterm birth and perinatal loss. Returning to the dose that previously achieved control, with an early review to confirm it has worked, directly addresses the cause of her deterioration. (Source: National Asthma Council Australia: Australian Asthma Handbook)
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australia: Australian Asthma Handbook

options.text: Stop the preventer entirely and use salbutamol whenever she has symptoms
options.rationale: Reliever only treatment is not an accepted strategy for persistent asthma at any time, and it would accelerate exactly the deterioration she is already showing. Escalating short acting beta agonist use is a marker of poor control rather than a treatment for it. (Source: National Asthma Council Australia: Australian Asthma Handbook)
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australia: Australian Asthma Handbook

options.text: Add montelukast in place of restoring the inhaled corticosteroid dose
options.rationale: Montelukast can be continued in pregnancy in women already established on it and stabilised by it, but it is a weaker controller than inhaled corticosteroid and is not a substitute for the dose she has withdrawn. Substituting it also leaves her original misconception about steroid safety uncorrected. (Source: National Asthma Council Australia: Australian Asthma Handbook)
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australia: Australian Asthma Handbook

options.text: Prescribe a two week course of oral prednisolone and continue the halved dose
options.rationale: Oral corticosteroid is used for acute exacerbations and is given in pregnancy when indicated, but this woman is not acutely exacerbating and is speaking in full sentences with normal oxygen saturation. Systemic steroid without restoring the preventer treats the symptom and leaves the cause in place. (Source: National Asthma Council Australia: Australian Asthma Handbook)
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australia: Australian Asthma Handbook

options.text: Arrange a chest radiograph and spirometry before altering any of her treatment
options.rationale: Investigation would be warranted if the diagnosis were uncertain or an alternative cause such as infection or embolism were suspected, and here the history explains the deterioration completely. Delaying treatment for tests postpones the correction of a problem you have already identified. (Source: National Asthma Council Australia: Australian Asthma Handbook)
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australia: Australian Asthma Handbook

explanation.summary: Roughly a third of pregnant women with asthma deteriorate during pregnancy, and self reduction of preventer medication out of concern for the foetus is one of the commonest reasons. The evidence is consistent that inhaled corticosteroids are safe in pregnancy while poorly controlled asthma is not, because maternal hypoxaemia is associated with fetal growth restriction, preterm birth, pre-eclampsia and perinatal mortality. This woman has clear markers of loss of control: daily reliever use, night waking and a peak flow at two thirds of her personal best. The correct response is to restore the dose that previously worked and review early to confirm the response. Explaining why the medication is safer than the disease is what prevents the same reduction happening again.
key_points: Inhaled corticosteroids are safe in pregnancy and should be continued at the dose that maintains control.
Uncontrolled asthma causes fetal growth restriction, preterm birth and perinatal mortality.
Night waking, daily reliever use and a peak flow below 80 percent of personal best all indicate poor control.
Oral corticosteroid is used for acute exacerbations in pregnancy and should not be withheld when indicated.
Asthma control should be reviewed at every antenatal visit and a written action plan provided.
explanation.pearls: Ask every pregnant woman with asthma whether she has changed her own dose since the pregnancy test, because self reduction of inhaled corticosteroid is the commonest cause of second trimester deterioration and is corrected by restoring the previous dose with a review inside two weeks.

sources.label: National Asthma Council Australia: Australian Asthma Handbook

subtopic_detail: recognising anterior pituitary failure when lactation never establishes after a major obstetric haemorrhage
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 32 year old woman ten weeks after the birth of her second child. Her delivery was complicated by a postpartum haemorrhage of 3 200 mL requiring six units of red cells and a period of hypotension in the operating theatre.

She tells you she was never able to produce enough milk despite persistent effort with a lactation consultant, and gave up at four weeks. She has had no periods since the birth, feels exhausted, is cold all the time and has become dizzy on standing. She has no headache and no visual disturbance. She is not breastfeeding now and a pregnancy test is negative. Her thyroid stimulating hormone is 0.8 mIU/L with a free thyroxine of 7 pmol/L, her 9 am cortisol is 62 nmol/L, and her prolactin is below the detection limit of the assay.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92/min, blood pressure 96/60 mmHg lying and 82/54 mmHg standing, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.2 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Pallor with dry skin, loss of axillary and pubic hair, no goitre, visual fields full to confrontation, no galactorrhoea, breasts soft and non engorged
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 0.8 mIU/L (0.4-4.0) with free thyroxine 7 pmol/L (10-20), 9 am cortisol 62 nmol/L (200-700), prolactin undetectable, sodium 129 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 4.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), beta human chorionic gonadotrophin negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Replace hydrocortisone first, then thyroxine, and image the pituitary
options.rationale: A low free thyroxine with an inappropriately normal thyroid stimulating hormone, an undetectable prolactin and a low 9 am cortisol together indicate panhypopituitarism, which in this context follows ischaemic necrosis of the pituitary after major obstetric haemorrhage. The order matters critically, because thyroxine accelerates cortisol clearance and giving it before glucocorticoid replacement can precipitate an adrenal crisis, and imaging then confirms the empty or shrunken gland. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia)

options.text: Start levothyroxine now and review her thyroid function again in six weeks
options.rationale: Thyroxine replacement is indeed needed, and starting it before glucocorticoid in a patient with unrecognised adrenal insufficiency increases metabolic demand and cortisol clearance and can precipitate a life threatening crisis. The sequence rather than the drug is the error. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia)

options.text: Reassure her that amenorrhoea and fatigue are expected in the postnatal period
options.rationale: Postnatal fatigue and lactational amenorrhoea are extremely common and would be the right interpretation in a woman who is breastfeeding and otherwise well. Failure of lactation, postural hypotension, hyponatraemia and loss of secondary sexual hair are not features of normal recovery. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia)

options.text: Commence the combined oral contraceptive pill to restore her menstrual cycle
options.rationale: Oestrogen replacement is part of long term management of the gonadotrophin deficiency and addresses only one of several failing axes. Prescribing it alone would produce withdrawal bleeds while leaving untreated the cortisol and thyroxine deficiencies that are making her unwell and putting her at risk. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia)

options.text: Measure thyroid autoantibodies and treat this as postpartum thyroiditis instead
options.rationale: Postpartum thyroiditis is common and causes a hypothyroid phase within the first year, and it produces a raised thyroid stimulating hormone because the pituitary responds normally to a failing thyroid. Her thyroid stimulating hormone is inappropriately normal with a low free thyroxine, which localises the problem to the pituitary. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia)

explanation.summary: Sheehan syndrome is infarction of the anterior pituitary caused by hypotension from major obstetric haemorrhage, occurring because the gland enlarges during pregnancy and outgrows its low pressure portal blood supply. The earliest and most characteristic clinical clue is failure of lactation, since prolactin secreting cells are affected, followed by amenorrhoea, fatigue, cold intolerance and loss of axillary and pubic hair. The biochemical signature is deficiency across several axes with inappropriately low or normal trophic hormones, and the key interpretive point is that a low free thyroxine with a normal thyroid stimulating hormone is a pituitary result rather than a normal one. Hyponatraemia from glucocorticoid deficiency is common. Hydrocortisone must be replaced before thyroxine, because thyroid hormone increases cortisol clearance and metabolic demand and can precipitate an adrenal crisis in an unreplaced patient.
key_points: Failure of lactation after major obstetric haemorrhage is the earliest clue to pituitary infarction.
A low free thyroxine with a normal thyroid stimulating hormone indicates pituitary rather than thyroid failure.
An undetectable prolactin in the postnatal period is strongly abnormal and supports the diagnosis.
Hyponatraemia with normal potassium reflects glucocorticoid deficiency with preserved mineralocorticoid function.
Glucocorticoid must always be replaced before thyroxine to avoid precipitating an adrenal crisis.
explanation.pearls: Always give hydrocortisone before levothyroxine when replacing multiple pituitary hormones, because thyroxine accelerates cortisol clearance and raises metabolic demand, and starting it first in an unreplaced patient can precipitate a fatal adrenal crisis within days.

subtopic_detail: responding to a thickened plaque arising within long standing white atrophic vulval skin
stem:
You are the gynaecologist reviewing a 64 year old woman who has had vulval itching for nine years, diagnosed as lichen sclerosus on biopsy six years ago and controlled with an ultrapotent topical corticosteroid used intermittently.

She has attended today because one area now feels different. Over the past four months a firm raised area has developed on the right labium majus, and it has not changed despite eight weeks of daily ultrapotent topical corticosteroid, which had always settled her symptoms before. She has no vaginal bleeding and no discharge. Her cervical screening history is complete and normal, and she has never smoked. On examination the vulval skin is generally pale, thinned and crinkled with loss of the labia minora and narrowing of the introitus, and within that skin there is a 15 mm firm indurated plaque on the right labium majus.

data_table.Examination: Generalised vulval pallor with thinned crinkled skin, resorption of the labia minora, introital narrowing, a discrete 15 mm firm indurated plaque on the right labium majus with an intact surface, no inguinal lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Vulval swab negative for candida and bacterial pathogens, previous vulval biopsy six years ago confirmed lichen sclerosus

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Escalate to a topical calcineurin inhibitor applied twice daily for three months
options.rationale: Tacrolimus and pimecrolimus are second line agents for lichen sclerosus that has not responded to corticosteroid, and using one here would treat a lesion that has not been characterised. Three months of a further topical agent delays the histological answer that a non responding indurated area demands. (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval disorders)

options.text: Biopsy the thickened area to exclude vulval intraepithelial neoplasia
options.rationale: Lichen sclerosus carries a lifetime risk of vulval squamous cell carcinoma of around four to five percent, and the transition is heralded by exactly this change: a localised area that becomes thickened, indurated, ulcerated or fails to respond to treatment that previously worked. Biopsy of the specific abnormal area, rather than of unaffected skin, is the only way to distinguish differentiated vulval intraepithelial neoplasia or an early carcinoma from hypertrophic lichen sclerosus. (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval disorders)

options.text: Reassure her that this represents hypertrophic disease and review in six months
options.rationale: Hypertrophic or thickened plaques do occur within lichen sclerosus and cannot be distinguished clinically from differentiated vulval intraepithelial neoplasia or early invasion, which is why they are biopsied rather than observed. Six months of review would allow an early carcinoma to progress to nodal disease. (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval disorders)
