options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis and groins before any biopsy
options.rationale: Cross sectional imaging stages disease once malignancy has been confirmed histologically and defines nodal involvement before surgery. Performed before any tissue diagnosis it cannot distinguish a benign plaque from a malignant one, because that distinction is cellular rather than anatomical. (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval disorders)

options.text: Refer for wide local excision of the entire affected vulval skin without biopsy
options.rationale: Wide excision is the treatment for confirmed neoplasia and its extent is determined by the histology and margins required, so operating before diagnosis risks both inadequate and unnecessarily mutilating surgery. Excising all lichen sclerosus affected skin would also be disfiguring and would not prevent recurrence elsewhere. (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval disorders)

explanation.summary: Lichen sclerosus is a chronic inflammatory dermatosis producing pallor, thinning and crinkling of vulval skin with architectural loss including resorption of the labia minora and introital narrowing. It is controlled rather than cured with ultrapotent topical corticosteroid, and long term maintenance treatment reduces both symptoms and the risk of malignant transformation. The lifetime risk of vulval squamous cell carcinoma is around four to five percent, and malignancy characteristically arises through differentiated vulval intraepithelial neoplasia, which is not associated with human papillomavirus and occurs in older women on a background of lichen sclerosus. The warning signs are a localised thickened, indurated, ulcerated or eroded area, or failure to respond to previously effective treatment. Any such area requires biopsy of the abnormal site rather than escalation of topical therapy or clinical observation.
key_points: Lichen sclerosus causes pallor, thinning, crinkling and architectural loss with introital narrowing.
Lifetime risk of vulval squamous cell carcinoma is about four to five percent.
Differentiated vulval intraepithelial neoplasia arises on lichen sclerosus and is not related to human papillomavirus.
Induration, ulceration or failure to respond to previously effective corticosteroid mandates biopsy.
Long term maintenance topical corticosteroid reduces symptoms, architectural damage and cancer risk.
explanation.pearls: Biopsy any area of lichen sclerosus that stops responding to a corticosteroid that previously worked, because differentiated vulval intraepithelial neoplasia cannot be distinguished clinically from a hypertrophic plaque and is the route by which around one in twenty of these women develop squamous cell carcinoma.

subtopic_detail: deciding whether to attempt instrumental birth in the room or move to theatre when the head is not as low as the caput suggests
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called to a birth suite for a 28 year old woman in her first pregnancy at 40 weeks. She has been pushing for two hours with an epidural in place and is becoming exhausted.

The cardiotocograph shows a baseline of 150 beats per minute with variable decelerations to 90 recovering within a minute, and normal variability. On abdominal palpation two fifths of the head is palpable above the pubic symphysis. On vaginal examination the cervix is fully dilated, the head is in the right occipitotransverse position, there is 3 plus caput and 2 plus moulding, and the presenting part feels to be at the level of the ischial spines. The liquor is clear. The birth suite is adjacent to the operating theatre and an anaesthetist is present in the unit.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96/min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 37.0 degrees C, fetal heart rate 150/min
data_table.Examination: Two fifths of the head palpable abdominally, cervix fully dilated, right occipitotransverse position, station at the ischial spines, caput 3 plus, moulding 2 plus, clear liquor, effective epidural in place
data_table.Investigations: Cardiotocograph baseline 150/min with normal variability and variable decelerations to 90/min recovering within one minute

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Apply non rotational forceps in the room and deliver in the current position
options.rationale: Non rotational forceps require an occipitoanterior position, and applying them to a head in the transverse position would be a misapplication with a high risk of facial nerve injury and severe maternal trauma. The position alone excludes this instrument. (Source: RANZCOG: Instrumental vaginal birth)

options.text: Continue pushing for a further hour with oxytocin augmentation commenced
options.rationale: Augmentation with more time is reasonable for inadequate contractions with a well applied head making gradual progress, and this woman has already pushed for two hours with significant caput and moulding indicating obstruction. Adding another hour increases the risks of obstructed labour without addressing why the head has not descended. (Source: RANZCOG: Instrumental vaginal birth)

options.text: Move to theatre for a trial of instrumental birth with immediate recourse to caesarean
options.rationale: Two fifths of the head palpable abdominally means that engagement is marginal and the station felt vaginally is being exaggerated by 3 plus caput and 2 plus moulding, which makes this a mid cavity birth with a transverse position and a genuine chance of failure. Conducting the attempt in theatre with the team assembled allows immediate progression to caesarean section if the instrument does not deliver, which is the arrangement that avoids a delayed second attempt with a deeply impacted head. (Source: RANZCOG: Instrumental vaginal birth)

options.text: Perform an immediate category one caesarean section without any vaginal attempt
options.rationale: A category one caesarean is for immediate threat to maternal or fetal life, and this cardiotocograph has normal variability with variable decelerations that recover within a minute, which does not meet that threshold. Committing straight to caesarean at full dilatation with the head at the spines also carries a real risk of a difficult impacted head. (Source: RANZCOG: Instrumental vaginal birth)

options.text: Attempt manual rotation and vacuum extraction in the room with paediatric support
options.rationale: Manual rotation followed by vacuum is a recognised technique for a transverse position and is appropriate when the head is well engaged with minimal caput and moulding. With two fifths palpable abdominally and marked caput, doing it in the room removes the immediate recourse to caesarean that this degree of uncertainty demands. (Source: RANZCOG: Instrumental vaginal birth)

explanation.summary: The critical skill in this scenario is recognising that caput and moulding make the vaginal station misleading, so abdominal palpation is the more reliable guide to descent. Two fifths of the head palpable abdominally with 3 plus caput and 2 plus moulding means the true station is higher than the spines suggests, placing this in mid cavity territory with an occipitotransverse position. Instrumental birth in these circumstances has a meaningfully higher failure rate, which is why the attempt belongs in theatre as a trial with the team prepared to proceed immediately to caesarean section. Non rotational forceps are excluded by the transverse position. The cardiotocograph does not meet category one criteria, so there is time to move the woman and prepare properly.
key_points: Caput and moulding falsely lower the apparent station, so abdominal palpation is the more reliable measure of descent.
More than one fifth of the head palpable abdominally makes instrumental birth substantially more likely to fail.
Non rotational forceps require an occipitoanterior position and are contraindicated in a transverse position.
A trial of instrumental birth in theatre allows immediate recourse to caesarean section without a second attempt.
Category one caesarean requires immediate threat to life, which normal variability with recovering variables does not meet.
explanation.pearls: Palpate the abdomen before every instrumental birth and treat more than one fifth palpable with 3 plus caput as a trial in theatre rather than a birth in the room, because caput and moulding routinely make a mid cavity head feel as though it is at the spines.

subtopic_detail: selecting bone protection in a recently menopausal woman with troublesome flushes and an intact uterus
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 53 year old woman whose last menstrual period was two years ago. She has twelve to fifteen hot flushes a day and wakes drenched most nights, and she has stopped attending her book club because of them.

Her mother fractured a hip at 70. She is a lifelong non smoker, drinks two standard drinks a week and walks daily. She has an intact uterus, has never had a venous thrombosis, has no personal or family history of breast cancer and her mammogram last month was normal. Her blood pressure is 118/74 mmHg and her body mass index is 24 kg/m2. A bone mineral density scan performed because of her family history shows a lumbar spine T score of minus 2.1 and a femoral neck T score of minus 1.9, and she has had no fractures. Her calcium, vitamin D and thyroid function are all normal.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 24 kg/m2, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, no breast masses, no spinal tenderness, height unchanged from her recorded height at age 40
data_table.Investigations: Lumbar spine T score minus 2.1, femoral neck T score minus 1.9, corrected calcium 2.35 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), 25 hydroxyvitamin D 78 nmol/L (50-150), thyroid stimulating hormone 2.1 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), mammogram normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Oral alendronate weekly with calcium and vitamin D supplementation added
options.rationale: A bisphosphonate is first line for established osteoporosis defined by a T score at or below minus 2.5 or a minimal trauma fracture, neither of which she has. It also does nothing for the vasomotor symptoms that are her presenting problem and are the reason she has withdrawn from her activities. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society)

options.text: Combined oestrogen and progestogen menopausal hormone therapy
options.rationale: She is within ten years of her final menstrual period and under 60, the window in which the balance of benefit and risk for hormone therapy is most favourable, and it is the most effective treatment for vasomotor symptoms while also preventing the accelerated bone loss of the early postmenopausal years. A progestogen must accompany the oestrogen because she has an intact uterus and unopposed oestrogen causes endometrial hyperplasia and carcinoma. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society)

options.text: Transdermal oestradiol used alone without any additional endometrial protection
options.rationale: The transdermal route is a sound choice and carries a lower venous thromboembolism risk than oral oestrogen, so the delivery method here is not the error. Giving oestrogen without a progestogen to a woman with an intact uterus is the error, because unopposed oestrogen drives endometrial hyperplasia and carcinoma. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society)

options.text: Denosumab by subcutaneous injection every six months with calcium monitoring
options.rationale: Denosumab is a potent antiresorptive used in established osteoporosis, often where bisphosphonates are unsuitable, and it requires uninterrupted six monthly dosing because cessation causes rapid rebound bone loss with vertebral fractures. Committing a 53 year old with osteopenia to that long term obligation is disproportionate. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Osteoporosis)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Osteoporosis

options.text: Venlafaxine at a low dose with weight bearing exercise and dietary calcium advice
options.rationale: A serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor is a reasonable non hormonal option for flushes in women who cannot take or decline hormone therapy, and it is less effective than oestrogen and offers no skeletal benefit. She has no contraindication to hormone therapy, so accepting a weaker option for both of her problems is not justified. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society)

explanation.summary: This woman has two problems that one treatment addresses: troublesome vasomotor symptoms and osteopenia with a family history of hip fracture. Menopausal hormone therapy is the most effective treatment for vasomotor symptoms and also prevents the rapid bone loss of the early postmenopausal years, which makes it the rational first choice. The timing hypothesis matters, since initiation under 60 years or within ten years of the final menstrual period carries a favourable balance of benefit and risk, whereas starting much later increases cardiovascular risk. A progestogen is mandatory alongside oestrogen in any woman with an intact uterus to prevent endometrial hyperplasia and carcinoma. Bisphosphonates and denosumab are reserved for established osteoporosis rather than osteopenia in a symptomatic woman of this age.
key_points: Hormone therapy is the most effective treatment for vasomotor symptoms and also preserves bone density.
The favourable window is initiation under 60 years or within ten years of the final menstrual period.
A progestogen is mandatory with systemic oestrogen in any woman who has an intact uterus.
Osteoporosis is defined by a T score at or below minus 2.5 or by a minimal trauma fracture.
Transdermal oestrogen carries a lower venous thromboembolism risk than the oral route.
explanation.pearls: Treat osteopenia in a symptomatic woman within ten years of her last period with menopausal hormone therapy rather than a bisphosphonate, because it addresses the flushes and the bone loss together, and never prescribe systemic oestrogen without a progestogen when the uterus is intact.

sources.label: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Osteoporosis

subtopic_detail: a visible cervical abnormality that must not be accepted as the cause of bleeding without exclusion
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 23 year old woman with three months of spotting after intercourse and occasional light bleeding between periods. She started the combined oral contraceptive pill five months ago and takes it reliably at the same time each day.

She has a new partner of four months and they use the pill alone for contraception. She has no pelvic pain, no discharge that she has noticed, no fevers and no weight loss. Her only cervical screening test was two years ago and reported no oncogenic human papillomavirus. On speculum examination there is a symmetrical ring of red velvety tissue extending from the external os onto the surrounding cervix, which bleeds lightly when touched by the swab. The uterus is normal sized and mobile with no adnexal mass or cervical motion tenderness.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Symmetrical circumferential red velvety area around the external os bleeding on contact, no ulceration, no irregular mass, uterus normal size and mobile, no adnexal mass or cervical motion tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Cervical screening two years ago negative for oncogenic human papillomavirus, pregnancy test negative today
data_table.Medications: Combined oral contraceptive pill containing 30 micrograms of ethinyloestradiol

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Take endocervical and vaginal swabs for chlamydia and gonorrhoea before attributing the bleeding
options.rationale: The appearance describes columnar epithelium extended onto the outer cervix, which is a normal finding in a young woman on oestrogen containing contraception and bleeds easily on contact. It is a common but unreliable explanation for the symptom, so infection must be excluded first, and chlamydial cervicitis in a woman with a new partner produces exactly this pattern of bleeding with no discharge or pain. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexually transmitted infections)

options.text: Refer for colposcopy because contact bleeding requires exclusion of cervical malignancy
options.rationale: Colposcopy is indicated for an irregular, ulcerated or friable mass, for persistent bleeding after infection has been excluded and treated, or for an abnormal screening result. A negative human papillomavirus test two years ago makes significant cervical disease very unlikely, and a symmetrical circumferential appearance is not the pattern of malignancy. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines)

options.text: Reassure her that the appearance is benign and review her only if the bleeding persists
options.rationale: The appearance genuinely is benign and does not itself require treatment, which is why this answer is tempting. Accepting it as the cause without excluding infection is how chlamydia is missed in exactly the group most likely to have it and most likely to suffer tubal damage from it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexually transmitted infections)

options.text: Perform cervical screening today, since a test more than twelve months old is unreliable
options.rationale: Screening under the renewed program is five yearly after a negative result, so hers is not due and repeating it early does not change her management. A screening test is also not the right instrument for investigating a symptom, which is assessed on its own merits. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines)

options.text: Change to a pill containing 20 micrograms of ethinyloestradiol to settle the bleeding
options.rationale: Breakthrough bleeding in the first months of a new pill often settles, and changing the formulation is a reasonable step once other causes have been excluded. Reducing the oestrogen dose usually makes breakthrough bleeding worse rather than better, and it does nothing about an untreated infection. (Source: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Combined oral contraception)
source_refs: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Combined oral contraception

explanation.summary: A symmetrical ring of red velvety tissue around the external os is columnar epithelium sitting on the outer cervix, which is a normal variant common in young women, in pregnancy and on oestrogen containing contraception. It bleeds on contact and is therefore an appealing explanation for postcoital bleeding, but it is present in many women without symptoms, so it is a finding rather than a diagnosis. The important differential in a sexually active woman with a new partner is chlamydial or gonococcal cervicitis, which commonly causes intermenstrual and postcoital bleeding with no discharge and no pain. Swabs are taken before the bleeding is attributed to the appearance, and treatment with partner notification follows a positive result. Colposcopy is reserved for a suspicious lesion, an abnormal screening result, or persistent bleeding once infection has been excluded and treated.
key_points: Columnar epithelium on the outer cervix is a normal variant that bleeds on contact.
It is present in many asymptomatic women, so it is a finding rather than a diagnosis.
Chlamydial cervicitis commonly causes contact bleeding with no discharge or pain.
A negative human papillomavirus result makes significant cervical disease unlikely.
Persistent bleeding after infection is excluded and treated warrants colposcopy.
explanation.pearls: Never let a visible ectropion close the consultation in a woman under thirty with a new partner, because chlamydia causes the same contact bleeding, is usually silent otherwise, and the tubal damage it causes is what she presents with in ten years time.

sources.label: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Combined oral contraception

subtopic_detail: whether immunoglobulin is owed for first trimester bleeding with a viable intrauterine pregnancy
stem:
You are the resident in the early pregnancy assessment service seeing a 29 year old woman in her first pregnancy at 9 weeks and 2 days with two days of light red spotting that needed a liner but not a pad. The bleeding has now stopped.

She has mild lower abdominal cramping that she rates 2 out of 10, no shoulder tip pain, no dizziness and no passage of tissue. She has had no procedures in this pregnancy, no trauma and no abdominal injury. Her booking bloods show blood group O rhesus D negative with a negative antibody screen. Transvaginal ultrasound today shows a single intrauterine gestation with a crown rump length matching dates, cardiac activity present, and a small subchorionic haematoma. Her cervix is closed on speculum examination.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78/min, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft with mild suprapubic tenderness, cervical os closed, minimal old blood in the vault, no adnexal mass
data_table.Investigations: Blood group O rhesus D negative, antibody screen negative, haemoglobin 128 g/L (115-155), ultrasound viable intrauterine pregnancy with small subchorionic haematoma

lead_in: What should you do about her rhesus status?

options.text: Send a Kleihauer test and give immunoglobulin only if fetomaternal haemorrhage is shown
options.rationale: Quantifying fetomaternal haemorrhage guides the dose after a sensitising event from 20 weeks, such as abdominal trauma or antepartum haemorrhage. Before 12 weeks the fetal red cell volume is below the detection threshold of the test, so a negative result carries no reassurance and no decision rests on it. (Source: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh(D) immunoglobulin)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh(D) immunoglobulin

options.text: Give 250 IU of anti D immunoglobulin today because she has bled in this pregnancy
options.rationale: That dose is the correct one for a sensitising event before 12 weeks, and such events include ectopic pregnancy, molar pregnancy, termination, miscarriage with instrumentation and chorionic villus sampling. Threatened miscarriage with a viable intrauterine pregnancy at this gestation is specifically not on that list. (Source: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh(D) immunoglobulin)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh(D) immunoglobulin

options.text: Give 625 IU of anti D immunoglobulin today and repeat the antibody screen in six weeks
options.rationale: The larger dose belongs to sensitising events from 12 weeks onward, so it is both the wrong indication and the wrong dose here. Repeating the antibody screen shortly after giving immunoglobulin is also unhelpful because passively acquired anti D cannot be distinguished from immune anti D on a routine screen. (Source: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh(D) immunoglobulin)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh(D) immunoglobulin

options.text: Arrange cell free fetal DNA typing to establish the fetal rhesus group before deciding
options.rationale: Fetal blood group typing from maternal plasma is used in some settings to avoid unnecessary prophylaxis, but it is not part of routine Australian care and is not reliable this early in pregnancy. It would also delay a decision that does not need the information. (Source: Lifeblood: Anti D in pregnancy)

options.text: Give no immunoglobulin now and arrange the routine dose in the third trimester
options.rationale: Prophylaxis is not recommended for threatened miscarriage below 12 weeks where the pregnancy is intrauterine and viable, because the fetomaternal haemorrhage at this gestation is too small to sensitise and the fetal red cell mass is minimal. She remains on the routine pathway, which is a dose at 28 weeks and again at 34 weeks, plus a dose after birth if the baby is rhesus D positive. (Source: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh(D) immunoglobulin)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh(D) immunoglobulin

explanation.summary: Rhesus D immunoglobulin prevents maternal sensitisation by clearing fetal red cells before the immune system responds to them, so the indication depends on whether enough fetal red cells could plausibly have entered the maternal circulation. Before 12 weeks the fetal red cell mass is tiny, and threatened miscarriage with a viable intrauterine pregnancy is not considered a sensitising event in Australian guidance. Events before 12 weeks that do warrant the 250 IU dose are ectopic pregnancy, molar pregnancy, termination, miscarriage involving instrumentation and chorionic villus sampling. From 12 weeks the dose rises to 625 IU, and from 20 weeks a Kleihauer test is used to determine whether additional doses are needed. This woman continues on routine antenatal prophylaxis at 28 and 34 weeks with a postnatal dose if the baby types as rhesus D positive.
key_points: Threatened miscarriage below 12 weeks with a viable intrauterine pregnancy does not require prophylaxis.
Sensitising events before 12 weeks warrant 250 IU, and from 12 weeks 625 IU.
Ectopic and molar pregnancy, termination and chorionic villus sampling are sensitising at any gestation.
Kleihauer testing guides additional dosing only from 20 weeks.
Routine antenatal prophylaxis is given at 28 and 34 weeks with a postnatal dose if the baby is positive.
explanation.pearls: Anchor on 12 weeks and on whether the uterus was instrumented: bleeding alone before 12 weeks in a viable intrauterine pregnancy earns no immunoglobulin, but the same bleeding after a curette or a chorionic villus sample earns 250 IU within 72 hours.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh(D) immunoglobulin

subtopic_detail: counselling on mode of birth after a repaired anal sphincter injury in a woman with no continence symptoms
stem:
You are the registrar in the antenatal clinic seeing a 31 year old woman at 30 weeks in her second pregnancy. Her first birth was a forceps delivery with a third degree tear repaired in theatre by a consultant, and she asks whether she should have a caesarean this time.

She has no leakage of wind or stool, no urgency and no soiling, and she says her bowel control feels the same as it did before her first baby. She had physiotherapy for six months afterwards and completes pelvic floor exercises most days. Anorectal manometry and endoanal ultrasound arranged by the perineal clinic eighteen months ago were reported as normal. This pregnancy has been uncomplicated, the foetus is cephalic with growth on the 55th centile, and the estimated fetal weight is similar to her first baby.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Symphysis fundal height 30 cm, cephalic presentation, fetal heart rate 142/min, perineum well healed with no scarring tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Anorectal manometry and endoanal ultrasound normal eighteen months ago, growth scan estimated fetal weight on the 55th centile

lead_in: What would you advise her about mode of birth?

options.text: Support a planned vaginal birth, noting her normal symptoms and normal investigations
options.rationale: A woman who has no continence symptoms and normal anorectal testing after a repaired sphincter injury has a low risk of lasting deterioration and can be supported toward vaginal birth. The recurrence risk of a further sphincter injury is around five to seven per cent, which does not by itself justify abdominal surgery in an asymptomatic woman. (Source: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears

options.text: Recommend vaginal birth with a routine episiotomy performed to protect the sphincter
options.rationale: Routine episiotomy does not prevent sphincter injury and midline episiotomy increases it, so it is performed for a clinical indication rather than as a prophylactic measure. Perineal protection during crowning and a warm compress have better evidence. (Source: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears

options.text: Plan vaginal birth but avoid instrumental delivery by proceeding directly to caesarean
options.rationale: Forceps carries a higher risk of sphincter injury than vacuum, so the operator can reasonably prefer vacuum if instrumental birth becomes necessary. Committing in advance to abdominal delivery rather than an assisted vaginal birth removes a safe option and increases the overall operative rate. (Source: RANZCOG: Instrumental vaginal birth)

options.text: Repeat the anorectal manometry and endoanal ultrasound before making any recommendation
options.rationale: Repeat testing is worthwhile where symptoms have developed or where the earlier studies were equivocal, since the result would then change the recommendation. With normal studies and unchanged symptoms, repeating them delays the discussion without altering it. (Source: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears

options.text: Recommend an elective caesarean because any previous sphincter injury makes it safer
options.rationale: Caesarean is recommended for women who remain symptomatic or who have abnormal endoanal ultrasound or manometry, because a further vaginal birth can convert compensated function into frank incontinence. Applying it to every woman with a previous tear exposes a large number to operative risk for no measurable gain. (Source: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears

explanation.summary: The decision after a repaired anal sphincter injury turns on current function rather than on the fact of the previous tear. A woman with no incontinence, no urgency and normal endoanal ultrasound and manometry has adequate reserve, and the recurrence risk of about five to seven per cent does not outweigh the risks of planned abdominal delivery. Caesarean is recommended where symptoms persist or where testing shows a residual sphincter defect or low pressures, because a further vaginal birth can decompensate a sphincter that is only just coping. Routine episiotomy is not protective and midline episiotomy makes injury more likely, so intrapartum care focuses on controlled delivery of the head and perineal support. If an instrumental birth becomes necessary, vacuum carries a lower risk of sphincter injury than forceps.
key_points: Current continence and anorectal testing, not the previous tear itself, drive the recommendation.
Recurrence risk of sphincter injury is approximately five to seven per cent.
Persistent symptoms or an abnormal study shift the recommendation toward caesarean.
Routine episiotomy does not protect the sphincter and midline episiotomy increases injury.
Vacuum extraction carries a lower sphincter injury risk than forceps.
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically about leakage of flatus rather than of stool, because women rarely volunteer it and it is the symptom that most often identifies the compensated sphincter that will decompensate after a second vaginal birth.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears

subtopic_detail: setting the timing of birth in twins according to the chorionicity determined in the first trimester
stem:
You are the registrar seeing a 33 year old woman at 32 weeks in a twin pregnancy conceived after in vitro fertilisation with two embryos transferred. She asks when her babies will be born and whether she needs a caesarean.

The dating scan at 12 weeks showed two separate placental masses with a thick dividing membrane and a lambda sign at the base. Growth scans every four weeks have shown both twins tracking on the 40th and 50th centiles with normal umbilical artery Doppler studies and normal liquor volumes. Her blood pressure has been normal throughout, her oral glucose tolerance test was normal, and she has had no bleeding, contractions or ruptured membranes. Twin one is cephalic and twin two is transverse today.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88/min, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Uterus large for dates as expected, twin one cephalic, twin two transverse, no uterine tenderness or contractions
data_table.Investigations: Dating scan lambda sign with two placental masses, growth scans both twins on the 40th and 50th centiles, normal umbilical artery Doppler studies, haemoglobin 108 g/L (110-140)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan for timing of birth?

options.text: Plan birth at 37 to 38 weeks and decide the mode closer to the time
options.rationale: The lambda sign with two placental masses establishes a dichorionic pregnancy, which does not carry the vascular anastomoses responsible for the sudden losses seen in monochorionic twins, so birth is planned later than in those pregnancies. Beyond 38 weeks the stillbirth risk in dichorionic twins rises, and the presentation of the second twin at 32 weeks does not predict the presentation at birth. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic and dichorionic twin pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic and dichorionic twin pregnancy

options.text: Plan birth at 36 to 37 weeks because of the risk of unexpected loss in twin pregnancy
options.rationale: That earlier window applies to monochorionic diamniotic pregnancies, where shared placental circulation creates a risk of sudden intrauterine death that increases from the late third trimester. Applying it to a dichorionic pregnancy delivers a large number of babies early for a risk they do not carry. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic and dichorionic twin pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic and dichorionic twin pregnancy

options.text: Continue to 40 weeks with twice weekly monitoring as for any uncomplicated pregnancy
options.rationale: Twin pregnancies have a higher stillbirth rate than singletons at every gestation and that rate climbs steeply beyond 38 weeks, which is why expectant management to term plus is not offered. Surveillance does not reliably predict the losses that occur in this window. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic and dichorionic twin pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic and dichorionic twin pregnancy

options.text: Plan an elective caesarean at 34 weeks with corticosteroids because twin two is transverse
options.rationale: The presentation of the second twin at 32 weeks changes frequently and is determined at the time of birth, not now, so it cannot drive the timing. Birth at 34 weeks in an uncomplicated pregnancy imposes substantial prematurity for no indication. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic and dichorionic twin pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic and dichorionic twin pregnancy

options.text: Plan birth at 32 to 34 weeks given the low haemoglobin and the twin pregnancy
options.rationale: A haemoglobin of 108 g/L reflects the physiological dilution that is more pronounced in twins, and it is managed with iron studies and replacement rather than by delivery. It is not an indication for preterm birth in a woman with normal growth and Doppler studies. (Source: RANZCOG: Iron deficiency in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Chorionicity determined in the first trimester governs almost every subsequent decision in twin pregnancy, including the frequency of scans and the timing of birth. The lambda sign with two separate placental masses identifies a dichorionic pregnancy, in which each twin has its own placental circulation and the risks of twin to twin transfusion and sudden co twin demise do not apply. Uncomplicated dichorionic twins are therefore delivered at 37 to 38 weeks, while monochorionic diamniotic twins are delivered at 36 to 37 weeks and monoamniotic pregnancies considerably earlier. The rationale for not continuing past 38 weeks is the steep rise in stillbirth beyond that gestation rather than any problem in this pregnancy. Mode of birth is decided near term and vaginal birth remains appropriate when the first twin is cephalic, whatever the second twin is doing weeks beforehand.
key_points: The lambda sign with two placental masses indicates dichorionicity.
Uncomplicated dichorionic twins are delivered at 37 to 38 weeks.
Monochorionic diamniotic twins are delivered earlier, at 36 to 37 weeks.
Stillbirth risk in twins rises steeply beyond 38 weeks.
The presentation of the second twin is determined at birth, not in the third trimester.
explanation.pearls: Go back to the 12 week images before you quote any timing, because chorionicity cannot be assigned reliably in the third trimester and getting it wrong shifts the planned birth by a full week in either direction.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic and dichorionic twin pregnancy

subtopic_detail: choosing between uterine sparing procedures when future pregnancy is intended
stem:
You are the registrar in the gynaecology clinic seeing a 34 year old woman with two years of increasing pelvic pressure, urinary frequency and a sensation of fullness in her lower abdomen. She and her partner intend to start trying to conceive next year.

Her periods are regular and moderately heavy but her haemoglobin is normal. She has no postcoital or intermenstrual bleeding. Examination reveals a firm irregular mass arising from the pelvis reaching to just below the umbilicus. Transvaginal and abdominal ultrasound shows a 9 cm intramural fibroid on the anterior uterine wall indenting the bladder, with a normal endometrial cavity and normal ovaries. Her cervical screening is up to date and normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Firm irregular pelvic mass palpable to just below the umbilicus, mobile, non tender, cervix normal on speculum
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound 9 cm anterior intramural fibroid indenting the bladder, endometrial cavity normal, ovaries normal, haemoglobin 131 g/L (115-155)

lead_in: Which treatment should you recommend?

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging to exclude malignancy before any treatment is offered
options.rationale: Imaging is escalated where rapid growth after the menopause, unusual features or a suspicious ultrasound raise the possibility of a sarcoma, which is rare and cannot be excluded by imaging in any case. A typical fibroid on ultrasound in a woman of 34 does not warrant that pathway, though magnetic resonance imaging does have a role in mapping multiple fibroids before surgery. (Source: RANZCOG: Uterine fibroids)

options.text: Insert a levonorgestrel releasing intrauterine device to control her symptoms medically
options.rationale: The device reduces menstrual blood loss effectively and is a reasonable choice where heavy bleeding is the dominant problem and the cavity is normal. It does nothing for the pressure and urinary symptoms that bulk produces, and it is contraception she does not want. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Heavy menstrual bleeding)

options.text: Refer for uterine artery embolisation as a less invasive way to shrink the fibroid
options.rationale: Embolisation is effective for bleeding and bulk symptoms and avoids surgery, which makes it attractive for women who have completed their families. It is not recommended where pregnancy is planned because of concerns about ovarian reserve, placentation and miscarriage, and because outcome data in subsequent pregnancy remain limited. (Source: RANZCOG: Uterine fibroids)

options.text: Start a gonadotropin releasing hormone agonist for six months to shrink the fibroid
options.rationale: An agonist reduces fibroid volume and is used before surgery to correct anaemia or to make an operation more feasible, so it is an adjunct rather than a treatment. Fibroids regrow within months of stopping, and the induced hypo oestrogenic state causes bone loss and prevents conception. (Source: RANZCOG: Uterine fibroids)

options.text: Refer for myomectomy with counselling about uterine scar risks in a future labour
options.rationale: Surgical removal of the fibroid preserves the uterus and relieves pressure symptoms caused by bulk, which is what she has, and it remains the option with the best evidence when pregnancy is intended. She needs to know that a myomectomy entering the myometrium changes the plan for a future birth and that fibroids may recur. (Source: RANZCOG: Uterine fibroids)

explanation.summary: Fibroid treatment is chosen by matching the intervention to the dominant symptom and to the woman's reproductive intentions. Bulk symptoms such as pressure, frequency and abdominal distension respond to procedures that remove or shrink the fibroid, not to medical treatments aimed at bleeding. Because she intends to conceive next year, uterine artery embolisation is avoided, since its effects on ovarian reserve and placentation and its limited pregnancy outcome data make it unsuitable when fertility matters. Myomectomy preserves the uterus and relieves bulk symptoms, at the cost of a uterine scar that influences the mode of a future birth and a recurrence rate that rises over subsequent years. A gonadotropin releasing hormone agonist has a place before surgery rather than instead of it.
key_points: Match the treatment to the dominant symptom: bulk symptoms need volume reduction.
Embolisation is avoided where future pregnancy is intended.
Myomectomy preserves the uterus but creates a scar that affects future birth planning.
A gonadotropin releasing hormone agonist is a preoperative adjunct, not definitive treatment.
The intrauterine device treats bleeding but not pressure symptoms.
explanation.pearls: Ask what she wants fixed and when she wants to conceive before choosing anything, because the intrauterine device and embolisation both look attractive on paper and both are the wrong answer for a woman whose complaint is pressure and whose plan is pregnancy within the year.

subtopic_detail: the sequence of assessment after a first report of reduced movements in the third trimester
stem:
You are the midwife coordinator's registrar receiving a 26 year old woman at 32 weeks and 4 days in her first pregnancy who telephoned the assessment unit because her baby has been moving less since yesterday afternoon. She has come in immediately as advised.

She describes the movements as fewer and weaker rather than absent, and she has felt three movements in the past hour while sitting quietly. She has had no bleeding, no abdominal pain, no fluid loss and no itching. Her pregnancy has been uncomplicated, her blood pressure has been normal at every visit and her morphology scan was normal. She smokes three cigarettes a day. On abdominal palpation the uterus is soft and non tender, the presentation is cephalic, and the symphysis fundal height measures 29 cm having been 30 cm two weeks ago.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 82/min, blood pressure 114/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C, fetal heart rate 145/min on auscultation
data_table.Examination: Uterus soft and non tender, cephalic presentation, symphysis fundal height 29 cm at 32 weeks and 4 days, no vaginal loss on inspection
data_table.Investigations: None performed since arrival

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give corticosteroids and admit her for continuous monitoring until the movements return
options.rationale: Corticosteroids are given when preterm birth within seven days is anticipated, which is a decision that follows the assessment rather than preceding it. Continuous monitoring at 32 weeks without an abnormal finding commits her to admission without adding information. (Source: RANZCOG: Antenatal corticosteroids)

options.text: Ask her to drink cold water, lie on her side and count movements for two hours
options.rationale: Formal movement counting protocols have not been shown to reduce stillbirth and they delay objective assessment in a woman who has already recognised a change and presented. Any manoeuvre intended to provoke movement is a substitute for the assessment rather than part of it. (Source: RANZCOG: Decreased fetal movements in the second half of pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Decreased fetal movements in the second half of pregnancy

options.text: Arrange a biophysical profile as the single assessment and omit the cardiotocograph
options.rationale: The biophysical profile includes cardiotocography as one of its components and adds ultrasound measures of tone, movement, breathing and liquor. It takes longer to organise and does not outperform the combination of an immediate trace with a growth and Doppler assessment in this setting. (Source: RANZCOG: Decreased fetal movements in the second half of pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Decreased fetal movements in the second half of pregnancy

options.text: Perform cardiotocography and discharge her home if the trace is normal with advice
options.rationale: A normal cardiotocograph reflects fetal wellbeing at that moment and is reassuring in the short term, which is why it is done first. It does not detect growth restriction, so discharging on the trace alone misses the pathology that reduced movements most often signal, particularly when the fundal height has fallen. (Source: RANZCOG: Decreased fetal movements in the second half of pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Decreased fetal movements in the second half of pregnancy

options.text: Perform cardiotocography now and arrange a growth scan with umbilical artery Doppler
options.rationale: Reduced movements are associated with growth restriction and placental insufficiency, so assessment has two parts: immediate assessment of fetal wellbeing by cardiotocography, and assessment of growth and placental function by ultrasound. Her fundal height has fallen behind and she smokes, both of which raise the pretest probability of a small or compromised foetus, so the scan is arranged rather than considered. (Source: RANZCOG: Decreased fetal movements in the second half of pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Decreased fetal movements in the second half of pregnancy

explanation.summary: Reduced fetal movement is a symptom rather than a diagnosis, and its importance lies in its association with growth restriction, placental insufficiency and subsequent stillbirth. Assessment therefore has two components that answer different questions: cardiotocography tells you how the foetus is now, and ultrasound for growth, liquor volume and umbilical artery Doppler tells you whether the placenta is failing. A normal trace is common in a foetus that is nonetheless growth restricted, so it cannot be used alone to close the episode. This woman has two additional risk factors, a fundal height that has fallen behind and ongoing smoking, which make the scan more important rather than less. Provoking movements with cold drinks or position change has no evidence base and delays assessment.
key_points: Reduced movements are associated with growth restriction and placental insufficiency.
Cardiotocography assesses current wellbeing and cannot detect growth restriction.
Ultrasound for growth, liquor and umbilical artery Doppler answers the placental question.
Symphysis fundal height falling behind or static is an indication for a growth scan.
Formal movement counting protocols have not been shown to reduce stillbirth.
explanation.pearls: Plot the fundal height against the previous measurement before deciding anything, because a static or falling height alongside reduced movements is the combination most likely to precede stillbirth and it converts a reassuring trace into an indication for a scan the same day.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Decreased fetal movements in the second half of pregnancy

subtopic_detail: contraceptive choice when the reliability of an oral method is compromised by altered gut anatomy
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 31 year old woman eight weeks after a Roux en Y gastric bypass. She has lost 14 kg and wants contraception, having been told by the surgical team to avoid pregnancy for the first eighteen months while her weight is changing rapidly.

She has two children, both born vaginally, and does not want more for at least three years. Her periods are regular and not heavy. She has no history of venous thromboembolism, no migraine of any kind, and she does not smoke. Her blood pressure today is 118/74 mmHg and her current body mass index is 38. She asks whether she can simply restart the combined pill she used before the operation, since she got on well with it.

data_table.Vital signs: Blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, pulse rate 72/min, other observations within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 38, abdominal wounds healed, no calf tenderness or swelling, no goitre
data_table.Investigations: Pregnancy test negative, haemoglobin 124 g/L (115-155), full blood count otherwise normal
data_table.Medications: Colecalciferol, a multivitamin and oral iron as prescribed after surgery

lead_in: What contraception should you recommend?

options.text: Condoms alone, since hormonal methods are less effective at a body mass index of 38
options.rationale: Body weight does reduce the effectiveness of emergency contraception with levonorgestrel and of the contraceptive patch, so weight is a genuine consideration in method choice. Condoms have a typical use failure rate around thirteen per cent a year, which is not acceptable for a woman advised that pregnancy would be unsafe for eighteen months. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of obesity in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of obesity in pregnancy

options.text: Restart the combined oral contraceptive pill she used successfully before the operation
options.rationale: It worked for her previously and her cardiovascular risk profile is otherwise unremarkable, which is why she is asking. The malabsorptive anatomy makes the oral route unreliable now, and the early postoperative period after a major abdominal operation is also the time of highest venous thromboembolism risk. (Source: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception after bariatric surgery)
source_refs: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception after bariatric surgery

options.text: An intrauterine device or the contraceptive implant, avoiding oral methods altogether
options.rationale: A bypass procedure shortens the absorptive surface and speeds transit, so the absorption of any oral contraceptive becomes unreliable and failure rates rise. A device or an implant bypasses the gut entirely, gives several years of cover for a woman who must avoid pregnancy for eighteen months, and does not depend on the weight loss and dietary changes still under way. (Source: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception after bariatric surgery)
source_refs: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception after bariatric surgery

options.text: The contraceptive vaginal ring, changed monthly, as an effective non oral hormonal option
options.rationale: The ring does bypass the gut and is a legitimate non oral option from an absorption point of view, so the reasoning is half right. It still delivers systemic oestrogen soon after major abdominal surgery, and it requires correct use every month rather than providing years of cover. (Source: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception after bariatric surgery)
source_refs: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception after bariatric surgery

options.text: A progestogen only pill taken at the same time each day with a written reminder
options.rationale: Moving from combined to progestogen only correctly removes the oestrogen and the associated thrombotic concern. It does not solve the problem, because absorption of the progestogen is affected by the same altered anatomy and this method already has the narrowest margin for a missed or delayed dose. (Source: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception after bariatric surgery)
source_refs: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception after bariatric surgery

explanation.summary: Bariatric procedures divide into restrictive operations such as sleeve gastrectomy, where oral absorption is largely preserved, and malabsorptive or combined procedures such as Roux en Y gastric bypass, where the shortened absorptive surface and accelerated transit make oral medicine absorption unreliable. After a bypass, oral contraceptives of any kind are avoided and a non oral method is recommended. Long acting reversible methods suit this situation particularly well because pregnancy must be avoided through a prolonged period of rapid weight change, during which nutritional deficiencies and poor fetal growth are the concern. The early postoperative months also carry an elevated venous thromboembolism risk, which is a further reason to avoid an oestrogen containing method at this point. Women who conceive after weight loss surgery need close nutritional monitoring in pregnancy.
key_points: Malabsorptive procedures make absorption of any oral contraceptive unreliable.
Restrictive procedures such as sleeve gastrectomy largely preserve oral absorption.
Long acting reversible methods bypass the gut and cover the whole period of weight change.
The early postoperative period carries elevated venous thromboembolism risk.
Pregnancy is generally avoided for twelve to eighteen months after surgery.
explanation.pearls: Ask which operation she had before choosing a method, because a sleeve gastrectomy leaves oral contraception perfectly viable while a bypass does not, and the two are routinely described by patients in the same words as weight loss surgery.

sources.label: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception after bariatric surgery
RANZCOG: Management of obesity in pregnancy

subtopic_detail: prepregnancy planning where the supplement dose and the medicine itself both need to change
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 26 year old woman who has been seizure free for three years on sodium valproate 800 mg twice daily for generalised epilepsy. She has stopped her contraceptive pill and says she and her husband want to start trying to conceive in the next couple of months.

She takes no other medication and has no other medical problems. She has read online that women planning pregnancy should take folic acid and has bought a supermarket multivitamin containing 500 micrograms of folic acid. She is otherwise well, her weight is stable with a body mass index of 24, and she has no family history of neural tube defects. She has not yet seen her neurologist about the pregnancy plan.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 24, neurological examination normal, no rash or gum hypertrophy
data_table.Investigations: None performed
data_table.Medications: Sodium valproate 800 mg twice daily, multivitamin containing folic acid 500 micrograms daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice at this visit?

options.text: Continue the current dose because three years seizure free makes a change too risky
options.rationale: Good seizure control is a genuine consideration and no change is made without a neurologist weighing it, which is why the referral is urgent rather than optional. Accepting a one in ten malformation risk without even attempting a switch is not a defensible position when effective alternatives exist. (Source: RANZCOG: Epilepsy in pregnancy)

options.text: Stop the valproate today and recheck her in four weeks to confirm she remains well
options.rationale: Abrupt withdrawal risks status epilepticus, and an uncontrolled generalised seizure in pregnancy threatens both the woman and the foetus through hypoxia and trauma. Any change is made gradually under specialist supervision with an alternative established first. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Antiepileptics)

options.text: Advise continuing contraception and arrange urgent neurology review to change her medicine
options.rationale: Valproate carries roughly a one in ten risk of major congenital malformation and a much higher risk of impaired neurodevelopment, and both are dose related, so the priority is a planned switch to a safer agent before conception rather than after. Contraception continues during the switch because the transition takes months and an unplanned pregnancy in the interim exposes the foetus to the highest risk period. (Source: RANZCOG: Epilepsy in pregnancy)

options.text: Refer for detailed fetal morphology imaging once she conceives and change nothing now
options.rationale: Detailed imaging at 18 to 20 weeks does detect many structural malformations and will form part of her care in pregnancy. It is surveillance rather than prevention, and it cannot detect the neurodevelopmental harm that is the larger part of the risk from this drug. (Source: RANZCOG: Epilepsy in pregnancy)

options.text: Increase her folic acid to 5 mg daily and tell her she can start trying immediately
options.rationale: The higher folate dose is correct for a woman taking an antiseizure medicine and should be started at least one month before conception. It reduces neural tube defect risk but does not protect against the other malformations or the neurodevelopmental effects of valproate, so starting it while leaving the drug unchanged addresses only part of the problem. (Source: RANZCOG: Epilepsy in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Valproate is the antiseizure medicine with the highest teratogenic risk, causing major congenital malformation in around one in ten exposed pregnancies and impaired neurodevelopment in a substantially larger proportion, with both effects rising with dose. Because organogenesis is largely complete before many women realise they are pregnant, the change must happen before conception, which means the referral is urgent and contraception continues until an alternative is established. Women taking any antiseizure medicine also need high dose folic acid of 5 mg daily started at least a month before conception, but folate does not mitigate the non neural tube effects of valproate. Abrupt cessation is dangerous because a generalised seizure carries its own risk of fetal hypoxia and maternal injury. Detailed morphology imaging remains part of antenatal care but detects rather than prevents harm.
key_points: Valproate causes major malformation in about one in ten exposed pregnancies.
Neurodevelopmental effects are dose related and are not prevented by folate.
Women on any antiseizure medicine take folic acid 5 mg daily from before conception.
Contraception continues until an alternative medicine is established.
Abrupt withdrawal risks status epilepticus and fetal hypoxia.
explanation.pearls: Do not let the folate conversation substitute for the drug conversation: 5 mg of folic acid lowers neural tube defect risk but does nothing about the neurodevelopmental harm from valproate, which is the larger risk and the reason the neurologist needs to see her before she conceives.

subtopic_detail: which investigations to order first when a couple has been trying for a year with regular cycles
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a couple who have been having regular unprotected intercourse for fourteen months without conceiving. She is 29, he is 31, and neither has children.

Her cycles are regular at 29 days with three days of moderate bleeding, no severe period pain and no pain with intercourse. She has never had pelvic inflammatory disease, abdominal surgery or an abnormal cervical screening result, and her body mass index is 23. He has no history of mumps orchitis, testicular surgery, undescended testis or chemotherapy, and he does not use anabolic steroids. Neither smokes. Her rubella serology from a previous visit shows immunity and she has been taking folic acid for three months.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 23, normal secondary sexual characteristics, no hirsutism, abdominal and pelvic examination unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: Rubella immune, cervical screening normal twelve months ago, no fertility investigations performed

lead_in: Which investigations should you arrange first?

options.text: Diagnostic laparoscopy with dye studies to assess tubal patency and pelvic disease
options.rationale: Laparoscopy directly visualises endometriosis and adhesions and is the right investigation where there is pelvic pain, painful intercourse or a suspicious history. As a first line test in a woman with no symptoms and no risk factors it exposes her to a general anaesthetic ahead of the non invasive assessments. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of infertility)

options.text: Semen analysis for him and a mid luteal progesterone for her with chlamydia testing
options.rationale: A male factor contributes in around half of couples and semen analysis is inexpensive, non invasive and abnormal often enough that it belongs in the first round for every couple. A mid luteal progesterone confirms that her regular cycles are genuinely ovulatory, and testing for chlamydia matters because previous asymptomatic infection is a common and treatable cause of tubal damage. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexually transmitted infections)

options.text: Advise timed intercourse with ovulation prediction kits and review again in six months
options.rationale: Advice about the fertile window is useful for couples who are mistiming intercourse, and reviewing frequency of intercourse is part of the history. Fourteen months of regular unprotected intercourse already meets the definition of infertility, so investigation is indicated now rather than after a further delay. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of infertility)

options.text: Anti Mullerian hormone with a day 3 follicle stimulating hormone and oestradiol for her
options.rationale: Ovarian reserve testing predicts the response to ovarian stimulation and is therefore useful once assisted reproduction is being planned. It is a poor predictor of natural conception in a woman of 29 with regular cycles and does not explain why this couple has not conceived. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of infertility)

options.text: Hysterosalpingogram now and referral to a fertility specialist for a treatment cycle
options.rationale: Tubal patency assessment is an important part of the workup and follows once ovulation and semen quality are known, since an abnormal semen analysis changes the whole pathway. Referring for treatment before any test has been done skips the step that determines which treatment is appropriate. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of infertility)

explanation.summary: Infertility is defined as failure to conceive after twelve months of regular unprotected intercourse, so this couple qualifies and investigation should begin rather than be deferred. The first round of tests addresses the three commonest causes in parallel: male factor, ovulatory dysfunction and tubal disease. Semen analysis is the single highest yield test because male factor contributes in about half of couples and the result changes the entire subsequent pathway. A mid luteal progesterone taken seven days before the expected period confirms ovulation even when cycles look regular, and chlamydia testing identifies a treatable and frequently asymptomatic cause of tubal damage. Ovarian reserve testing, hysterosalpingography and laparoscopy each have a place but follow this first round rather than preceding it.
key_points: Infertility is defined at twelve months of regular unprotected intercourse.
Male factor contributes in about half of couples, so semen analysis comes first.
Mid luteal progesterone is taken seven days before the expected period.
Regular cycles do not guarantee ovulation and are confirmed biochemically.
Ovarian reserve testing predicts stimulation response rather than natural conception.
explanation.pearls: Investigate both partners at the same visit rather than working through her first, because half of these couples have a male factor and a delayed semen analysis is the commonest reason a workup takes a year instead of a month.

subtopic_detail: the headache feature that makes combined hormonal contraception unacceptable rather than merely cautious
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 24 year old woman who wants to start the combined oral contraceptive pill because her friend found it helped her skin. She has no children and does not want to conceive for several years.

She describes headaches about once a month, each preceded for twenty minutes by a shimmering zigzag in her right visual field, followed by a throbbing left sided headache with nausea and light sensitivity lasting most of a day. The visual disturbance resolves completely before the headache begins. She does not smoke, her blood pressure today is 112/70 mmHg, and her body mass index is 22. She has no personal or family history of venous thromboembolism or stroke, and she takes no regular medication.

data_table.Vital signs: Blood pressure 112/70 mmHg, pulse rate 68/min, other observations within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 22, neurological examination normal between episodes, visual fields full to confrontation, fundoscopy normal
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What contraception should you recommend?

options.text: A progestogen only method such as the implant, the intrauterine device or the pill
options.rationale: Focal neurological symptoms preceding a headache and resolving before it starts identify migraine with aura, which raises ischaemic stroke risk, and combined hormonal contraception multiplies that risk further, so it is unacceptable regardless of age or other risk factors. Progestogen only methods carry no such stroke association and are unrestricted in these women, which leaves her the full range of long acting and oral options. (Source: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception and migraine)
source_refs: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception and migraine

options.text: A low dose combined pill containing 20 micrograms of ethinyloestradiol with monitoring
options.rationale: Lowering the oestrogen dose reduces venous thromboembolism risk but does not remove the arterial risk that matters here, and no dose of oestrogen is considered acceptable alongside aura. Monitoring cannot detect an impending stroke. (Source: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception and migraine)
source_refs: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception and migraine

options.text: A combined pill taken continuously, since her headaches occur in the hormone free week
options.rationale: Continuous regimens genuinely reduce the oestrogen withdrawal headaches that occur in the hormone free interval, which is useful for migraine without aura. That strategy does not apply to a woman who should not be taking oestrogen at all, and her headaches currently occur without any hormonal cycling. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Migraine)

options.text: Copper intrauterine device only, because hormonal contraception is unsafe in migraine
options.rationale: The copper device is a perfectly reasonable option for her and carries no hormonal risk at all. Restricting her to it alone misstates the evidence, because it is oestrogen rather than hormonal contraception in general that is contraindicated, and it may worsen the heavy bleeding some women experience. (Source: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception and migraine)
source_refs: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception and migraine

options.text: A combined vaginal ring, since non oral delivery avoids the first pass hepatic effect
options.rationale: Route of administration changes hepatic exposure and some metabolic effects, but the systemic oestrogen and the arterial risk remain, so the ring and the patch are restricted in exactly the same way as the pill. The contraindication follows the hormone rather than the delivery method. (Source: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception and migraine)
source_refs: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception and migraine

explanation.summary: Aura is defined by fully reversible focal neurological symptoms that develop over several minutes and precede or accompany the headache, most often visual and most often described as zigzag lines or a shimmering scotoma. Its importance in contraceptive prescribing is that migraine with aura roughly doubles ischaemic stroke risk, and combined hormonal contraception multiplies that risk further, so oestrogen containing methods are unacceptable at any age and any dose. The restriction applies to the pill, the patch and the ring equally, because it follows the systemic oestrogen rather than the route. Progestogen only methods and the copper intrauterine device carry no such association and are all available to her. Migraine without aura is treated differently and combined contraception can usually be used with review.
key_points: Aura consists of fully reversible focal symptoms developing over minutes before the headache.
Migraine with aura roughly doubles ischaemic stroke risk.
Combined hormonal contraception is unacceptable with aura at any oestrogen dose.
The restriction applies equally to the pill, the patch and the ring.
Progestogen only methods and the copper device carry no arterial risk restriction.
explanation.pearls: Ask whether the visual symptom comes before the headache and goes away completely, because photophobia and blurred vision during a migraine are not aura, while twenty minutes of zigzag lines beforehand rules out every oestrogen containing method she might ask for.

sources.label: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception and migraine

subtopic_detail: whether laparoscopy is needed before treating cyclical pelvic pain with a typical history
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 24 year old woman with four years of pelvic pain that begins two days before each period, continues through the heaviest days, and has recently started to occur with deep penetration during intercourse. She misses one or two days of work most months.

Ibuprofen taken when the pain is already severe helps a little. She has never been pregnant, does not want to conceive for at least four years and currently uses condoms. There is no bleeding between periods, no bowel or bladder symptoms, and no fevers or weight loss. Her mother had a hysterectomy in her thirties for pelvic pain. Examination shows a mobile anteverted uterus with mild tenderness in the posterior fornix and no palpable mass or nodularity. Pelvic ultrasound reports normal ovaries with no endometrioma.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Anteverted mobile uterus, mild posterior fornix tenderness, no adnexal mass, no palpable nodularity, speculum examination normal
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound normal ovaries with no endometrioma, chlamydia nucleic acid test negative, full blood count normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first treatment?

options.text: A gonadotropin releasing hormone agonist with add back hormone therapy for six months
options.rationale: Agonist treatment is effective and is used when first line hormonal treatment has failed or is not tolerated, with add back therapy to limit bone loss and vasomotor symptoms. Starting with it in a woman who has not yet tried simpler options exposes her to those adverse effects unnecessarily. (Source: RANZCOG: Australian clinical practice guideline for the diagnosis and management of endometriosis)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Australian clinical practice guideline for the diagnosis and management of endometriosis

options.text: Refer to a pelvic pain physiotherapist and a psychologist as the initial management plan
options.rationale: Pelvic floor physiotherapy and pain psychology are genuinely valuable in persistent pelvic pain and belong in the longer term plan, particularly where central sensitisation has developed. Offering them instead of hormonal suppression at the first visit withholds the treatment that addresses the cyclical mechanism driving her pain. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endometriosis)

options.text: Diagnostic laparoscopy with excision of any lesions before starting medical treatment
options.rationale: Laparoscopy establishes the diagnosis histologically and treats lesions at the same time, and it is appropriate where medical treatment has failed, where fertility is an immediate concern or where deep disease is suspected. Requiring it before any treatment delays relief by months and exposes a young woman to surgery she may never need. (Source: RANZCOG: Australian clinical practice guideline for the diagnosis and management of endometriosis)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Australian clinical practice guideline for the diagnosis and management of endometriosis

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis to stage the disease before choosing treatment
options.rationale: Imaging is valuable for mapping deep infiltrating disease and endometrioma before surgery, and transvaginal ultrasound by an experienced operator detects much of this. Superficial peritoneal disease is invisible on all imaging, so a normal scan neither excludes the condition nor changes the first line medical plan. (Source: RANZCOG: Australian clinical practice guideline for the diagnosis and management of endometriosis)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Australian clinical practice guideline for the diagnosis and management of endometriosis

options.text: Continuous combined hormonal contraception with a regular anti inflammatory before pain starts
options.rationale: Suppressing ovulation and menstruation treats the cyclical pain of this condition and is offered on the clinical picture without waiting for surgical confirmation, since laparoscopy is no longer required to begin treatment. Taking the anti inflammatory regularly from before the pain begins works far better than taking it once the pain is established, and she also gains the contraception she currently lacks. (Source: RANZCOG: Australian clinical practice guideline for the diagnosis and management of endometriosis)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Australian clinical practice guideline for the diagnosis and management of endometriosis

explanation.summary: Cyclical pelvic pain beginning before the period, continuing through it and accompanied by deep pain during intercourse is a typical history for endometriosis, and a normal ultrasound does not argue against it because superficial peritoneal disease cannot be seen on any imaging. Australian guidance has moved away from requiring laparoscopic confirmation before treatment, so medical management is started on the clinical picture and the diagnosis is supported by the response. Continuous combined hormonal contraception suppresses ovulation and menstruation and addresses the cyclical mechanism, and it suits a woman who also needs contraception. Anti inflammatories work best taken regularly from before the pain begins rather than as rescue once it is established. Surgery, agonist therapy and multidisciplinary pain management all remain available if this approach fails or if fertility becomes the presenting issue.
key_points: A normal pelvic ultrasound does not exclude superficial peritoneal disease.
Treatment is started on the clinical picture without requiring laparoscopic confirmation.
Continuous hormonal suppression targets the cyclical mechanism of the pain.
Anti inflammatories are most effective taken regularly from before the pain starts.
Agonist therapy with add back is reserved for failure of first line hormonal treatment.
explanation.pearls: Tell her to start the anti inflammatory the day before her period is due rather than when the pain arrives, because prostaglandin release has already happened by the time she reaches for the tablet and that single change in timing often doubles the benefit she gets from it.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Australian clinical practice guideline for the diagnosis and management of endometriosis

subtopic_detail: explaining what a high chance result on a maternal plasma screening test does and does not establish
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 39 year old woman at 10 weeks in her third pregnancy who asks for the blood test that checks the baby's chromosomes. She says a friend had it and was told everything was fine, and she wants to avoid the needle in the abdomen that her sister had.

She has two healthy children born at term, no family history of chromosomal or genetic conditions, and no consanguinity. She takes folic acid and no other medication. Her dating scan yesterday showed a single viable intrauterine pregnancy at 10 weeks and 1 day with a normal appearance. She has private health insurance and asks whether the test is covered by Medicare.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Uterus not palpable abdominally, no abnormality on general examination
data_table.Investigations: Dating ultrasound single viable intrauterine pregnancy at 10 weeks and 1 day, booking bloods unremarkable

lead_in: What is the most important point to cover when counselling her?

options.text: Her age of 39 makes the test mandatory before any further antenatal care proceeds
options.rationale: Advancing maternal age does raise the chance of trisomy and makes the offer of screening more relevant, so the discussion is appropriate. All prenatal screening is voluntary and declining it is a legitimate choice that does not affect the rest of her care. (Source: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing for fetal chromosomal and genetic conditions)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing for fetal chromosomal and genetic conditions

options.text: A low chance result excludes chromosomal and genetic conditions in this pregnancy
options.rationale: Detection is very high for trisomy 21 and good for trisomies 18 and 13, which is why a low chance result is genuinely reassuring for those conditions. It says nothing about the many single gene disorders, microdeletions and structural anomalies that the test does not examine. (Source: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing for fetal chromosomal and genetic conditions)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing for fetal chromosomal and genetic conditions

options.text: The test replaces the need for the nuchal translucency and morphology ultrasounds
options.rationale: Screening for chromosomal conditions from maternal plasma does not assess fetal structure, and ultrasound remains necessary to detect structural anomalies, to confirm dating and viability and to assess the placenta. The first trimester scan also identifies findings such as a markedly increased nuchal translucency that carry their own implications. (Source: Australian Government Department of Health: Antenatal care clinical practice guidelines)
source_refs: Australian Government Department of Health: Antenatal care clinical practice guidelines

options.text: A high chance result estimates risk and needs a diagnostic test to confirm it
options.rationale: The test analyses placental DNA circulating in maternal plasma and returns a probability rather than a diagnosis, so a high chance result must be confirmed by chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis before any irreversible decision is made.
