Confined placental mosaicism, a vanishing twin and maternal chromosomal variation all produce results that do not reflect the fetal karyotype. (Source: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing for fetal chromosomal and genetic conditions)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing for fetal chromosomal and genetic conditions

options.text: The test is rebated through Medicare for all women aged 35 years and over
options.rationale: Cost matters to families and should be discussed, because this test is paid for privately in Australia and the amount is not trivial. There is no age based rebate, and getting this wrong sends women away expecting a refund that will not come. (Source: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing for fetal chromosomal and genetic conditions)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing for fetal chromosomal and genetic conditions

explanation.summary: Screening of cell free DNA in maternal plasma analyses fragments derived from the placenta, which usually but not always reflect the fetal karyotype. It performs very well for trisomy 21 and reasonably for trisomies 18 and 13, but it returns a probability rather than a diagnosis, and the positive predictive value falls considerably for rarer conditions and in younger women. Confined placental mosaicism, a vanishing twin, maternal mosaicism and maternal malignancy all generate results that do not reflect the foetus, which is why chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis is required before any irreversible decision. The test does not assess fetal structure, so the first trimester and morphology ultrasounds remain part of care. It is not rebated by Medicare in Australia and all prenatal screening is voluntary.
key_points: The test analyses placental DNA and returns a probability, not a diagnosis.
A high chance result requires chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis to confirm.
Confined placental mosaicism and a vanishing twin are recognised causes of discordant results.
The test does not assess fetal structure and does not replace ultrasound.
It is not rebated by Medicare and all prenatal screening is voluntary.
explanation.pearls: Say the words screening test and diagnostic test explicitly in the consultation and write them down, because women commonly leave believing they have had the baby's chromosomes checked, and that misunderstanding is what drives decisions made on an unconfirmed high chance result.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing for fetal chromosomal and genetic conditions
Australian Government Department of Health: Antenatal care clinical practice guidelines

subtopic_detail: Timing of birth for intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy when the bile acid level exceeds one hundred micromol per litre
stem:
A 31 year old woman at 33 weeks in her first pregnancy attends your antenatal clinic with three weeks of itching, worst on her palms and the soles of her feet and worse at night. She has no rash apart from scratch marks.

Her pregnancy has otherwise been uncomplicated with normal growth on serial scans and normal blood pressure throughout. Her urine shows no protein. A viral hepatitis screen and liver autoantibodies are negative, and a liver ultrasound shows no biliary dilatation or gallstones. Her fasting bile acid level today is 128 micromol/L, having been 46 micromol/L two weeks ago.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 84/min, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C, fetal heart rate 142/min
data_table.Investigations: Bile acids 128 micromol/L (<10), alanine aminotransferase 96 U/L (<35), bilirubin 12 micromol/L (<20), platelets 245 x10^9/L (150-400)
data_table.Imaging: Liver ultrasound shows no biliary dilatation and no gallstones, fetal growth on the 45th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan for timing of birth?

options.text: Plan birth at 35 to 36 weeks after a course of antenatal corticosteroids
options.rationale: Stillbirth risk rises steeply once bile acids exceed 100 micromol/L, and this threshold defines the group in whom earlier planned birth is justified. Corticosteroids are given because birth at this gestation carries neonatal respiratory risk. (Source: RANZCOG: Obstetric cholestasis)

options.text: Plan birth at 38 to 39 weeks with weekly bile acid monitoring until then
options.rationale: This timing suits women whose bile acids remain below 40 micromol/L, where the excess stillbirth risk is not clearly increased. It underestimates the risk carried by a level above 100 micromol/L. (Source: RANZCOG: Obstetric cholestasis)

options.text: Plan birth at 37 weeks with twice weekly cardiotocography until then
options.rationale: Cardiotocography does not predict the sudden stillbirth associated with this condition, so surveillance cannot substitute for earlier birth. The timing also does not reflect the severity band she now occupies. (Source: RANZCOG: Obstetric cholestasis)

options.text: Plan birth at 40 weeks and treat the itch with ursodeoxycholic acid until then
options.rationale: Ursodeoxycholic acid improves itch and biochemistry but has not been shown to reduce stillbirth, so it cannot justify expectant management to term. Treating the symptom does not address the risk. (Source: RANZCOG: Obstetric cholestasis)

options.text: Arrange birth within the next 24 hours by induction regardless of cervical status
options.rationale: Birth at 33 weeks would expose the baby to substantial prematurity risk that outweighs the stillbirth risk at this gestation. Immediate birth is reserved for other deteriorating features such as jaundice with coagulopathy. (Source: RANZCOG: Obstetric cholestasis)

explanation.summary: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy is diagnosed by pruritus without a primary rash together with raised bile acids, after excluding other liver disease. Its significance is almost entirely fetal, and the pivotal insight from large cohort data is that risk is not uniform across the diagnosis but is concentrated in women with severe biochemical disease. Peak bile acid concentration stratifies that risk, with levels below 40 micromol/L carrying little excess stillbirth risk and levels of 100 micromol/L or above carrying a markedly elevated risk that justifies planned late preterm birth. Because the stillbirth is typically sudden rather than preceded by growth restriction or abnormal Dopplers, antenatal surveillance offers false reassurance and timing of birth is the only intervention shown to matter.
key_points: Diagnosis requires pruritus with raised bile acids and exclusion of other liver disease
Peak bile acid concentration stratifies stillbirth risk within the diagnosis
Levels of 100 micromol/L or above justify planned birth at 35 to 36 weeks
Cardiotocography and Doppler do not predict the sudden stillbirth
Ursodeoxycholic acid improves itch and biochemistry but not stillbirth risk
explanation.pearls: The 100 micromol/L bile acid threshold is the single number that changes management in cholestasis of pregnancy, moving planned birth from around 38 weeks to 35 to 36 weeks with corticosteroid cover.

subtopic_detail: Anti-D requirement for a woman with a rhesus negative blood group and light bleeding at ten weeks with a closed cervix
stem:
A 27 year old woman in her second pregnancy attends your early pregnancy assessment unit at 10 weeks with two days of light vaginal bleeding, described as spotting that does not fill a pad. She has mild period like cramping that settles with paracetamol.

Her first pregnancy ended in a normal vaginal birth three years ago and she received anti-D immunoglobulin after that birth. Speculum examination shows a closed cervical os with a small amount of old blood in the vagina, and no products are visible. Ultrasound today confirms a single intrauterine pregnancy with a fetal heart rate of 164/min and a crown rump length consistent with dates. Her blood group is confirmed as O negative and her antibody screen is negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Closed cervical os, small amount of old blood in the vagina, no products of conception visible, uterus non-tender
data_table.Investigations: Blood group O negative, antibody screen negative, haemoglobin 128 g/L (115-155)
data_table.Imaging: Single intrauterine pregnancy, fetal heart rate 164/min, crown rump length consistent with 10 weeks

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her rhesus status?

options.text: Give 250 IU of anti-D immunoglobulin now and repeat the dose if bleeding continues
options.rationale: Giving anti-D for a threatened miscarriage at this gestation exposes her to a blood product without evidence of benefit. The 250 IU dose is correct for first trimester sensitising events, but this is not one. (Source: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh D immunoglobulin)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh D immunoglobulin

options.text: Withhold anti-D immunoglobulin and manage expectantly with review if bleeding worsens
options.rationale: Anti-D is not required for threatened miscarriage before 12 weeks where the pregnancy remains viable and there has been no instrumentation, because the foeto-maternal transfusion volume is negligible. Routine prophylaxis will still be given in the third trimester. (Source: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh D immunoglobulin)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh D immunoglobulin

options.text: Give 625 IU of anti-D immunoglobulin now and arrange a Kleihauer test the same day
options.rationale: The larger dose and quantification of foeto-maternal haemorrhage apply to sensitising events after 12 weeks, not to first trimester bleeding. Both the dose and the test are mismatched to the gestation. (Source: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh D immunoglobulin)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh D immunoglobulin

options.text: Arrange non-invasive fetal rhesus genotyping now and give anti-D only if the result is positive
options.rationale: Fetal genotyping from maternal blood is not part of routine Australian practice and would not alter management at this gestation. The decision here rests on whether a sensitising event has occurred. (Source: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh D immunoglobulin)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh D immunoglobulin

options.text: Withhold anti-D immunoglobulin now and omit the routine third trimester doses as well
options.rationale: Routine antenatal prophylaxis at 28 and 34 weeks is given to all rhesus negative women regardless of first trimester events. Omitting it would leave her unprotected against silent sensitisation. (Source: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh D immunoglobulin)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh D immunoglobulin

explanation.summary: Rhesus D alloimmunisation is prevented by giving anti-D immunoglobulin routinely in the third trimester, after birth of a rhesus positive baby, and after potentially sensitising events. The distinction that causes most difficulty in early pregnancy is between a threatened miscarriage with a viable pregnancy and a genuine sensitising event such as miscarriage with instrumentation, ectopic pregnancy, termination, or chorionic villus sampling. Before 12 weeks the foeto-maternal transfusion volume in uncomplicated threatened miscarriage is too small to sensitise, so anti-D is not indicated. Dose also varies by gestation, with 250 IU covering first trimester events and 625 IU used after 12 weeks alongside a Kleihauer test to detect a larger bleed requiring additional doses.
key_points: Threatened miscarriage before 12 weeks with a viable pregnancy does not need anti-D
Instrumentation, ectopic pregnancy and termination are sensitising at any gestation
First trimester sensitising events are covered by a 250 IU dose
After 12 weeks the dose is 625 IU with a Kleihauer test to quantify the bleed
Routine prophylaxis at 28 and 34 weeks is given irrespective of earlier events
explanation.pearls: Anti-D must be given within 72 hours of a sensitising event to be reliably effective, though it is still worth giving up to ten days later if the window has been missed.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh D immunoglobulin
National Blood Authority Australia: Anti-D immunoglobulin

subtopic_detail: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes at thirty weeks with no clinical infection and a cephalic presentation
stem:
A 29 year old woman at 30 weeks in her second pregnancy presents to your birth suite after a sudden gush of clear fluid four hours ago, with continued leaking since. She has no abdominal pain and reports normal fetal movements.

Sterile speculum examination shows a pool of clear liquor in the posterior fornix with a closed cervix and no offensive odour. Her uterus is soft and non-tender on palpation, and the presentation is cephalic on ultrasound with an amniotic fluid index at the lower limit of normal. Cardiotocography shows a baseline of 140/min with normal variability, accelerations present and no decelerations. Her observations and blood results are reassuring.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 82/min, blood pressure 114/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C, fetal heart rate baseline 140/min
data_table.Examination: Pool of clear liquor in the posterior fornix, closed cervix, no offensive odour, soft non-tender uterus
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 9.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C-reactive protein 4 mg/L (<5), low vaginal swab sent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Oral amoxicillin with clavulanate and corticosteroids with inpatient expectant surveillance
options.rationale: This combination is specifically avoided in this setting because it is associated with an increased rate of neonatal necrotising enterocolitis. The principle of latency antibiotics is right but the agent is wrong. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.text: Oral erythromycin with antenatal corticosteroids and inpatient expectant surveillance
options.rationale: Latency antibiotics prolong pregnancy and reduce neonatal morbidity, and corticosteroids reduce respiratory distress, intraventricular haemorrhage and necrotising enterocolitis at this gestation. With no evidence of infection or fetal compromise, expectant management allows further maturation. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.text: Antenatal corticosteroids with tocolysis for 48 hours and inpatient expectant surveillance
options.rationale: Tocolysis is not recommended once membranes have ruptured because it does not improve outcomes and may prolong exposure to intrauterine infection. She is not contracting in any case. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.text: Antenatal corticosteroids with induction of labour once the second dose has been given
options.rationale: Immediate birth at 30 weeks exchanges a small infection risk for substantial prematurity, and expectant management is preferred while surveillance remains reassuring. Planned birth becomes appropriate closer to 37 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.text: Antenatal corticosteroids with amnioinfusion and inpatient expectant surveillance
options.rationale: Amnioinfusion has no established role in managing ruptured membranes remote from term and introduces an additional intrauterine procedure. The fluid volume here is in any case at the lower limit of normal. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

explanation.summary: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes is confirmed on sterile speculum examination rather than by digital examination, which should be avoided because it introduces infection and shortens latency. Management balances the risk of ascending infection against the risks of prematurity, and while both surveillance and the threshold for birth shift with gestation, expectant management is preferred well before term. Latency antibiotics are given to prolong the interval to birth, with a macrolide chosen because co-amoxiclav increases neonatal necrotising enterocolitis. Antenatal corticosteroids are given for fetal lung maturity, and magnesium sulfate is added for neuroprotection when birth is anticipated before 30 weeks. Signs of chorioamnionitis, including maternal fever, uterine tenderness, offensive liquor, maternal tachycardia or fetal tachycardia, convert the plan to immediate birth with intravenous antibiotics.
key_points: Diagnosis is by sterile speculum examination, avoiding digital examination
Latency antibiotics use a macrolide, not amoxicillin with clavulanate
Tocolysis is not recommended after membranes rupture
Magnesium sulfate is given for neuroprotection when birth is expected before 30 weeks
Chorioamnionitis converts management from expectant to immediate birth
explanation.pearls: Amoxicillin with clavulanate is specifically avoided as the latency antibiotic in ruptured preterm membranes because of the increased rate of neonatal necrotising enterocolitis demonstrated in the ORACLE trial.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

subtopic_detail: Antenatal surveillance and birth planning after a low anterior placenta is reported in a woman with two previous caesareans
stem:
A 34 year old woman at 21 weeks in her third pregnancy attends your antenatal clinic to discuss her morphology scan. Her two previous births were both by caesarean section, the first for breech presentation and the second as a planned repeat procedure.

She is well with no bleeding and no pain. The morphology scan reports an anterior placenta that reaches the internal os, with loss of the normal hypoechoic retroplacental clear zone and several irregular vascular lacunae within the placental substance in the region overlying the previous uterine scar. Fetal growth and anatomy are normal. She tells you she has read that a low placenta usually moves up, and asks whether she can plan to give birth at her local unit as she did last time.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Imaging: Anterior placenta reaching the internal os, loss of the retroplacental clear zone, irregular vascular lacunae overlying the previous uterine scar, normal fetal growth and anatomy
data_table.Obstetric history: Two previous caesarean sections, no antepartum bleeding in this pregnancy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan?

options.text: Refer to a tertiary centre for specialist imaging and a planned caesarean with surgical backup
options.rationale: Loss of the clear zone with lacunae in an anterior placenta overlying a previous scar indicates abnormal placental invasion rather than simple praevia. Outcomes are substantially better when birth occurs in a centre with interventional radiology, blood bank and gynaecological oncology or urology support available. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta accreta spectrum)

options.text: Repeat the transvaginal scan at 32 weeks and plan a caesarean locally if it remains low
options.rationale: This is the correct pathway for uncomplicated placenta praevia, where migration is common and local birth is reasonable. The invasion features here mean the problem is not the position of the placenta but its attachment. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia)

options.text: Reassure her that most low placentas resolve and review the position again at 36 weeks
options.rationale: Reassurance based on migration ignores the sonographic features of invasion, which do not resolve and carry a high risk of catastrophic haemorrhage. It also defers referral past the point where planning is useful. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta accreta spectrum)

options.text: Admit her from 28 weeks for inpatient observation with a planned caesarean at her local unit
options.rationale: Prolonged admission does not address the need for a surgical team and resources capable of managing massive haemorrhage. Where the birth happens matters more than how long she is observed beforehand. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta accreta spectrum)

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging now and plan a caesarean hysterectomy at 34 weeks locally
options.rationale: Imaging may refine the assessment but committing to hysterectomy at this gestation and at a unit without the necessary support reverses the priorities. The location of birth is the decision that changes outcome. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta accreta spectrum)

explanation.summary: Placenta accreta spectrum describes abnormally adherent or invasive placentation, and its incidence has risen in step with caesarean section rates. The combination that should prompt suspicion is an anterior low lying placenta in a woman with previous uterine surgery, since the placenta implants over a scarred, poorly decidualised segment. Sonographic markers include loss of the retroplacental hypoechoic clear zone, irregular vascular lacunae, bladder wall interface irregularity and increased subplacental vascularity on Doppler. The single intervention that most reduces maternal morbidity is planned birth at around 34 to 36 weeks in a centre with a multidisciplinary team, massive transfusion capability and interventional radiology, since unanticipated accreta discovered at an emergency caesarean carries far higher rates of massive haemorrhage, intensive care admission and death.
key_points: Anterior low placenta plus previous caesarean is the classic risk combination
Loss of the clear zone and vascular lacunae suggest invasion rather than praevia
Invasion features do not resolve with advancing gestation
Planned birth in a tertiary centre is the main determinant of maternal outcome
Unanticipated accreta at emergency caesarean carries the worst outcomes
explanation.pearls: A woman with an anterior placenta praevia and two previous caesareans has a risk of placenta accreta spectrum of roughly forty per cent, which is why the finding prompts tertiary referral rather than a repeat scan.

subtopic_detail: Loss of the presenting part and a fetal bradycardia during labour in a woman with one previous caesarean
stem:
You are called to review a 32 year old woman at 39 weeks labouring spontaneously after one previous caesarean section for failure to progress. She has been progressing well and was 7 cm dilated with the head at the level of the spines thirty minutes ago.

Her epidural has been working well, but over the last few minutes she has become distressed by constant lower abdominal pain that persists between contractions, which is new. The cardiotocograph now shows a prolonged deceleration to 70/min lasting four minutes with no recovery. On vaginal examination the presenting part is now high and difficult to reach. Her contractions, which had been regular, have become infrequent and weak, and there is light fresh vaginal bleeding.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 126/min, blood pressure 96/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.9 °C, fetal heart rate 70/min
data_table.Examination: Constant lower abdominal pain between contractions, presenting part high and difficult to reach, light fresh vaginal bleeding, contractions infrequent and weak
data_table.Monitoring: Prolonged deceleration to 70/min for four minutes with no recovery

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Give a subcutaneous tocolytic and reassess the fetal heart rate over the next ten minutes
options.rationale: Acute tocolysis is used for fetal distress from uterine hyperstimulation, where contractions are excessive rather than fading. It would delay definitive treatment of a mechanical catastrophe. (Source: RANZCOG: Intrapartum fetal surveillance)

options.text: Perform an amniotomy and apply a fetal scalp electrode to improve the quality of the trace
options.rationale: Improving trace quality addresses monitoring rather than the underlying event, and the presenting part is now too high to attach an electrode safely. The clinical picture already establishes urgency. (Source: RANZCOG: Intrapartum fetal surveillance)

options.text: Reposition her into the left lateral position and give a fluid bolus with high flow oxygen
options.rationale: Intrauterine resuscitation measures are appropriate for a deceleration from cord compression or hypotension, neither of which explains the loss of station and constant pain. They should not delay transfer to theatre here. (Source: RANZCOG: Intrapartum fetal surveillance)

options.text: Commence an oxytocin infusion to restore contractions and reassess progress in thirty minutes
options.rationale: Augmenting a uterus that may have ruptured risks extending the defect and causing catastrophic haemorrhage. Weakening contractions here reflect loss of uterine integrity rather than inadequate labour. (Source: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section

options.text: Call the theatre team for immediate laparotomy with the neonatal and anaesthetic teams
options.rationale: Loss of station with constant pain, a deteriorating fetal heart rate and altered contractions in a scarred uterus indicates scar rupture, and both mother and baby are salvaged only by immediate operative delivery. Delay to confirm the diagnosis worsens outcomes for both. (Source: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section

explanation.summary: Vaginal birth after caesarean section is offered to suitable women in Australian practice, with uterine scar rupture the principal risk at roughly one in two hundred labours. Because rupture is uncommon, its recognition depends on assembling several individually unremarkable findings rather than on any single sign. An abnormal cardiotocograph is the commonest and earliest feature, and it is often accompanied by constant abdominal pain between contractions, cessation or weakening of previously effective contractions, loss of station of the presenting part, vaginal bleeding, haematuria, and maternal tachycardia with hypotension. Scar pain alone is a poor discriminator, particularly with an epidural in place. Management is immediate laparotomy, and the interval from diagnosis to delivery is the strongest determinant of neonatal outcome, so no investigation should precede transfer to theatre.
key_points: Scar rupture complicates roughly one in two hundred labours after caesarean
An abnormal cardiotocograph is the commonest and earliest sign
Loss of station and fading contractions indicate loss of uterine integrity
Epidural analgesia masks scar pain and reduces its diagnostic value
Time from diagnosis to delivery determines neonatal outcome
explanation.pearls: Weakening contractions in a woman labouring with a uterine scar is an ominous rather than a reassuring change, and augmenting with oxytocin at that moment can extend an existing rupture.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section

subtopic_detail: Maternal collapse with a mass visible at the introitus immediately after the placenta is delivered
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called to a 24 year old woman who has just given birth to her first baby. The placenta was delivered a few minutes ago and she immediately became pale and clammy with severe lower abdominal pain, and her blood pressure has fallen sharply.

Estimated blood loss so far is about 500 mL, which does not account for the degree of shock. On examination you cannot feel the uterine fundus abdominally where you would expect it. A dark red mass is visible at the introitus with the placenta already separated from it. Her midwife tells you she gave the routine oxytocin with the birth of the anterior shoulder and applied cord traction as the placenta delivered.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 58/min, blood pressure 74/38 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.5 °C
data_table.Examination: Uterine fundus not palpable abdominally, dark red mass visible at the introitus with the placenta separated, pale and clammy
data_table.Blood loss: Estimated 500 mL, disproportionate to the degree of shock

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Replace the fundus manually at once while further uterotonic drugs are withheld
options.rationale: Immediate replacement is the priority because the constriction ring tightens with time and makes later reduction progressively harder. Uterotonics are withheld until the fundus is replaced because they contract the ring and lock the inversion in place. (Source: RANZCOG: Acute uterine inversion)

options.text: Give a bolus of intravenous oxytocin at once and then attempt to replace the fundus
options.rationale: A uterotonic given before reduction tightens the cervical ring around the inverted fundus and can make manual replacement impossible. The sequence is what matters, not the drug itself. (Source: RANZCOG: Acute uterine inversion)

options.text: Insert an intrauterine balloon tamponade device and inflate it to control the bleeding
options.rationale: Tamponade treats atonic bleeding from a correctly positioned uterus and cannot be deployed into an inverted one. The shock here is largely neurogenic rather than from measured loss. (Source: RANZCOG: Postpartum haemorrhage)

options.text: Apply bimanual uterine compression and commence a rapid crystalloid fluid infusion
options.rationale: Compression is a holding measure for atony and does nothing to correct the anatomical abnormality that is causing the collapse. Fluids alone will not reverse the vagal response. (Source: RANZCOG: Postpartum haemorrhage)

options.text: Transfer immediately to theatre for laparotomy and surgical correction of the abnormality
options.rationale: Surgical reduction is reserved for failure of manual replacement, and the delay involved in transfer allows the ring to tighten further. Manual replacement should be attempted first at the bedside. (Source: RANZCOG: Acute uterine inversion)

explanation.summary: Acute uterine inversion is rare but is one of the few obstetric emergencies where the correct first move is counterintuitive and the wrong one makes the situation irretrievable. It is suspected when shock is out of proportion to measured blood loss, the fundus cannot be palpated abdominally, and a mass is found in the vagina or at the introitus, usually after excessive cord traction with a fundal placenta. The profound bradycardia reflects vagal stimulation from traction on the infundibulopelvic ligaments and distinguishes it from hypovolaemic shock, in which tachycardia is expected. Immediate manual replacement by pushing the fundus back through the cervix gives the best chance of success, and uterotonics are deliberately withheld until the uterus is restored, after which they are given to maintain tone. If manual replacement fails, hydrostatic reduction or surgical approaches are used, with tocolysis to relax the constriction ring.
key_points: Shock disproportionate to blood loss with an impalpable fundus suggests inversion
Bradycardia rather than tachycardia reflects the vagal mechanism
Excessive cord traction with a fundal placenta is the usual precipitant
Uterotonics are withheld until the fundus has been replaced
Hydrostatic or surgical reduction follows failed manual replacement
explanation.pearls: Bradycardia in a shocked woman immediately after birth should prompt palpation for the fundus, because vagally mediated bradycardia with an impalpable fundus is uterine inversion until proven otherwise.

subtopic_detail: Failure to establish breastfeeding with lethargy and low sodium in a woman who had a large blood loss at birth
stem:
A 29 year old woman is reviewed on your postnatal ward on day nine after a birth complicated by a 2.8 litre haemorrhage requiring transfusion of six units of red cells and a period of hypotension in theatre.

She has been readmitted with four days of increasing tiredness, dizziness on standing and poor appetite. She has produced almost no breast milk despite regular expressing and good support from the lactation consultant, and she has noticed she feels cold all the time. Her lochia is normal and her uterus is well involuted and non-tender. Her haemoglobin has been stable since discharge and her iron studies are satisfactory after the transfusion.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92/min, blood pressure 88/54 mmHg lying with a fall on standing, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.1 °C
data_table.Examination: Uterus well involuted and non-tender, normal lochia, no calf tenderness, minimal breast fullness despite regular expressing
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 126 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 4.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), glucose 3.1 mmol/L (3.5-7.8), haemoglobin 104 g/L (115-155), thyroid stimulating hormone 0.4 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), free thyroxine 7 pmol/L (9-19)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Oral thyroxine replacement started now with hydrocortisone added once the results return
options.rationale: Giving thyroxine to a cortisol deficient patient accelerates cortisol clearance and can precipitate a crisis, which is why the order of replacement is fixed. The hormone choice is right but the sequence is dangerous. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Fluid restriction to 1 litre daily with paired serum and urine osmolality measurements
options.rationale: This is the approach to the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis, which does not cause postural hypotension, hypoglycaemia or failure of lactation. Restricting fluid here would worsen her volume depletion. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Intravenous hydrocortisone given before any thyroid hormone replacement is started
options.rationale: Pituitary failure after obstetric haemorrhage produces combined cortisol and thyroid deficiency, and cortisol must be replaced first because thyroxine raises metabolic demand and can precipitate an adrenal crisis. The low sodium with hypoglycaemia and postural hypotension reflects the cortisol deficit. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Domperidone to stimulate lactation with dietitian review and iron supplementation
options.rationale: Treating the lactation failure in isolation misses the systemic endocrine cause and leaves the dangerous cortisol deficiency untreated. Her iron status is already satisfactory. (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association)

options.text: Hypertonic saline infusion to correct the sodium with close neurological observation
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline is reserved for seizures or severe neurological symptoms from hyponatraemia, and she has neither. Her sodium will correct as the hormone deficiency is treated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Sheehan syndrome is postpartum hypopituitarism caused by infarction of a pituitary gland that has enlarged during pregnancy and is vulnerable to a period of hypotension from obstetric haemorrhage. Its presentation is easily missed because the early symptoms of fatigue, dizziness and poor appetite are ubiquitous after a difficult birth, and the most specific early clue, failure of lactation, is frequently attributed to stress or poor technique. The biochemical signature is a combination of deficiencies rather than a single abnormality, typically hyponatraemia with hypoglycaemia from cortisol deficiency and a low free thyroxine with an inappropriately normal or low thyroid stimulating hormone, which distinguishes central from primary hypothyroidism. Later features include amenorrhoea and loss of secondary sexual hair. Replacement is lifelong and the order of starting matters critically.
key_points: Obstetric haemorrhage with hypotension is the precipitating event
Failure of lactation is the earliest specific clue and is easily dismissed
Low free thyroxine with a normal or low thyroid stimulating hormone indicates central failure
Hydrocortisone is always started before thyroxine replacement
Hyponatraemia with hypoglycaemia reflects cortisol rather than thyroid deficiency
explanation.pearls: A normal thyroid stimulating hormone alongside a low free thyroxine is the finding that reveals pituitary rather than thyroid failure, and in this setting it means hydrocortisone must precede the first thyroxine dose.

subtopic_detail: Anticoagulation planning before conception for a woman with a mechanical mitral valve prosthesis
stem:
A 30 year old woman attends your general practice to discuss trying for a pregnancy. She had a mechanical mitral valve replacement four years ago for rheumatic valve disease and takes warfarin 4 mg daily, with a target international normalised ratio of 3.0 and consistently stable readings.

She is otherwise well with good exercise tolerance and no breathlessness or palpitations. She has read online that warfarin harms the baby and tells you she has already decided to stop it as soon as her pregnancy test is positive. She has not yet stopped contraception. Her most recent echocardiogram showed a normally functioning prosthesis with good ventricular function.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Mechanical first heart sound audible, no murmur of prosthetic dysfunction, no peripheral oedema, good exercise tolerance
data_table.Investigations: International normalised ratio 3.0 and stable on warfarin 4 mg daily, echocardiogram shows normally functioning prosthesis with good ventricular function

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice?

options.text: Refer now for a joint cardiac and obstetric plan before she stops any anticoagulant
options.rationale: Every anticoagulation strategy in this setting trades maternal valve thrombosis against fetal risk, and the choice depends on her warfarin dose, valve position and preference, so it needs specialist discussion before conception. Stopping anticoagulation without a bridging plan carries a high risk of valve thrombosis, which is the leading cause of maternal death in this group. (Source: RANZCOG: Cardiac disease in pregnancy)

options.text: Agree with her plan to stop warfarin as soon as a pregnancy test is positive
options.rationale: An unbridged gap in anticoagulation risks prosthetic valve thrombosis, which carries high maternal mortality and often occurs before she would be reviewed. Any change must be planned with an alternative agent already in place. (Source: RANZCOG: Cardiac disease in pregnancy)

options.text: Advise her to switch to a direct oral anticoagulant before she stops contraception
options.rationale: Direct oral anticoagulants are contraindicated with mechanical valves because trials showed increased thromboembolism and bleeding compared with warfarin. They are also not recommended in pregnancy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Advise her to switch to aspirin with clopidogrel before she stops contraception
options.rationale: Antiplatelet therapy does not prevent thrombosis on a mechanical valve, which requires anticoagulation. Substituting it would leave the prosthesis effectively unprotected. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Reassure her that warfarin is safe throughout pregnancy and no change will be needed
options.rationale: Warfarin crosses the placenta and carries a dose related embryopathy risk in the first trimester as well as fetal bleeding risk later, so it cannot be presented as free of fetal consequence. Blanket reassurance would remove her ability to make an informed choice. (Source: RANZCOG: Cardiac disease in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: A mechanical heart valve in pregnancy is one of the highest risk maternal cardiac situations, because pregnancy is prothrombotic while the anticoagulant that best protects the valve is the one that harms the foetus. Warfarin gives the lowest rate of valve thrombosis but crosses the placenta, causing a dose related embryopathy when taken between six and twelve weeks and increasing fetal intracranial haemorrhage near term. Low molecular weight heparin does not cross the placenta but requires weight adjusted twice daily dosing with regular anti-Xa monitoring, and inadequate dosing has been associated with fatal valve thrombosis. Strategies therefore include continuing warfarin throughout with a switch near term, or substituting heparin during the embryopathy window, with the decision influenced by whether the daily warfarin dose exceeds 5 mg. All of this requires pre-pregnancy counselling by a multidisciplinary team, and the single most dangerous action is an unplanned unilateral cessation of anticoagulation.
key_points: Pregnancy is prothrombotic and mechanical valves need uninterrupted anticoagulation
Warfarin embryopathy risk is dose related and concentrated between six and twelve weeks
Low molecular weight heparin needs weight adjusted dosing with anti-Xa monitoring
Direct oral anticoagulants are contraindicated with mechanical valves
Pre-pregnancy multidisciplinary counselling precedes any change in therapy
explanation.pearls: A warfarin maintenance dose of 5 mg daily or less carries a substantially lower embryopathy risk, which is why the actual daily dose is the number that shapes the first trimester anticoagulation plan.

subtopic_detail: Absent periods at sixteen with short stature and minimal breast development in a girl whose pubic hair is normal
stem:
A 16 year old girl attends your practice with her mother because she has never had a period. Her mother reached menarche at 13 and her older sister at 12.

She has always been the shortest in her class and her height today is well below the third centile, against a mid-parental target on the 50th. Breast development is minimal, while pubic and axillary hair are normal for her age. She has no headaches, no visual symptoms and a normal sense of smell, and she is not underweight and does not exercise excessively. On examination she has a broad chest with widely spaced nipples and there is a soft mid-systolic murmur at the left sternal edge. Her pregnancy test is negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 74/min, blood pressure 128/82 mmHg in the right arm, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Height well below the third centile, breast stage 2, normal pubic and axillary hair, broad chest with widely spaced nipples, soft mid-systolic murmur at the left sternal edge
data_table.Investigations: Pregnancy test negative, thyroid function and prolactin within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start combined oral contraceptive therapy now to induce withdrawal bleeding and breast development
options.rationale: Giving oestrogen before the diagnosis is established removes the diagnostic value of the gonadotrophins and may close the epiphyses prematurely in a girl who could benefit from growth treatment. Sequencing matters before any hormone is given. (Source: RANZCOG: Primary amenorrhoea)

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary before any other investigation is undertaken
options.rationale: Pituitary imaging is directed at hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism, suggested by headache, visual field loss or impaired smell, none of which is present. Her short stature and dysmorphic features point elsewhere. (Source: RANZCOG: Primary amenorrhoea)

options.text: Reassure her that this represents constitutional delay and review her again in twelve months
options.rationale: Constitutional delay usually follows a family pattern and does not produce height this far below the mid-parental target with dysmorphic features. Waiting a further year would forfeit the window for growth intervention. (Source: RANZCOG: Primary amenorrhoea)

options.text: Measure gonadotrophins and arrange a karyotype before any hormone treatment is started
options.rationale: Short stature with absent breast development but normal adrenal driven pubic hair indicates gonadal failure, and raised gonadotrophins would confirm the ovary rather than the pituitary as the site. A karyotype is essential because a chromosomal cause carries cardiac, renal and aortic implications that change lifelong care. (Source: RANZCOG: Primary amenorrhoea)

options.text: Measure total testosterone and arrange a pelvic ultrasound to assess for androgen excess
options.rationale: Androgen excess would be suggested by hirsutism, acne and virilisation with normal or advanced growth, and she has none of these. Her pubic hair is normal rather than excessive. (Source: RANZCOG: Primary amenorrhoea)

explanation.summary: Primary amenorrhoea is investigated by first establishing whether secondary sexual characteristics have developed, because that single observation splits the differential efficiently. Absent breast development indicates absent oestrogen exposure, and gonadotrophins then separate a failing gonad, which drives them up, from a failing hypothalamus or pituitary, which leaves them low. Turner syndrome is the commonest chromosomal cause of gonadal failure and should be suspected whenever short stature accompanies absent breast development, with supportive features including a broad chest, widely spaced nipples, a webbed neck, a low hairline, lymphoedema and cubitus valgus. Because the pubic and axillary hair are driven by adrenal androgens rather than by the ovary, they develop normally and their presence is reassuring only about the adrenal axis. Diagnosis matters well beyond fertility, since it prompts screening for bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation, aortic root dilatation, renal anomalies, hypothyroidism and coeliac disease, and growth hormone can improve final height if started early enough.
key_points: Presence or absence of breast development is the first branch point
Raised gonadotrophins localise the problem to the gonad rather than the pituitary
Pubic hair is adrenal driven and can be normal despite ovarian failure
Short stature with absent breast development should prompt a karyotype
Diagnosis triggers cardiac, aortic, renal and thyroid surveillance
explanation.pearls: Aortic root dilatation with a risk of dissection is the complication of Turner syndrome that persists into adult life and into pregnancy, so the karyotype result changes cardiac surveillance rather than only explaining the amenorrhoea.

subtopic_detail: Investigation offered to a couple after a third consecutive first trimester loss with no living children
stem:
A 31 year old woman attends your practice with her partner two weeks after a third consecutive miscarriage, all at between seven and nine weeks. They have no living children and she conceives readily each time.

Her cycles are regular at 29 days and she has no history of pelvic infection, uterine surgery or termination. She is a non-smoker with a body mass index of 24 kg/m2 and takes no regular medication. Her thyroid function and a random glucose are normal, and her cervical screening is up to date. The couple are distressed and want to know what can be looked for before they try again.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Unremarkable abdominal and pelvic examination, no adnexal mass or tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid function within normal limits, random glucose 4.9 mmol/L (3.5-7.8), full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What investigations would you arrange?

options.text: Test for inherited thrombophilias and image the uterine cavity, with parental karyotyping discussed
options.rationale: Routine inherited thrombophilia screening is not recommended for recurrent first trimester loss because the association is weak and anticoagulation has not improved outcomes. The acquired antibody syndrome is a different matter. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage)

options.text: Test for natural killer cell activity and image the uterine cavity, with parental karyotyping discussed
options.rationale: Peripheral natural killer cell testing has no established relationship with uterine immune function and is offered mainly outside the evidence base. Acting on the result exposes women to unproven immunotherapy. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage)

options.text: Test for antiphospholipid antibodies and image the uterine cavity, with parental karyotyping discussed
options.rationale: Antiphospholipid syndrome is the one cause of recurrent loss with a treatment that clearly improves live birth rates, and structural uterine anomalies are the other reliably identifiable factor. Parental karyotyping is offered selectively because a balanced translocation in a parent changes counselling. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage)

options.text: Test sperm DNA fragmentation and image the uterine cavity, with parental karyotyping discussed
options.rationale: Sperm DNA fragmentation testing is not part of standard recurrent miscarriage assessment and no intervention based on it has been shown to improve live birth. It would not alter management here. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage)

options.text: Arrange no investigations at this stage and advise trying again with reassurance about the prognosis
options.rationale: Three consecutive losses meets the threshold at which investigation is offered, and a treatable cause would otherwise be missed. Reassurance about prognosis is appropriate but accompanies rather than replaces assessment. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage)

explanation.summary: Recurrent miscarriage is conventionally defined as three or more consecutive pregnancy losses, though investigation is often begun after two in older women or where there is another concern. The great majority of sporadic first trimester losses are caused by fetal chromosomal abnormality, and even after three losses no cause is identified in around half of couples, which is important to convey because the prognosis for a subsequent live birth remains good. The investigations that are worth doing are those attached to an intervention or to meaningful counselling: antiphospholipid antibodies, because aspirin with low molecular weight heparin improves live birth rates in confirmed cases, imaging of the uterine cavity for structural anomalies, and thyroid function. Antiphospholipid testing requires two positive results at least twelve weeks apart to confirm the diagnosis. A wide range of other tests, including inherited thrombophilia panels and immune assays, are frequently marketed to distressed couples but are not supported and can lead to unproven and potentially harmful treatment.
key_points: Three consecutive losses is the conventional threshold for investigation
No cause is found in around half of couples and the prognosis remains good
Antiphospholipid syndrome is the cause with the clearest effective treatment
Confirmation requires two positive antibody results twelve weeks apart
Inherited thrombophilia and immune panels are not part of standard assessment
explanation.pearls: Antiphospholipid antibodies must be positive on two occasions at least twelve weeks apart before the diagnosis is made, because transient positivity after an acute event is common and would otherwise commit a woman to unnecessary anticoagulation.

subtopic_detail: Magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection in established very preterm labour in a normotensive woman
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar on the birth suite reviewing a woman at 28 weeks and 3 days in her second pregnancy. She was admitted six hours ago with regular painful contractions and her membranes ruptured spontaneously thirty minutes ago.

Her cervix is now 5 cm dilated and the midwife expects birth within a few hours. She completed a course of betamethasone yesterday after her first assessment. Her blood pressure has been normal throughout the pregnancy, her reflexes are normal and her urine shows no protein. The neonatal team has been called to attend.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92/min, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.9 °C, fetal heart rate 148/min
data_table.Examination: Cervix 5 cm dilated, cephalic presentation, clear liquor draining
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis shows no protein, full blood count and renal function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate addition to her management?

options.text: Withhold magnesium because her blood pressure and reflexes are normal
options.rationale: Normal blood pressure excludes the seizure prophylaxis indication but is irrelevant to the neuroprotective one, which depends only on gestation and the imminence of birth. Conflating the two indications is the commonest reason this treatment is missed. (Source: Antenatal Magnesium Sulphate Prior to Preterm Birth: Australian Clinical Practice Guidelines)
source_refs: Antenatal Magnesium Sulphate Prior to Preterm Birth: Australian Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.text: Give magnesium sulfate only if she develops signs of pre-eclampsia
options.rationale: This restricts magnesium to eclampsia prophylaxis, which is a separate indication with a different rationale and dosing intent. The neuroprotective benefit is lost entirely if treatment waits for hypertensive features that may never appear. (Source: Antenatal Magnesium Sulphate Prior to Preterm Birth: Australian Clinical Practice Guidelines)
source_refs: Antenatal Magnesium Sulphate Prior to Preterm Birth: Australian Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.text: Give nifedipine alone to delay birth and omit magnesium altogether
options.rationale: Tocolysis is not effective once the cervix is 5 cm with ruptured membranes, and its purpose is to buy time for steroids and transfer rather than to replace neuroprotection. Omitting magnesium forfeits a benefit that applies whether or not birth is delayed. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm labour and birth)

options.text: Give magnesium sulfate now for fetal neuroprotection before birth
options.rationale: Magnesium sulfate given to women before 30 weeks when birth is planned or expected within 24 hours reduces cerebral palsy and gross motor dysfunction in the surviving child, and this benefit is independent of blood pressure. At 28 weeks and 3 days with a cervix of 5 cm she meets both the gestational and the timing criteria. (Source: Antenatal Magnesium Sulphate Prior to Preterm Birth: Australian Clinical Practice Guidelines)
source_refs: Antenatal Magnesium Sulphate Prior to Preterm Birth: Australian Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.text: Defer magnesium until after birth and give it to the baby directly
options.rationale: The neuroprotective effect depends on magnesium crossing the placenta and being present in the fetal circulation during labour and birth, so postnatal administration to the neonate does not reproduce it. Neonatal magnesium is used for different indications entirely. (Source: Antenatal Magnesium Sulphate Prior to Preterm Birth: Australian Clinical Practice Guidelines)
source_refs: Antenatal Magnesium Sulphate Prior to Preterm Birth: Australian Clinical Practice Guidelines

explanation.summary: Magnesium sulfate has two entirely separate obstetric indications that share a drug and nothing else. As eclampsia prophylaxis it is given for severe pre-eclampsia to prevent seizures, while as a neuroprotective agent it is given to women in very preterm labour to reduce cerebral palsy in the child, with roughly one case of cerebral palsy avoided for every 60 or so women treated. The Australian guideline applies the neuroprotective indication before 30 weeks of gestation when birth is planned or anticipated within 24 hours, regardless of the cause of the preterm birth, the plurality of the pregnancy or the mode of birth. Administration requires monitoring of respiratory rate, reflexes and urine output, since toxicity manifests as loss of deep tendon reflexes before respiratory depression, and calcium gluconate should be available.
key_points: Neuroprotection and eclampsia prophylaxis are separate indications for the same drug
The neuroprotective indication applies before 30 weeks with birth expected within 24 hours
Blood pressure and proteinuria are irrelevant to the neuroprotective decision
Benefit requires antenatal administration so the foetus is exposed before birth
Monitor reflexes, respiratory rate and urine output during the infusion
explanation.pearls: Loss of deep tendon reflexes is the earliest sign of magnesium toxicity and precedes respiratory depression, so hourly reflex checks matter more than routine serum magnesium levels in a woman with normal renal function.

sources.label: Antenatal Magnesium Sulphate Prior to Preterm Birth: Australian Clinical Practice Guidelines

subtopic_detail: Definitive drainage technique for a recurrent vulval gland abscess after repeated simple incision
stem:
A 32 year old woman presents to your practice with a painful swelling at the entrance to the vagina that has grown over three days and now makes sitting and walking uncomfortable.

This is her third such episode in eighteen months. On each of the two previous occasions she attended an emergency department, where the swelling was cut and drained under local anaesthetic, and each time it returned within a few months. On examination there is a tender fluctuant swelling about 4 cm across in the posterior part of the vulva on the right, with surrounding erythema but no spreading cellulitis. She is systemically well and has no other symptoms.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Tender fluctuant 4 cm swelling in the right posterior vulva, overlying erythema, no induration of surrounding tissue
data_table.Past history: Two previous episodes each treated by simple incision and drainage, both recurring within months

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of this episode?

options.text: Simple incision and drainage under local anaesthetic in the department
options.rationale: Simple incision relieves pain but the edges seal within days, which reforms a closed cavity and explains why this has now happened twice. It is the intervention that has already failed her. (Source: RANZCOG: Bartholin cyst and abscess)

options.text: Oral antibiotics alone with warm compresses and review in one week
options.rationale: An established fluctuant abscess needs drainage, and antibiotics alone will not resolve a walled off collection of this size. Antibiotics are added when there is surrounding cellulitis or systemic features, neither of which is present. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Complete surgical excision of the gland under general anaesthetic
options.rationale: Excision is reserved for repeated failure of drainage procedures because it carries significant bleeding risk, scarring and dyspareunia. It is too morbid a step while a simpler definitive option has not yet been tried. (Source: RANZCOG: Bartholin cyst and abscess)

options.text: Needle aspiration of the swelling with a wide bore needle in clinic
options.rationale: Aspiration decompresses the cavity temporarily but leaves no drainage tract at all, so the recurrence rate is higher than with simple incision. It offers no advantage over the approach that has already failed. (Source: RANZCOG: Bartholin cyst and abscess)

options.text: Insertion of a Word catheter to create a permanently draining tract
options.rationale: The balloon tipped catheter is left in place for several weeks so the tract epithelialises, creating a lasting drainage channel and reducing recurrence far below that of simple incision. It is performed under local anaesthetic and preserves gland function and lubrication. (Source: RANZCOG: Bartholin cyst and abscess)

explanation.summary: Bartholin gland cysts and abscesses arise when the duct at the posterior introitus obstructs, and the central management principle is that the problem is the blocked duct rather than the fluid inside it. Procedures that simply evacuate the contents, including needle aspiration and simple incision and drainage, allow the opening to seal and carry recurrence rates that rise with each episode. Definitive management creates a permanent epithelialised channel, achieved either by a Word catheter left in for two to four weeks or by marsupialisation, where the cyst wall is sutured to the vulval skin. Antibiotics are added only for surrounding cellulitis, systemic features or sexually transmitted infection, and a new solid or persistent mass in a woman over 40 warrants biopsy because vulval gland carcinoma, although rare, presents this way.
key_points: The pathology is duct obstruction, so drainage alone predictably recurs
A Word catheter or marsupialisation creates a lasting epithelialised tract
The catheter stays in for two to four weeks to allow epithelialisation
Antibiotics are reserved for cellulitis or systemic involvement
A persistent mass over the age of 40 requires biopsy to exclude carcinoma
explanation.pearls: A new or persistent Bartholin mass in a woman over 40 should be biopsied rather than simply drained, because adenocarcinoma of the gland presents as an apparently benign recurrent swelling.

subtopic_detail: Sequencing thiamine before glucose containing fluid in prolonged vomiting of early pregnancy
stem:
You are the medical officer admitting a woman at 11 weeks in her first pregnancy who has been vomiting many times a day for four weeks and can no longer keep down fluids.

She has lost 6 kg since her booking weight and looks dry, with reduced skin turgor and dry mucous membranes. Her urine shows heavy ketones. The resident has already written up an initial litre of five per cent dextrose and an antiemetic, and asks you to check the chart before it is hung. She has taken no supplements since the vomiting began and her only other history is mild asthma.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 112/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.5 °C
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor, no abdominal tenderness, no goitre
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis shows heavy ketones, potassium 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), sodium 133 mmol/L (135-145), thyroid function within normal limits
data_table.Weight: Loss of 6 kg from a booking weight of 68 kg

lead_in: What change to the prescribed fluid plan is most important?

options.text: Start five per cent dextrose and add an antiemetic once she settles
options.rationale: This is the plan as written and carries the specific hazard of precipitating an acute thiamine deficient encephalopathy in a woman whose stores are depleted after four weeks without intake. Dextrose is also a poor resuscitation fluid because it distributes across total body water. (Source: RANZCOG: Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy and hyperemesis gravidarum)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy and hyperemesis gravidarum

options.text: Start normal saline and give oral thiamine tablets once she can swallow
options.rationale: Choosing saline over dextrose is correct, but deferring thiamine to the oral route in a woman who cannot keep fluids down means she effectively receives none. Replacement must be parenteral until absorption is reliable. (Source: RANZCOG: Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy and hyperemesis gravidarum)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy and hyperemesis gravidarum

options.text: Give parenteral thiamine before starting any glucose containing fluid
options.rationale: Four weeks of vomiting exhausts thiamine stores, and a glucose load consumes the remaining thiamine as a cofactor, which can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy within hours. Parenteral thiamine is therefore given first, and rehydration then proceeds with normal saline and added potassium. (Source: RANZCOG: Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy and hyperemesis gravidarum)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy and hyperemesis gravidarum

options.text: Start potassium replacement first and withhold thiamine until admission
options.rationale: Her potassium does need replacing, but it can be added to the rehydration fluid rather than sequenced ahead of everything else, and withholding thiamine leaves the encephalopathy risk unaddressed. Potassium at this level is not immediately life threatening. (Source: RANZCOG: Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy and hyperemesis gravidarum)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy and hyperemesis gravidarum

options.text: Start total parenteral nutrition given the degree of weight she has lost
options.rationale: Parenteral nutrition is a last resort in hyperemesis because of line sepsis and thrombosis risk, and it is considered only after antiemetics, rehydration and enteral options have failed. Introducing a large glucose load without thiamine would compound the same hazard. (Source: RANZCOG: Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy and hyperemesis gravidarum)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy and hyperemesis gravidarum

explanation.summary: Hyperemesis gravidarum is distinguished from ordinary nausea and vomiting of pregnancy by weight loss exceeding about five per cent of body weight, dehydration, ketosis and electrolyte disturbance. Management combines rehydration with normal saline, potassium replacement guided by levels, and a stepwise antiemetic ladder, while thyroid function is checked because a transient biochemical hyperthyroidism driven by human chorionic gonadotrophin is common and rarely needs treatment. The critical prescribing point is thiamine: stores last only a few weeks, and administering glucose to a depleted woman consumes the last of the cofactor needed for carbohydrate metabolism, which can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy with confusion, ophthalmoplegia and ataxia. Wernicke encephalopathy in pregnancy carries a high rate of lasting cognitive deficit and fetal loss, and is entirely preventable by giving thiamine first.
key_points: Hyperemesis requires weight loss, dehydration and ketosis, not just vomiting
Rehydrate with normal saline rather than dextrose containing fluid
Parenteral thiamine precedes any glucose load after prolonged vomiting
Transient hCG driven biochemical hyperthyroidism rarely needs treatment
Parenteral nutrition is a last resort because of line related complications
explanation.pearls: Any woman vomiting in pregnancy for more than three weeks should receive parenteral thiamine before intravenous glucose, because Wernicke encephalopathy can be precipitated by a single litre of dextrose.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy and hyperemesis gravidarum

subtopic_detail: Preventive therapy for culture proven recurrent urinary infection after menopause with a normal tract
stem:
A 68 year old woman attends your practice frustrated by repeated urinary infections. She has had four culture proven episodes in the past twelve months, each with dysuria and frequency, and each settling promptly with a short course of antibiotics.

She went through menopause at 51 and has never used hormone therapy. She describes vaginal dryness and discomfort with intercourse. On examination the vulval and vaginal tissues are pale and thin with loss of rugae, and there is no prolapse beyond the hymen. A bladder scan after voiding shows a negligible residual volume, and an ultrasound of the renal tract arranged by a colleague was reported as normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Pale thin vaginal epithelium with loss of rugae, no prolapse beyond the hymen, no suprapubic tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Four culture proven infections in twelve months with fully sensitive Escherichia coli, post void residual negligible, renal tract ultrasound reported as normal
data_table.Glucose: Fasting glucose and HbA1c within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate preventive treatment?

options.text: Long term low dose trimethoprim taken each night for the next six months
options.rationale: Continuous antibiotic prophylaxis does reduce episodes while it is taken, but benefit stops when it stops and it drives resistance in an organism that is currently fully sensitive. It is reserved for women in whom non antibiotic measures have failed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: A further course of antibiotics given at the onset of each new episode
options.rationale: Treating each episode as it arises is what she is already doing, and it leaves the underlying mucosal change untouched so the pattern simply continues. Self start therapy is a reasonable adjunct but is not preventive. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Cranberry capsules taken daily together with an increased fluid intake
options.rationale: Increased fluid intake has modest supporting evidence and is worth advising, but cranberry products have not shown consistent benefit in trials and neither addresses the oestrogen deficient epithelium. These are adjuncts rather than the principal treatment. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society: Genitourinary syndrome of menopause)
source_refs: Australasian Menopause Society: Genitourinary syndrome of menopause

options.text: Topical vaginal oestrogen used regularly as ongoing preventive therapy
options.rationale: Oestrogen deficiency thins the urogenital epithelium and raises vaginal pH, which allows uropathogens to replace the protective lactobacilli, and topical replacement reverses both changes and significantly reduces recurrence. Systemic absorption from low dose vaginal preparations is minimal, so a progestogen is not required for endometrial protection. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society: Genitourinary syndrome of menopause)
source_refs: Australasian Menopause Society: Genitourinary syndrome of menopause

options.text: Referral for cystoscopy to exclude a structural cause for the infections
options.rationale: Imaging and cystoscopy are indicated where there is haematuria between episodes, infection with urea splitting organisms, suspected stones or a significant post void residual, none of which is present. Her tract has already been imaged and shown to be normal. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Recurrent urinary tract infection is defined as two episodes in six months or three in a year, and in postmenopausal women with a structurally normal tract the dominant mechanism is the genitourinary syndrome of menopause. Falling oestrogen thins the urogenital epithelium, raises vaginal pH and depletes lactobacilli, which permits colonisation by bowel uropathogens, so restoring local oestrogen addresses the cause rather than suppressing the consequence. Vaginal oestrogen has good trial evidence for reducing recurrence and is preferred to continuous antibiotic prophylaxis, which works only while taken and selects for resistance. Investigation for a structural cause is reserved for red flags such as persistent haematuria, infection with urea splitting organisms, a significant post void residual or failure to respond to appropriate therapy.
key_points: Recurrent infection means two episodes in six months or three in twelve
Oestrogen deficiency raises vaginal pH and depletes protective lactobacilli
Vaginal oestrogen is preferred over continuous antibiotic prophylaxis
Low dose vaginal oestrogen needs no progestogen for endometrial protection
Imaging is reserved for haematuria, stones, residual volume or treatment failure
explanation.pearls: Low dose vaginal oestrogen produces serum levels within the postmenopausal range, so it can be offered to most women with a history of oestrogen receptor positive breast cancer after discussion with their oncologist rather than being automatically withheld.

sources.label: Australasian Menopause Society: Genitourinary syndrome of menopause

subtopic_detail: Timing of combined hormonal contraception for a breastfeeding woman in the first week after birth
stem:
You are reviewing a 30 year old woman on the postnatal ward on day 5 after an uncomplicated vaginal birth of her second child. She is fully breastfeeding and the baby is feeding well.

She used a combined oral contraceptive pill before this pregnancy, got on well with it, and asks to restart the same brand before she goes home today so that nothing is forgotten. She has no personal or family history of venous thromboembolism, does not smoke, and her blood pressure and body mass index are both normal. Her first child was conceived sooner than she had planned and she is anxious to avoid that happening again.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Uterus well contracted, lochia normal, calves soft and non tender
data_table.History: Fully breastfeeding, no thrombotic history, non smoker, body mass index 23 kg/m2
data_table.Birth details: Uncomplicated vaginal birth at term, estimated blood loss 300 mL

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice about her contraceptive request?

options.text: Defer combined hormonal contraception until six weeks after the birth
options.rationale: Combined preparations are avoided in the first six weeks in a breastfeeding woman because oestrogen can reduce milk supply while lactation is being established, and the postpartum thrombotic risk remains elevated in the early weeks. A progestogen only method or an intrauterine device can be started now if she wants cover before then. (Source: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception after childbirth)
source_refs: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception after childbirth

options.text: Start combined hormonal contraception today before she goes home
options.rationale: Day 5 falls inside the period of greatest postpartum thrombotic risk and coincides with the establishment of milk supply, which oestrogen can suppress. The convenience of starting before discharge does not outweigh either concern. (Source: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception after childbirth)
source_refs: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception after childbirth

options.text: Start combined hormonal contraception at three weeks after the birth
options.rationale: Three weeks is the usual earliest start for a woman who is not breastfeeding and has no additional thrombotic risk factors, and applying it here ignores the lactation consideration. The breastfeeding threshold is six weeks. (Source: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception after childbirth)
source_refs: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception after childbirth

options.text: Advise that breastfeeding alone gives reliable contraception for a year
options.rationale: Lactational amenorrhoea is only reliable while all three conditions hold together: full breastfeeding, amenorrhoea and an infant under six months. Presenting it as twelve months of cover misstates the method and invites exactly the unplanned pregnancy she is trying to avoid. (Source: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception after childbirth)
source_refs: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception after childbirth

options.text: Defer all hormonal contraception until she has stopped breastfeeding
options.rationale: Progestogen only methods do not affect milk supply and can be started immediately after birth, so withholding all hormonal options is unnecessarily restrictive. Only the oestrogen containing methods carry the lactation concern. (Source: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception after childbirth)
source_refs: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception after childbirth

explanation.summary: Contraceptive choice after birth is governed by two considerations that move on different timelines: venous thromboembolism risk, which is highest in the first three weeks and has largely resolved by six, and the effect of oestrogen on establishing lactation. Progestogen only pills, implants and injections do not affect milk supply and can be started at any time from immediately after birth, and both intrauterine device types can be inserted within the first 48 hours or from four weeks onwards. Combined hormonal methods are deferred to six weeks in a woman who is breastfeeding, and to three weeks in a woman who is not and has no additional thrombotic risk factors. Ovulation can return from about day 21 in a woman who is not fully breastfeeding, so a plan should be made before discharge even when the chosen method starts later.
key_points: Progestogen only methods can start immediately and do not affect milk supply
Combined methods are deferred to six weeks while breastfeeding
Combined methods may start at three weeks if not breastfeeding and low risk
Lactational amenorrhoea requires full breastfeeding, amenorrhoea and age under six months
Ovulation can precede the first postpartum period, so counsel before discharge
explanation.pearls: An intrauterine device inserted within 48 hours of birth is acceptable, but insertion between 48 hours and four weeks carries a markedly higher perforation and expulsion rate and should be avoided.

sources.label: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception after childbirth
Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and reproductive health

subtopic_detail: Stratifying a complex adnexal mass in a postmenopausal woman to decide the surgical pathway
stem:
A 62 year old woman attends your practice with three months of abdominal bloating, feeling full after small meals and a vague dragging discomfort in the pelvis. She has lost 4 kg without trying.

She went through menopause at 50 and has had no bleeding since. Her abdomen is distended with shifting dullness, and bimanual examination reveals a firm irregular mass arising from the pelvis. She has no family history of breast or ovarian cancer. Her bowel habit is unchanged and a faecal occult blood test arranged by a colleague was negative. The imaging and tumour marker you requested have now returned.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Distended abdomen with shifting dullness, firm irregular pelvic mass, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Ultrasound: 9 cm multilocular right adnexal mass with solid areas and internal vascularity, moderate ascites, normal endometrial thickness

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Arrange laparoscopic ovarian cystectomy at the local hospital next month
options.rationale: Cystectomy is an operation for a benign cyst in a woman wishing to preserve ovarian tissue, and performing it here risks rupturing a malignant cyst and upstaging the disease. Fertility preservation is not a consideration at this age. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Ovarian cancer)

options.text: Repeat the ultrasound and tumour marker in three months to see if they change
options.rationale: Interval surveillance is appropriate for a simple unilocular cyst under 5 cm with a normal marker in a postmenopausal woman. With solid areas, ascites and a markedly raised marker, a three month delay allows progression of a disease whose outcome depends on early complete surgery. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Ovarian cancer)

options.text: Arrange image guided percutaneous biopsy of the mass before any referral
