options.rationale: Percutaneous sampling of an apparently operable ovarian mass risks seeding the peritoneum and the needle track, and the diagnosis is normally made at definitive surgery instead. Biopsy is reserved for advanced disease where chemotherapy will precede surgery. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Ovarian cancer)

options.text: Refer to the general gynaecology list for laparoscopic oophorectomy locally
options.rationale: Survival in ovarian cancer depends strongly on complete cytoreduction performed by a trained subspecialist, and operating outside such a unit is associated with incomplete staging and worse outcomes. The referral destination is itself part of the treatment decision. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Ovarian cancer)

options.text: Calculate the risk of malignancy index and refer to gynaecological oncology
options.rationale: The index combines menopausal status, ultrasound morphology and the CA125 value, and a score above 200 identifies a high probability of malignancy warranting referral to a specialist centre. Her postmenopausal status, multiple suspicious ultrasound features and markedly raised marker place her far above that threshold. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Ovarian cancer)

explanation.summary: Ovarian cancer presents with vague abdominal symptoms such as bloating, early satiety, urinary frequency and pelvic discomfort, and the persistence and newness of these symptoms in a woman over 50 is what should trigger investigation rather than their individual specificity. Initial assessment combines pelvic ultrasound with serum CA125, and these feed with menopausal status into the risk of malignancy index, where a score above 200 indicates referral to a gynaecological oncology centre. The reason the referral destination matters so much is that survival correlates with the completeness of cytoreduction achieved at the first operation, which is consistently better in specialist units. CA125 must be interpreted with care, since it rises in endometriosis, fibroids, pelvic infection, pregnancy and any peritoneal irritation, which is why the index weights it alongside imaging rather than using it alone.
key_points: Persistent new bloating and early satiety over 50 warrant investigation
Initial assessment is pelvic ultrasound plus serum CA125
The risk of malignancy index combines menopausal status, ultrasound and CA125
A score above 200 mandates referral to a gynaecological oncology unit
Survival depends on complete cytoreduction at the first operation
explanation.pearls: CA125 is raised in only about half of early stage ovarian cancers, so a normal value never excludes malignancy in a woman with a suspicious mass on ultrasound.

subtopic_detail: Choosing intrapartum prophylaxis when the recorded penicillin reaction is a delayed childhood rash
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar asked to write up intrapartum antibiotics for a woman at 39 weeks who is 4 cm dilated with intact membranes. Her screening swab at 36 weeks grew group B streptococcus.

Her notes carry an allergy label for penicillin. When you ask her about it directly, she describes a flat blotchy rash over her tummy and back that appeared three or four days into a course of amoxicillin for a sore throat when she was about six years old. It settled over a week without treatment. She has never had swelling of the lips or tongue, wheeze, faintness or blistering, and she has taken cephalexin for a urinary infection since then without trouble.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88/min, blood pressure 122/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C, fetal heart rate 140/min
data_table.Screening: Vaginal and rectal swab at 36 weeks positive for group B streptococcus, susceptibility not requested
data_table.Allergy history: Delayed maculopapular rash on day three or four of amoxicillin at age six, no mucosal or respiratory involvement, subsequent cephalexin tolerated
data_table.Labour: Cervix 4 cm dilated, membranes intact, contracting three in ten minutes

lead_in: Which intrapartum antibiotic is most appropriate?

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin despite the allergy recorded in her notes
options.rationale: Benzylpenicillin is the agent of choice where no allergy exists, and a delayed rash is indeed low risk, but a recorded penicillin label is not simply overridden at the bedside in labour without formal assessment. The cephalosporin achieves comparable cover while respecting the label. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous vancomycin because she reports an allergy to penicillin
options.rationale: Vancomycin is reserved for women at high risk of anaphylaxis whose isolate is resistant to clindamycin or whose susceptibility is unknown, and it crosses the placenta less reliably. Using it for a low risk rash history exposes mother and baby to a broader agent without benefit. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous cefazolin because her reported reaction was not severe
options.rationale: A delayed maculopapular rash without mucosal, respiratory or systemic involvement is a low risk history, and the cross reactivity between penicillins and cefazolin is negligible because they share no side chain, which her subsequent tolerance of cephalexin supports. Cefazolin crosses the placenta well and achieves adequate fetal levels, making it the preferred choice in low risk allergy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous clindamycin without testing the isolate for susceptibility
options.rationale: Clindamycin is an option only for severe allergy and only when the isolate has been shown susceptible, since resistance rates in group B streptococcus are appreciable and no susceptibility was requested here. Giving it blind risks ineffective prophylaxis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Oral amoxicillin once labour is established and repeated six hourly
options.rationale: Prophylaxis must be intravenous to achieve adequate and rapid amniotic fluid concentrations before birth, and the oral route cannot do this reliably. It also ignores the recorded allergy to the same drug class. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis prevents early onset neonatal group B streptococcal sepsis and is most effective when the first dose is given at least four hours before birth. Benzylpenicillin is first choice, and the decision tree for a woman with a penicillin label turns entirely on how severe the reported reaction was. A low risk history is an isolated delayed rash without mucosal involvement, systemic features or blistering, and such women receive cefazolin, which shares no side chain with the penicillins and carries negligible cross reactivity. A high risk history, meaning anaphylaxis, angioedema, respiratory compromise or a severe cutaneous adverse reaction, moves the choice to clindamycin if the isolate is proven susceptible and otherwise to vancomycin. Because most penicillin allergy labels are inaccurate, taking a proper allergy history in the antenatal period is a concrete clinical intervention rather than a formality.
key_points: Benzylpenicillin is first line when no allergy label exists
Severity of the reported reaction determines the alternative chosen
Delayed rash without systemic features is a low risk history
Cefazolin shares no side chain with penicillins and is preferred in low risk allergy
Clindamycin requires demonstrated susceptibility of the isolate
explanation.pearls: Request clindamycin susceptibility at the time of the 36 week group B streptococcus swab for any woman with a penicillin allergy label, because the result is unavailable once she presents in labour.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Deciding on a repeat antenatal corticosteroid course four weeks after the first when birth again appears likely
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a woman at 30 weeks and 2 days who has been readmitted with regular painful contractions and a cervix that has shortened on transvaginal scan since her last assessment.

She was admitted four weeks ago with threatened preterm labour, received a complete course of betamethasone then, and settled without giving birth. On that occasion the contractions stopped within a day. This time her contractions are stronger and more frequent, her cervical length has fallen considerably and the consultant judges that birth within the next week is likely. Her membranes are intact, her observations are normal and there is no evidence of infection.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 90/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 17/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.9 °C, fetal heart rate 144/min
data_table.Previous treatment: Complete betamethasone course given four weeks ago at 26 weeks and 2 days
data_table.Current findings: Cervical length 12 mm on transvaginal ultrasound, contracting three in ten minutes, membranes intact
data_table.Investigations: White cell count and C reactive protein within normal limits, glucose within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate decision regarding corticosteroids?

options.text: Give a full new two dose course every week until she gives birth
options.rationale: Weekly repeated courses have been associated with reduced birthweight and smaller head circumference without additional respiratory benefit, so repetition is deliberately limited. The evidence supports a single repeat rather than a rolling schedule. (Source: RANZCOG: Antenatal corticosteroids)

options.text: Withhold repeat steroids because a course has already been given
options.rationale: The benefit of the original course wanes after about seven days, so a woman who did not give birth within that window and now faces imminent birth stands to gain from a repeat. Treating the first course as permanently sufficient forfeits that benefit. (Source: RANZCOG: Antenatal corticosteroids)

options.text: Withhold repeat steroids because she is now beyond 30 weeks gestation
options.rationale: The accepted gestational ceiling for a repeat course extends beyond 30 weeks, so this gestation does not exclude her. Respiratory morbidity remains substantial at this gestation and the treatment still reduces it. (Source: RANZCOG: Antenatal corticosteroids)

options.text: Give a repeat course only once the membranes have actually ruptured
options.rationale: Membrane rupture is neither necessary nor sufficient as a trigger, since the decision rests on the likelihood of birth within the next seven days. Waiting for rupture may mean the course is given too late to take effect. (Source: RANZCOG: Antenatal corticosteroids)

options.text: Give a single repeat course as birth is likely within the next week
options.rationale: A single repeat course is indicated when more than seven days have elapsed since the first, the woman remains below the gestational ceiling and birth is judged likely within the next seven days, all of which apply here. The Australian randomised evidence showed reduced respiratory distress and less oxygen requirement with a single repeat, without the growth effects seen with weekly dosing. (Source: RANZCOG: Antenatal corticosteroids)

explanation.summary: A single course of antenatal betamethasone before preterm birth reduces respiratory distress syndrome, intraventricular haemorrhage and neonatal death, and the effect is greatest when birth occurs between 24 hours and seven days after the course. The clinical difficulty arises with the substantial group of women who receive a course during a threatened preterm labour that then settles, and who represent again weeks later. Australian randomised evidence established that a single repeat course in that situation reduces respiratory morbidity, whereas weekly repetition reduces birthweight and head circumference without further respiratory gain. The decision therefore requires three conditions together: more than seven days since the previous course, a gestation still within the treatable range, and a genuine judgement that birth is likely within the next week. Corticosteroids also raise maternal blood glucose for several days, which matters when diabetes complicates the pregnancy.
key_points: Maximal benefit falls between 24 hours and seven days after administration
A single repeat course is supported when more than seven days have elapsed
Weekly repeated courses reduce birthweight and head circumference
The judgement that birth is likely within seven days is part of the indication
Maternal blood glucose rises for several days after a course
explanation.pearls: Australian practice was shaped by a randomised trial showing that one repeat betamethasone course reduced neonatal respiratory morbidity, which is why the repeat is offered once rather than on a weekly schedule.

subtopic_detail: Management of a positive routine antenatal urine culture in a woman without urinary symptoms
stem:
A 26 year old woman at 16 weeks in her first pregnancy attends your practice to discuss the results of her booking investigations. She feels well and is getting on with the pregnancy without difficulty.

She has no urinary frequency, dysuria, urgency, haematuria or loin pain, and she has had no fevers. The midstream specimen collected at her booking visit has grown a significant pure growth of Escherichia coli, fully sensitive on the panel reported. Her renal function is within normal limits and she has no history of urinary tract infection or renal tract abnormality.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non tender, no renal angle tenderness
data_table.Microbiology: Midstream urine culture with a significant pure growth of Escherichia coli, fully sensitive
data_table.Other results: Renal function within normal limits, no proteinuria, full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Treat with an oral antibiotic guided by susceptibility and repeat the culture
options.rationale: Asymptomatic bacteriuria is treated in pregnancy because up to a third of untreated women progress to pyelonephritis, with associated preterm birth and low birthweight, and treatment substantially reduces that risk. A test of cure culture after treatment confirms clearance, since persistence is common and warrants further courses or prophylaxis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Repeat the urine culture and treat only if symptoms develop later
options.rationale: Waiting for symptoms defeats the purpose of screening, because the complication being prevented is ascending infection that often announces itself as established pyelonephritis. The screening programme exists precisely to treat before symptoms occur. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: No treatment as bacteriuria without symptoms needs no antibiotic
options.rationale: This is the correct approach outside pregnancy, and in older adults and catheterised patients treating asymptomatic bacteriuria causes harm without benefit. Pregnancy is the major exception because of the physiological ureteric dilatation and stasis that favour ascending infection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Treat only if a repeat culture also grows the same organism in a week
options.rationale: A significant pure growth on a properly collected specimen is sufficient to act on, and requiring a second confirmatory culture delays treatment without improving accuracy. Repeat culture has a role as a test of cure rather than as a precondition for treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Refer for renal tract ultrasound before considering any antibiotic
options.rationale: Imaging is reserved for recurrent infection, suspected stones or structural abnormality, none of which is suggested by a single positive screening culture. It would delay a simple and effective treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Screening for asymptomatic bacteriuria with a midstream urine culture at the first antenatal visit is one of the few screening tests in pregnancy that clearly prevents a serious maternal complication. Progesterone mediated smooth muscle relaxation and mechanical compression by the gravid uterus produce ureteric dilatation and urinary stasis, so bacteria that would remain confined to the bladder outside pregnancy ascend readily to the kidneys. Untreated, a substantial minority of affected women develop pyelonephritis, which is associated with preterm birth, low birthweight, maternal sepsis and acute kidney injury. Antibiotic choice follows susceptibility while respecting pregnancy safety, and a test of cure culture is taken after treatment because persistent or recurrent bacteriuria is common and may require repeat treatment or suppressive prophylaxis for the remainder of the pregnancy. Group B streptococcus isolated in the urine at any point is a separate matter and indicates intrapartum prophylaxis regardless of the swab result later in pregnancy.
key_points: Pregnancy is the main exception to not treating asymptomatic bacteriuria
Ureteric dilatation and stasis favour ascending infection
Untreated bacteriuria progresses to pyelonephritis in a substantial minority
A test of cure culture follows treatment because persistence is common
Group B streptococcus in urine mandates intrapartum prophylaxis
explanation.pearls: Group B streptococcus cultured from the urine at any stage of pregnancy indicates heavy genital colonisation and is an indication for intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis, irrespective of what the 36 week swab shows.

subtopic_detail: Initial ward management of a first bleed at 32 weeks when the placenta covers the internal os
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called to the assessment unit to see a 34 year old woman in her third pregnancy at 32 weeks. She was sitting watching television when she felt a sudden gush and found bright red blood soaking her clothing.

She has had no abdominal pain at any point and felt no contractions. The bleeding amounted to roughly 200 mL and has now settled to light spotting. Her uterus is soft and completely non tender on palpation, and the baby has been moving normally. Her morphology scan reported a low placenta and a repeat transvaginal scan a fortnight ago confirmed that it covers the internal os. Her blood group is O positive and her haemoglobin is within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92/min, blood pressure 116/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C, fetal heart rate 142/min
data_table.Examination: Soft non tender uterus, cephalic presentation high, light fresh spotting on the pad, no contractions palpable
data_table.Imaging: Transvaginal ultrasound a fortnight ago shows the placenta covering the internal os
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin within normal limits, blood group O positive, coagulation profile within normal limits, group and hold sent
data_table.Cardiotocograph: Baseline 142/min with normal variability and no decelerations

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Perform a digital vaginal examination to assess the cervix for dilatation
options.rationale: Digital examination in the presence of a placenta covering the os can disrupt the placental edge and provoke torrential haemorrhage, and it is the single manoeuvre to avoid in this situation. Any assessment of the cervix is made by speculum or ultrasound instead. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and placenta accreta spectrum)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and placenta accreta spectrum

options.text: Admit for observation and corticosteroids, avoiding digital vaginal examination
options.rationale: A first bleed that settles in a stable woman with a reassuring cardiotocograph is managed expectantly as an inpatient, because a further and heavier bleed can occur without warning and she needs to be where blood and theatre are available. Corticosteroids are given for fetal lung maturity since birth before term is now considerably more likely. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and placenta accreta spectrum)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and placenta accreta spectrum

options.text: Discharge home with advice to return if the bleeding recurs or worsens
options.rationale: Outpatient management is considered only after a period of inpatient stability in a woman who lives close to the hospital with ready transport and support. Discharging on the day of a first significant bleed leaves her distant from care when the next one occurs. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and placenta accreta spectrum)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and placenta accreta spectrum

options.text: Proceed to immediate caesarean section regardless of the bleeding settling
options.rationale: Immediate birth is reserved for maternal haemodynamic compromise, a non reassuring cardiotocograph or bleeding that does not settle, none of which applies. Delivering a stable 32 week pregnancy now would impose avoidable prematurity. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and placenta accreta spectrum)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and placenta accreta spectrum

options.text: Induce labour with prostaglandin now that the bleeding has settled down
options.rationale: A placenta covering the internal os is an absolute contraindication to labour and to vaginal birth, because the presenting part cannot descend without disrupting the placenta. Birth must be by caesarean section. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and placenta accreta spectrum)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and placenta accreta spectrum

explanation.summary: Antepartum haemorrhage after 20 weeks is separated clinically by the presence or absence of pain and uterine tone: painless bright red bleeding with a soft non tender uterus suggests placenta praevia, whereas pain with a tense tender uterus suggests abruption. A low lying placenta found at the morphology scan is common and most resolve as the lower segment develops, so the diagnosis is confirmed by transvaginal ultrasound in the third trimester, which is safe and more accurate than the transabdominal route. The governing rule of management is that no digital vaginal examination is performed until praevia has been excluded, since it can provoke catastrophic bleeding. A first bleed that settles in a stable woman is managed by admission, corticosteroids for lung maturity, anti-D for a woman who is rhesus negative, group and hold with attention to haemoglobin, and planned caesarean section, typically between 36 and 37 weeks or sooner if bleeding recurs.
key_points: Painless bleeding with a soft uterus suggests praevia; pain with a tense uterus suggests abruption
Transvaginal ultrasound is safe and confirms the placental position
No digital vaginal examination until praevia has been excluded
A settled first bleed is managed by admission with corticosteroids
Birth is by planned caesarean section, usually at 36 to 37 weeks
explanation.pearls: Ask about previous caesarean sections whenever praevia is diagnosed, because a placenta praevia overlying a uterine scar carries a substantially increased risk of placenta accreta spectrum and changes the planning of the birth entirely.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and placenta accreta spectrum

subtopic_detail: Continuing and monitoring an anticonvulsant whose clearance rises sharply through pregnancy
stem:
A 29 year old woman attends your clinic at 7 weeks in a pregnancy she is pleased about but had not planned. She has focal epilepsy and has been free of seizures for three years on lamotrigine monotherapy.

She drives to work and cares for a toddler. Having read about medication in pregnancy overnight, she tells you she has already missed this morning's dose and intends to stop the tablets altogether until the baby is born. She has no other medical history, takes no other medication and had not been taking folic acid before conception. Her last seizure was a focal to bilateral tonic clonic event.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Epilepsy history: Focal epilepsy, seizure free for three years on lamotrigine monotherapy, last event was focal to bilateral tonic clonic
data_table.Medication: Lamotrigine monotherapy, no other medication, no preconception folic acid
data_table.Social: Holds a current driver licence, sole daytime carer for a toddler

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice?

options.text: Continue the lamotrigine and monitor drug levels through each trimester
options.rationale: Lamotrigine clearance rises markedly during pregnancy through induced glucuronidation, so levels fall progressively and seizures can recur on an unchanged dose, which makes scheduled level monitoring with dose adjustment the core of management. Continuing treatment is safer than stopping, because a generalised convulsion carries hypoxic risk to the foetus and a real risk of maternal death. (Source: RANZCOG: Epilepsy in pregnancy)

options.text: Stop the lamotrigine now because it is unsafe in the first trimester
options.rationale: Lamotrigine is among the anticonvulsants with the most reassuring data on major congenital malformation, and abrupt cessation in a woman with a history of bilateral tonic clonic seizures risks status epilepticus. Stopping poses a far greater threat to both than continuing. (Source: RANZCOG: Epilepsy in pregnancy)

options.text: Switch to sodium valproate which is better studied during pregnancy
options.rationale: Valproate carries the highest rates of major congenital malformation and of impaired neurodevelopment of any anticonvulsant and is specifically avoided in pregnancy wherever an alternative exists. Switching towards it would be the worst available choice. (Source: RANZCOG: Epilepsy in pregnancy)

options.text: Halve the lamotrigine dose to reduce fetal exposure during organogenesis
options.rationale: Halving the dose moves in exactly the wrong direction given that pregnancy already lowers levels substantially, and it would leave her subtherapeutic at the point her seizure risk is rising. Partial dosing delivers the risks of exposure without the protection. (Source: RANZCOG: Epilepsy in pregnancy)

options.text: Continue the current dose without any monitoring of drug levels
options.rationale: Continuing is right but doing so blindly ignores the pharmacokinetic change that distinguishes this drug, and breakthrough seizures in the second and third trimesters are the predictable result. Lamotrigine is one of the anticonvulsants where level monitoring genuinely alters management. (Source: RANZCOG: Epilepsy in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Most women with epilepsy have uncomplicated pregnancies, and the overriding principle is that uncontrolled convulsive seizures are more dangerous to mother and foetus than the anticonvulsants used to prevent them. Lamotrigine and levetiracetam are the preferred agents because of comparatively reassuring malformation and neurodevelopmental data, while valproate is avoided wherever possible and topiramate carries cleft and growth restriction concerns. Lamotrigine is pharmacokinetically distinctive: oestrogen driven induction of glucuronidation increases its clearance so that plasma levels can fall by half or more as pregnancy advances, producing breakthrough seizures on a dose that was previously adequate. Levels are therefore checked before pregnancy where possible and through each trimester, with the dose increased to maintain the preconception concentration and reduced again over the first weeks after birth to avoid toxicity as clearance returns to baseline. High dose folic acid is started as soon as pregnancy is recognised, and women should be advised about safer bathing and infant handling practices.
key_points: Uncontrolled convulsive seizures pose greater risk than anticonvulsant exposure
Lamotrigine and levetiracetam are the preferred agents in pregnancy
Pregnancy raises lamotrigine clearance so levels fall substantially
Check levels each trimester and adjust the dose to the preconception level
Reduce the dose again in the weeks after birth as clearance normalises
explanation.pearls: Reduce the lamotrigine dose over the first two to three weeks postpartum towards the preconception dose, because clearance falls rapidly after birth and women who remain on the increased pregnancy dose develop toxicity with ataxia and diplopia.

subtopic_detail: Antithyroid drug selection by trimester in a woman with Graves disease who has just conceived
stem:
A 27 year old woman telephones your clinic to say her pregnancy test is positive. Her last menstrual period was six weeks ago and the pregnancy was planned.

She has Graves disease diagnosed two years ago and has been stable on carbimazole for the past nine months, with thyroid function in the target range at her last two checks and no goitre symptoms. She has no palpitations, tremor or weight loss at present. She asks whether she should keep taking her tablets now that she is pregnant, and mentions that she stopped her regular blood tests a few months ago because everything had been stable.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Small smooth goitre, no tremor, no lid lag, no proptosis
data_table.Thyroid function: Free thyroxine and thyroid stimulating hormone within the target range on the two most recent checks
data_table.Medication: Carbimazole at a stable dose for nine months

lead_in: What is the most appropriate change to her treatment?

options.text: Stop all antithyroid medication and monitor thyroid function monthly
options.rationale: Stopping altogether risks relapse of thyrotoxicosis, which is associated with miscarriage, preterm birth, growth restriction and maternal heart failure. Withdrawal is considered only in women with mild disease in long remission and is not a default on discovering pregnancy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Change to propylthiouracil for the first trimester and then review
options.rationale: Carbimazole and its active metabolite are associated with a specific embryopathy including aplasia cutis, choanal and oesophageal atresia, with the risk concentrated in the period of organogenesis, so propylthiouracil is preferred through the first trimester. Because propylthiouracil carries a small risk of severe hepatotoxicity, most units switch back afterwards, which is why the plan is framed as a change with later review. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Continue carbimazole at the same dose throughout the whole pregnancy
options.rationale: This leaves her on the agent associated with embryopathy during precisely the weeks when organogenesis occurs. Carbimazole becomes the preferred drug again after the first trimester, not during it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Add levothyroxine alongside carbimazole to block and replace instead
options.rationale: A block and replace regimen requires higher antithyroid drug doses, and since these cross the placenta while thyroxine does so poorly, the foetus is rendered hypothyroid with goitre. It is specifically avoided in pregnancy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Refer for thyroidectomy in the first trimester to avoid drug exposure
options.rationale: Surgery is reserved for severe or refractory disease or drug intolerance and, when needed, is timed to the second trimester to minimise miscarriage and preterm labour risk. It is disproportionate for well controlled disease. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Graves disease in pregnancy requires balancing the harms of uncontrolled thyrotoxicosis against the harms of the drugs that control it, and the balance shifts with gestation. Carbimazole and methimazole are associated with an embryopathy comprising aplasia cutis, choanal atresia, oesophageal atresia and dysmorphic features, with risk concentrated during organogenesis, so propylthiouracil is preferred through the first trimester. Propylthiouracil in turn carries a rare but serious risk of fulminant hepatic failure, which is why many units switch back after the first trimester. Both drugs cross the placenta, so the aim is the lowest dose that keeps free thyroxine in the upper part of the normal range, accepting a suppressed thyroid stimulating hormone, and block and replace regimens are avoided because the higher antithyroid dose reaches the foetus while the replacement thyroxine does not. Thyroid stimulating hormone receptor antibodies should be measured because they cross the placenta and can cause fetal or neonatal thyrotoxicosis even in a mother who has been rendered euthyroid by surgery or radioiodine.
key_points: Carbimazole embryopathy risk is concentrated during first trimester organogenesis
Propylthiouracil is preferred in the first trimester despite hepatotoxicity risk
Aim for free thyroxine in the upper normal range on the lowest effective dose
Block and replace regimens cause fetal hypothyroidism and are avoided
Receptor antibodies cross the placenta and can cause neonatal thyrotoxicosis
explanation.pearls: Measure thyroid stimulating hormone receptor antibodies even in a woman previously treated with radioiodine or surgery, because the antibodies persist and cross the placenta to cause fetal thyrotoxicosis in a mother who is herself euthyroid or hypothyroid.

subtopic_detail: Severe localised pain over a known fibroid in the second trimester with a closed cervix
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 33 year old woman at 22 weeks in her first pregnancy who presented overnight with severe constant pain in the left side of her abdomen that began two days ago and has steadily worsened.

She has a fibroid uterus documented at her morphology scan, with the largest measuring 8 cm on the left side of the fundus. The pain is sharply localised and she can point to it with one finger. Her uterus is soft between examinations and is tender only directly over the fibroid, with no generalised tenderness. Her cervix is long and closed on speculum examination and there is no bleeding or fluid loss. Her urine culture is negative and her cardiotocograph is reassuring.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 37.6 °C, fetal heart rate 148/min
data_table.Examination: Tenderness localised over the left fundal fibroid only, uterus soft elsewhere, cervix long and closed, no bleeding
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 13.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C reactive protein 32 mg/L (less than 5), urine culture negative
data_table.Imaging: Ultrasound shows an 8 cm left fundal fibroid with heterogeneous echotexture, normal liquor volume, normal fetal growth

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Urgent laparotomy and myomectomy to remove the painful fibroid
options.rationale: Myomectomy during pregnancy carries a high risk of torrential haemorrhage from the vascular gravid uterus and of pregnancy loss, so it is avoided except in extreme circumstances such as a torted pedunculated fibroid. The pain here is self limiting and does not justify that risk. (Source: RANZCOG: Fibroids in pregnancy)

options.text: Start intravenous antibiotics for presumed intrauterine infection
options.rationale: Chorioamnionitis produces generalised uterine tenderness with maternal and fetal tachycardia and usually follows membrane rupture, whereas her tenderness is confined to the fibroid with intact membranes and a closed cervix. The mild fever and inflammatory response here reflect tissue infarction rather than infection. (Source: RANZCOG: Fibroids in pregnancy)

options.text: Analgesia and observation without any operative intervention
options.rationale: Red degeneration occurs when a fibroid outgrows its blood supply during the rapid growth of the second trimester, producing localised pain with a low grade fever and mildly raised inflammatory markers that mimic infection. It is self limiting over one to two weeks, so management is adequate analgesia, hydration and observation, avoiding prolonged nonsteroidal use beyond 32 weeks because of ductal constriction. (Source: RANZCOG: Fibroids in pregnancy)

options.text: Uterine artery embolisation to infarct the fibroid and relieve pain
options.rationale: Embolisation is contraindicated in pregnancy because it would compromise the uteroplacental circulation and expose the foetus to radiation. It is a treatment for symptomatic fibroids outside pregnancy in women who have completed childbearing. (Source: RANZCOG: Fibroids in pregnancy)

options.text: Induce labour because the pain indicates the pregnancy cannot continue
options.rationale: Birth at 22 weeks would be pre viable and the underlying process is a self limiting one that resolves with time and analgesia. There is no maternal or fetal compromise that would justify ending the pregnancy. (Source: RANZCOG: Fibroids in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Fibroids grow under oestrogen stimulation during pregnancy, and a large fibroid can outgrow its blood supply and undergo haemorrhagic infarction, known as red or carneous degeneration. The presentation is severe pain localised precisely over the fibroid, often with a low grade fever, mild leucocytosis and raised inflammatory markers, which makes infection the obvious but incorrect first thought. The features that separate it are tenderness confined to the fibroid with a soft non tender uterus elsewhere, intact membranes, a closed cervix and a reassuring cardiotocograph. Treatment is supportive with adequate analgesia, hydration and observation, and the pain settles over one to two weeks, with nonsteroidal anti inflammatory drugs limited in duration and avoided after 32 weeks because of premature ductal constriction. Surgery is avoided because the gravid uterus bleeds heavily, and fibroids are reassessed after the puerperium when they commonly shrink.
key_points: Fibroids enlarge under oestrogen stimulation and can outgrow their blood supply
Pain is sharply localised over the fibroid with a soft uterus elsewhere
Low grade fever and raised inflammatory markers mimic infection
Management is analgesia, hydration and observation over one to two weeks
Myomectomy in pregnancy risks torrential haemorrhage and is avoided
explanation.pearls: Avoid nonsteroidal anti inflammatory drugs after 32 weeks and limit courses to about 48 hours before then, because prolonged exposure constricts the ductus arteriosus and reduces fetal urine output causing oligohydramnios.

subtopic_detail: Preconception planning for a woman established on an antiepileptic drug
stem:
A 28 year old woman attends your general practice to discuss trying for a baby in the next few months. She has focal epilepsy and has been seizure free for three years on lamotrigine 200 mg twice daily.

She takes no other regular medication, has no history of neural tube defect in her family and her body mass index is 24 kg/m2. She has read online that epilepsy medication causes birth defects and has already stopped taking her tablets for the last four days. She has not yet conceived and her last menstrual period was ten days ago.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Neurological examination normal, no focal deficit
data_table.Medication: Lamotrigine 200 mg twice daily, self ceased four days ago, no other regular medication
data_table.History: Focal epilepsy, seizure free for three years, no family history of neural tube defect, body mass index 24 kg/m2

lead_in: What would you first recommend?

options.text: Support stopping lamotrigine and begin folic acid 5 mg daily
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation after three years of control risks status epilepticus and loss of her driving licence, and a generalised seizure in pregnancy causes fetal hypoxia and placental abruption. Withdrawal is a specialist decision made before conception is attempted, not a self directed one. (Source: RANZCOG: Pre pregnancy counselling)

options.text: Switch her to sodium valproate and begin folic acid 5 mg daily
options.rationale: Valproate carries the highest risk of major congenital malformation and neurodevelopmental harm of the commonly used antiepileptics and should be avoided in anyone who could become pregnant. Moving towards it is the opposite of the required direction. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Restart lamotrigine now and begin folic acid 0.5 mg daily
options.rationale: Restarting the drug is right but 0.5 mg is the dose for women at standard risk. Antiepileptic therapy places her in the higher risk group for whom 5 mg daily is recommended, and the folate antagonism of several agents is the reason. (Source: RANZCOG: Pre pregnancy counselling)

options.text: Restart lamotrigine now and begin folic acid 5 mg daily
options.rationale: Uncontrolled seizures carry a greater risk to mother and foetus than lamotrigine, which is among the antiepileptics with the lowest teratogenic risk, so the drug is resumed rather than stopped. Women taking any antiepileptic are advised to take the higher 5 mg folic acid dose from at least one month before conception through the first trimester. (Source: RANZCOG: Pre pregnancy counselling)

options.text: Defer any change until she has a positive pregnancy test
options.rationale: Neural tube closure is complete by 28 days after conception, which is usually before a woman knows she is pregnant, so folate supplementation and drug optimisation must be in place beforehand. (Source: RANZCOG: Pre pregnancy counselling)

explanation.summary: Preconception care for a woman with epilepsy balances two risks that pull in opposite directions: the teratogenicity of antiepileptic drugs and the harm caused by uncontrolled seizures. For most women established on an agent with a favourable profile, continuing treatment is safer than stopping it, and any change to the regimen is planned with a neurologist before conception rather than reactively in early pregnancy. High dose folic acid at 5 mg daily is recommended for women on antiepileptic therapy, in contrast to the 0.5 mg standard dose, and should begin at least one month before conception. Neural tube closure completes before most pregnancies are recognised, which is why the timing matters.
key_points: Seizure control is protective for the pregnancy; abrupt self cessation is the greater immediate danger
Folic acid 5 mg daily rather than 0.5 mg for women on antiepileptic drugs, previous affected pregnancy, diabetes or a body mass index above 30 kg/m2
Sodium valproate is avoided in anyone of reproductive potential because of malformation and neurodevelopmental risk
Lamotrigine concentrations fall substantially during pregnancy and require monitoring with dose adjustment
explanation.pearls: Lamotrigine clearance rises through pregnancy so levels can fall by more than half by the third trimester; establish a preconception baseline concentration while she is seizure free, because that is the target to titrate against later.

subtopic_detail: Timing of pertussis containing vaccine within the current pregnancy
stem:
A 30 year old woman attends your antenatal clinic at 22 weeks in her second pregnancy. She asks about whooping cough because a colleague's baby was admitted to hospital with it last month.

She received a pertussis containing vaccine during her first pregnancy three years ago and tells you she assumed that would still cover this baby. She has had an influenza vaccine this season. She has no allergy to vaccine components, no immunosuppression and has had no adverse reaction to previous vaccination. The pregnancy is uncomplicated with normal growth on ultrasound. She plans to breastfeed.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 80 beats per minute, blood pressure 110/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 145 beats per minute
data_table.Examination: Symphysis fundal height 22 cm, no abnormality detected
data_table.Immunisation history: Pertussis containing vaccine in a previous pregnancy three years ago, influenza vaccine this season, no vaccine allergy
data_table.Pregnancy: Uncomplicated, normal growth on ultrasound, 22 weeks gestation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice about pertussis vaccination?

options.text: Explain that her previous dose protects this baby as well
options.rationale: Antibody from a dose given three years ago has waned and is not transferred in protective quantity to the current foetus, which is why a dose is recommended in each pregnancy rather than once only. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Defer the vaccine until she has given birth to this baby
options.rationale: Postpartum vaccination protects the mother from becoming a source of infection but gives the newborn no transplacental antibody, leaving the infant unprotected during the first weeks when the disease is most lethal. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Defer the vaccine until she reaches thirty six weeks gestation
options.rationale: A dose this late leaves insufficient time for maternal antibody production and placental transfer before birth, particularly if she delivers early, which is why the recommended window closes at 32 weeks. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Vaccinate the household contacts instead of vaccinating her
options.rationale: Vaccinating close contacts reduces exposure and is recommended alongside maternal vaccination, but it does not provide the infant with circulating antibody and is markedly less effective on its own. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Give the vaccine now between twenty and thirty two weeks
options.rationale: A pertussis containing vaccine is recommended in every pregnancy regardless of previous doses, because the protection that matters is the transfer of maternal antibody to this particular foetus, and antibody levels wane within months. The optimal window is 20 to 32 weeks, which maximises transplacental transfer before birth. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

explanation.summary: Pertussis causes its greatest mortality in infants under 6 months, who are too young to have completed their own primary course, so protection in those first weeks depends on maternal antibody acquired across the placenta. A pertussis containing vaccine is therefore recommended in every pregnancy, irrespective of when the woman was last vaccinated, because antibody levels fall substantially within a year. The recommended window is 20 to 32 weeks, which allows time for the maternal antibody response and its transfer before birth while still covering preterm delivery. Vaccinating household contacts is complementary but does not replace maternal vaccination.
key_points: A dose is recommended in every pregnancy, not once per lifetime
The window of 20 to 32 weeks balances antibody production against the risk of preterm birth
Maternal vaccination is more effective at protecting the newborn than vaccinating contacts
It is safe during breastfeeding and can be given postpartum if missed in pregnancy
explanation.pearls: If a woman presents after 32 weeks, still vaccinate rather than defer to the postnatal period: a late dose transfers less antibody than an ideally timed one but still transfers some, and the alternative leaves the infant with none at all.

subtopic_detail: Determining chorionicity in a newly confirmed twin pregnancy
stem:
A 27 year old woman attends your general practice at 8 weeks in her first pregnancy. A dating ultrasound arranged after a positive test has reported two gestational sacs with two live embryos of equal size.

The report does not comment on the membrane or on the number of placentas. She is well, has no bleeding and no pain, and has already started folic acid and iodine supplementation. She has no family history of twins and conceived spontaneously. She asks whether the twins are identical and what this means for her care. Her body mass index is 23 kg/m2 and her booking bloods are unremarkable.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Abdominal and pelvic examination unremarkable
data_table.Ultrasound: Two gestational sacs each containing a live embryo of equal crown rump length, membrane characteristics and placental number not reported
data_table.History: Spontaneous conception, first pregnancy, folic acid and iodine already commenced

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange ultrasound between eleven and thirteen weeks to assess the membrane
options.rationale: Chorionicity determines the entire antenatal plan and is most reliably established between 11 and 13 weeks, when the membrane insertion can be seen as either a thick triangular projection of placental tissue or a thin T shaped junction. Determination becomes progressively less reliable as gestation advances, so the window should not be missed. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy

options.text: Arrange non invasive prenatal testing to determine whether they are identical
options.rationale: Cell free DNA testing screens for common aneuploidies and does not establish chorionicity, which is an anatomical question about the placenta rather than a genetic one. Zygosity and chorionicity are also not the same thing. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy

options.text: Arrange a repeat ultrasound at twenty weeks with the morphology scan
options.rationale: Waiting until the morphology scan misses the window in which the membrane is most easily characterised and delays the fortnightly surveillance that a monochorionic pregnancy requires from 16 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy

options.text: Reassure her that two separate sacs means the twins are not identical
options.rationale: Two sacs seen early may still represent a monochorionic diamniotic pregnancy, and identical twins are commonly diamniotic, so sac number alone does not establish either zygosity or chorionicity. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy

options.text: Refer her directly for fortnightly scans from sixteen weeks onwards
options.rationale: Intensive surveillance is appropriate for a monochorionic pregnancy but represents considerable unnecessary scanning and anxiety if the pregnancy proves dichorionic, so the chorionicity is established first. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy

explanation.summary: Chorionicity, not zygosity, determines the risk profile and the surveillance plan of a twin pregnancy, because monochorionic twins share a placenta with vascular anastomoses and are at risk of twin to twin transfusion, selective growth restriction and anaemia polycythaemia sequence. It is determined by ultrasound between 11 and 13 weeks, when the membrane insertion shows either a thick triangular wedge of placental tissue indicating two chorions or a thin T shaped junction indicating one. After about 14 weeks the sign becomes progressively harder to identify. Monochorionic pregnancies require fortnightly ultrasound from 16 weeks and earlier planned birth, whereas dichorionic pregnancies are scanned less frequently.
key_points: Chorionicity drives management; zygosity is largely of academic interest
The membrane sign is most reliable between 11 and 13 weeks
Monochorionic pregnancies need fortnightly surveillance from 16 weeks
Two sacs on an early scan does not exclude a shared placenta
explanation.pearls: Make sure chorionicity is recorded in the handheld record and on every subsequent report: when the information is lost, later scans default to treating the pregnancy as monochorionic, and a woman can end up with months of unnecessary fortnightly surveillance or, far worse, a missed diagnosis of twin to twin transfusion.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Rubella non immune status identified on booking bloods and acted on after birth
stem:
You are the resident doing the postnatal round on day one. A 26 year old woman gave birth yesterday to a healthy term boy and is establishing breastfeeding well.

Her booking bloods, which you are reviewing before discharge, show that she is rubella non immune. She was born overseas and has no record of childhood immunisation. Her blood group is O rhesus D positive, her full blood count is normal and she had no antenatal complications. She tells you she and her partner would like another baby fairly soon and asks whether anything needs doing before they start trying.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Uterus well contracted, lochia normal, perineum intact, breastfeeding established
data_table.Investigations: Rubella immunoglobulin G non immune on booking bloods, blood group O rhesus D positive, full blood count within normal limits, hepatitis B surface antigen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Give rubella immunoglobulin before she goes home tomorrow
options.rationale: Immunoglobulin provides short lived passive protection after an exposure and does not generate the lasting immunity needed to protect a subsequent pregnancy. It has no role in a woman who has not been exposed. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Give measles mumps rubella vaccine before she goes home
options.rationale: Rubella containing vaccine is a live vaccine that cannot be given during pregnancy, so the immediate postpartum period before discharge is the standard opportunity to protect future pregnancies, and it is safe during breastfeeding. She is advised to avoid pregnancy for 28 days after the dose. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Arrange vaccination once she has finished breastfeeding him
options.rationale: Breastfeeding is not a contraindication to live rubella containing vaccine, and deferring until weaning risks a further pregnancy occurring while she is still susceptible. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Repeat her rubella serology in six weeks before deciding
options.rationale: Repeating the antibody test will not change a non immune result obtained in pregnancy and postpones the vaccination past the point at which she is most reliably in contact with the health service. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Vaccinate her partner and the baby to protect her instead
options.rationale: Household immunity limits exposure but does not protect the foetus of a susceptible mother, and the infant is not eligible for a rubella containing vaccine until 12 months of age. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

explanation.summary: Rubella serology is checked at booking in every Australian pregnancy because congenital rubella syndrome is devastating and entirely preventable. A live rubella containing vaccine cannot be given during pregnancy, so a non immune woman is vaccinated immediately after birth, before discharge, while she is still in contact with the service. Breastfeeding is not a contraindication. She should be advised to avoid pregnancy for 28 days afterwards, although inadvertent vaccination in early pregnancy has not been shown to cause congenital rubella syndrome and is not an indication for termination.
key_points: Vaccinate postpartum before discharge, because the opportunity is easily lost at follow up
Live rubella containing vaccine is contraindicated in pregnancy but safe during breastfeeding
Advise avoiding pregnancy for 28 days after the dose
Immunoglobulin is not a substitute for vaccination and has no role without an exposure
explanation.pearls: A second dose is needed for durable protection in someone with no documented childhood immunisation, so arrange the second measles mumps rubella dose at least 28 days later rather than assuming the postnatal dose has completed the course.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Routine antenatal assessment in the absence of pregnancy complications

subtopic_detail: Primary amenorrhoea with short stature and absent breast development
stem:
A 16 year old girl attends your general practice with her mother because she has never had a period. Her mother says she has always been the shortest in her year and that she has not grown noticeably since she was about 13.

She has no headaches, no visual symptoms and a normal sense of smell. She is not underweight, does not exercise excessively and has no features of androgen excess. She has no cyclical pelvic pain. Examination shows Tanner stage 1 breast development with sparse pubic hair, a high arched palate, a wide chest with widely spaced nipples and a low posterior hairline. Blood pressure is equal in both arms and femoral pulses are palpable.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 76 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg in both arms, respiratory rate 15 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Height 142 cm well below the 3rd centile, body mass index 22 kg/m2, Tanner stage 1 breast development, sparse pubic hair, high arched palate, wide carrying angle, low posterior hairline, femoral pulses present
data_table.Investigations: Follicle stimulating hormone 62 IU/L (3-10 follicular), luteinising hormone 28 IU/L, oestradiol less than 50 pmol/L, prolactin and thyroid function within normal limits, pregnancy test negative
data_table.Imaging: Pelvic ultrasound shows a small uterus with streak ovaries

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Request pituitary imaging studies
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary is indicated when gonadotrophins are low, indicating a central cause. Here they are high, which localises the problem to the ovary and makes a pituitary lesion very unlikely. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea investigation)

options.text: Measure her serum testosterone
options.rationale: Androgen measurement is directed at virilisation or at a disorder of androgen action, and she has neither hirsutism nor clitoromegaly. It would not explain the short stature or the raised gonadotrophins. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea investigation)

options.text: Request a peripheral blood karyotype
options.rationale: A raised follicle stimulating hormone with absent secondary sexual characteristics identifies primary gonadal failure, and in a girl with short stature and the associated dysmorphic features the cause is a sex chromosome abnormality until proven otherwise. The karyotype also determines whether Y chromosome material is present, which carries a risk of gonadal malignancy and changes management. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea investigation)

options.text: Arrange a progestogen challenge
options.rationale: A withdrawal bleed test assesses whether the endometrium has been oestrogenised, but the oestradiol is already known to be undetectable so the result is predictable and adds nothing. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea investigation)

options.text: Arrange coeliac disease serology
options.rationale: Coeliac disease is a recognised cause of short stature and delayed puberty, but it acts through chronic illness and undernutrition and produces low rather than high gonadotrophins, and her body mass index is normal. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea investigation)

explanation.summary: Primary amenorrhoea is investigated by first establishing whether secondary sexual characteristics are present and then measuring gonadotrophins, which separates ovarian from central causes. A high follicle stimulating hormone with absent breast development indicates primary ovarian failure, and when it occurs alongside short stature and characteristic features such as a webbed neck, wide carrying angle and widely spaced nipples the diagnosis is a sex chromosome abnormality. Karyotype is therefore the definitive investigation. It matters practically because the presence of Y chromosome material mandates gonadectomy for malignancy risk, and because associated cardiac, renal, thyroid and hearing problems need screening.
key_points: High gonadotrophins localise the lesion to the gonad; low gonadotrophins point to the hypothalamus or pituitary
Short stature with primary amenorrhoea should prompt karyotype rather than further hormonal testing
Y chromosome material in a phenotypic female requires gonadectomy because of gonadoblastoma risk
Associated anomalies include bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation, horseshoe kidney, autoimmune thyroid disease and conductive hearing loss
explanation.pearls: Arrange transthoracic echocardiography at diagnosis even when femoral pulses are normal and blood pressures are equal: bicuspid aortic valve occurs in up to a third of these girls and predisposes to aortic dissection in later pregnancy.

subtopic_detail: Rapidly progressive fever and hypotension on day two after a vaginal birth
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called to the postnatal ward at 2 am. A 30 year old woman who gave birth vaginally 36 hours ago has become rapidly unwell over the past three hours with rigors and severe lower abdominal pain.

Her midwife reports the lochia has an offensive smell. Her 4 year old was sent home from childcare last week with a sore throat. The perineum is intact with no tear and no haematoma, the calves are soft and non tender, and there is no cough, no dysuria and no breast erythema. She is drowsy but rousable and her capillary refill is 4 seconds.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 138 beats per minute, blood pressure 82/44 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute, SpO2 95 percent on room air, temperature 39.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, capillary refill 4 seconds, marked uterine tenderness with a bulky uterus, offensive lochia, perineum intact, calves soft, chest clear
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 2.1 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C reactive protein 280 mg/L (less than 5), lactate 4.8 mmol/L (less than 2), creatinine 148 micromol/L (45-90), platelets 88 x10^9/L (150-400)
data_table.Social history: Household contact with a child who had a sore throat in the past week

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate antimicrobial management?

options.text: Give intravenous cefazolin with metronidazole now
options.rationale: This combination is reasonable empirical cover for polymicrobial endometritis but lacks the antitoxin effect of a protein synthesis inhibitor, which is what limits toxic shock in invasive streptococcal disease. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Give oral amoxicillin with clavulanate and observe closely
options.rationale: Oral therapy is inadequate in a woman with hypotension, a raised lactate and organ dysfunction, in whom gastrointestinal absorption is unreliable and delay costs survival. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Await blood culture results before starting any antibiotic
options.rationale: Cultures must be taken but mortality in invasive streptococcal sepsis rises with every hour of delay to effective therapy, and results take at least 12 to 24 hours. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Give intravenous benzylpenicillin with clindamycin now
options.rationale: Fulminant sepsis within 48 hours of birth with uterine tenderness, offensive lochia, a low white cell count and a recent household sore throat points to invasive group A streptococcal infection, for which benzylpenicillin is the definitive agent and clindamycin is added to suppress exotoxin production. Treatment is given immediately after cultures rather than after imaging. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Give intravenous gentamicin alone and arrange urgent imaging
options.rationale: An aminoglycoside gives no useful cover against group A streptococcus, and imaging to look for retained products should follow resuscitation and antibiotics rather than precede them. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Invasive group A streptococcal infection remains a leading cause of direct maternal death in Australia and characteristically presents with an extremely rapid course in the first few days after birth. The clues are severe pain out of proportion to findings, high fever with rigors, uterine tenderness with offensive lochia, and a household contact with pharyngitis, often in a young child. A low rather than high white cell count is a recognised and ominous feature. Management is immediate resuscitation with benzylpenicillin plus clindamycin, the latter for its suppression of exotoxin synthesis, alongside cultures, senior involvement and consideration of source control.
key_points: A falling or low white cell count in sepsis is a marker of severity, not of mild disease
Clindamycin is added for exotoxin suppression, not for its spectrum
A household contact with sore throat is a classic and frequently missed piece of history
Consider intravenous immunoglobulin and early surgical review if toxic shock or necrotising infection develops
explanation.pearls: Ask every septic postnatal woman about sore throat in the household: group A streptococcus is carried in the throats of young children, and that single question often separates this diagnosis from ordinary polymicrobial endometritis before any culture returns.

subtopic_detail: Counselling about mode of birth after a repaired third degree perineal tear
stem:
A 32 year old woman attends your clinic to plan her second pregnancy. Two years ago she had a forceps birth complicated by a third degree perineal tear, which was repaired in theatre by a consultant at the time.

She tells you that she still cannot always hold wind, and that about once a fortnight she has to rush to the toilet and has twice not made it in time. She completed a course of pelvic floor physiotherapy after the birth with some improvement that then plateaued. Endoanal ultrasound arranged by the perineal clinic shows a persistent external anal sphincter defect and anorectal manometry shows a reduced squeeze pressure.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Well healed perineal scar, reduced voluntary anal squeeze on digital examination, no prolapse
data_table.Investigations: Endoanal ultrasound shows a persistent external anal sphincter defect, anorectal manometry shows reduced squeeze pressure, resting pressure preserved
data_table.Symptoms: Flatus incontinence most days and two episodes of faecal urgency incontinence in the past six months
data_table.Obstetric history: One forceps birth with a repaired third degree tear, no other deliveries

lead_in: What would you first recommend for her next birth?

options.text: Plan a vaginal birth with an elective mediolateral episiotomy
options.rationale: Routine episiotomy does not reliably protect a previously injured sphincter, and subjecting an already symptomatic and structurally deficient sphincter to another vaginal birth is the situation in which continence most often deteriorates permanently. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of obstetric anal sphincter injury)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of obstetric anal sphincter injury

options.text: Plan a vaginal birth and repeat the physiotherapy beforehand
options.rationale: Pelvic floor physiotherapy is valuable and should continue, but she has already had a course with a plateau in response, and conservative therapy cannot restore a structural sphincter defect before another vaginal birth. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of obstetric anal sphincter injury)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of obstetric anal sphincter injury

options.text: Plan a vaginal birth but avoid any instrumental assistance
options.rationale: Avoiding forceps reduces but does not remove the risk to the sphincter, since spontaneous birth also stretches and can further disrupt a deficient muscle, and the plan gives no protection if instrumental birth becomes necessary. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of obstetric anal sphincter injury)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of obstetric anal sphincter injury

options.text: Refer for secondary sphincter repair then plan a vaginal birth
options.rationale: Delayed sphincter repair is considered for severe incontinence in women who have completed their families, because its results deteriorate over time and are undone by subsequent vaginal birth. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of obstetric anal sphincter injury)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of obstetric anal sphincter injury

options.text: Plan an elective caesarean section for her next birth
options.rationale: A woman who remains symptomatic after a previous obstetric anal sphincter injury, with objective evidence of a persisting defect and reduced squeeze pressure, should be offered planned caesarean because a further vaginal birth risks irreversible deterioration to frank faecal incontinence. Women who are asymptomatic with normal investigations can be offered vaginal birth. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of obstetric anal sphincter injury)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of obstetric anal sphincter injury

explanation.summary: Counselling after obstetric anal sphincter injury turns on whether the woman is symptomatic and what objective testing shows. A woman who is fully continent with a normal endoanal ultrasound and normal manometry can be offered vaginal birth with a small risk of recurrence. A woman with persisting incontinence, a demonstrable sphincter defect or reduced squeeze pressure should be offered planned caesarean, because a further vaginal birth carries a substantial risk of permanent worsening. Secondary sphincter repair is reserved for women with severe symptoms who have completed childbearing, since its benefit degrades over time and is lost with another vaginal birth.
key_points: Symptoms plus objective sphincter deficiency is the combination that shifts the recommendation to caesarean
Asymptomatic women with normal investigations may be offered vaginal birth
Elective episiotomy does not reliably protect a previously injured sphincter
Flatus incontinence counts as a symptom and should be asked about directly
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically about flatus control and faecal urgency rather than asking whether she is incontinent: women very rarely volunteer these symptoms, and urgency with a plateaued physiotherapy response is what converts a routine counselling conversation into a recommendation for caesarean.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Management of obstetric anal sphincter injury

subtopic_detail: When contraception can be stopped in a woman using progestogen only pills at fifty three
stem:
A 53 year old woman attends your general practice for a repeat prescription. She has taken a progestogen only pill continuously for nine years and has had no bleeding at all for the past four years.

She asks whether she still needs contraception, saying she is certain she has gone through the menopause and that her friend was told to have a blood test to prove it. She has no hot flushes and no vaginal dryness. She is a non smoker, her blood pressure is normal, and she has no personal or family history of venous thromboembolism or breast cancer.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 70 beats per minute, blood pressure 122/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 15 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 26 kg/m2, no abnormality on abdominal or pelvic examination
data_table.Contraceptive history: Progestogen only pill for nine years, amenorrhoeic for four years, no missed pills
data_table.Other: Non smoker, no vasomotor symptoms, cervical screening up to date and negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice?

options.text: Continue the pill until she is 55 and then stop it
options.rationale: Contraception is recommended until age 55, by which age natural conception is exceptionally rare, and it can then be stopped without any hormonal testing. Amenorrhoea on a progestogen only pill is caused by the pill itself and cannot be used as evidence that ovulation has ceased. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception in the perimenopause)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia: Contraception in the perimenopause

options.text: Stop the pill now given four years without any bleeding
options.rationale: Amenorrhoea is an expected effect of continuous progestogen and does not indicate loss of ovarian function, so stopping on that basis leaves her at risk of a late and unintended pregnancy. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception in the perimenopause)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia: Contraception in the perimenopause

options.text: Check two follicle stimulating hormone levels and then stop
options.rationale: Measuring follicle stimulating hormone is an option in women aged 50 or over using progestogen only methods, but results fluctuate widely in the perimenopause and a raised value does not exclude a subsequent ovulation. Continuing to 55 avoids the ambiguity altogether. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception in the perimenopause)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia: Contraception in the perimenopause

options.text: Change to the combined oral contraceptive pill until age 55
options.rationale: Combined hormonal contraception is generally avoided from age 50 because the cardiovascular and thromboembolic risks outweigh its benefits, and she has no indication for oestrogen. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception in the perimenopause)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia: Contraception in the perimenopause

options.text: Stop the pill and use condoms alone until she turns 55
options.rationale: Barrier methods are far less effective than a progestogen only pill she is already taking without problems, and there is no clinical reason to downgrade her contraceptive efficacy at this stage. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception in the perimenopause)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia: Contraception in the perimenopause

explanation.summary: Fertility falls sharply but does not disappear in the late forties and early fifties, and unintended pregnancy at this age carries high maternal and fetal risk. The simplest and safest rule is to continue contraception until age 55, at which point it can be stopped regardless of bleeding pattern and without hormonal testing. Amenorrhoea while taking a progestogen only method is caused by the method and says nothing about ovarian activity, which is the central trap in this scenario. Combined hormonal contraception is generally discontinued at age 50 in favour of progestogen only or intrauterine methods.
key_points: Age 55 is the point at which contraception can be stopped without testing
Amenorrhoea on progestogen is method induced and is not evidence of menopause
Follicle stimulating hormone testing is optional from age 50 on progestogen only methods but is unreliable in isolation
A levonorgestrel intrauterine system fitted at 45 or older may be retained until 55 if used for contraception alone
explanation.pearls: If she later needs hormone replacement therapy for vasomotor symptoms, remember that standard hormone replacement is not contraceptive: she needs a separate contraceptive method alongside it until 55.

sources.label: Family Planning Australia: Contraception in the perimenopause
Australasian Menopause Society: Contraception and the perimenopause

subtopic_detail: Severe hot flushes in a woman taking tamoxifen after breast cancer
stem:
A 49 year old woman attends your general practice with severe hot flushes occurring around fifteen times a day and waking her four or five times each night. She has been exhausted for months and has started declining work and social commitments.

She completed treatment for an oestrogen receptor positive breast cancer eighteen months ago and takes tamoxifen. Her periods stopped during chemotherapy. She has tried reducing caffeine and alcohol, layered clothing and a bedroom fan without benefit. She has no depression on assessment, no vaginal bleeding, and her mood is low only in proportion to the sleep deprivation. She is not taking any antidepressant and has no history of seizures.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 76 beats per minute, blood pressure 124/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 15 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 25 kg/m2, no lymphadenopathy, surgical breast examination unremarkable, no abnormality on abdominal examination
data_table.Symptom burden: Approximately fifteen daytime flushes and four to five night time waking episodes daily
data_table.Oncology history: Oestrogen receptor positive breast cancer treated eighteen months ago, currently on tamoxifen
data_table.Measures already tried: Caffeine and alcohol reduction, clothing layering, bedroom cooling, without benefit

lead_in: What would you first recommend?

options.text: Start systemic oestrogen therapy at the lowest effective dose
options.rationale: Systemic oestrogen is contraindicated after an oestrogen receptor positive breast cancer because of the risk of stimulating recurrence, regardless of how severe the vasomotor symptoms are. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society: Non hormonal treatments for menopausal symptoms)
source_refs: Australasian Menopause Society: Non hormonal treatments for menopausal symptoms

options.text: Start venlafaxine rather than any hormonal preparation
options.rationale: Venlafaxine has the best evidence among non hormonal agents for reducing vasomotor symptom frequency and severity and is a preferred choice in women taking tamoxifen because it does not meaningfully inhibit the enzyme that converts tamoxifen to its active metabolite. Her symptom burden is well past the point at which lifestyle measures alone suffice. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society: Non hormonal treatments for menopausal symptoms)
source_refs: Australasian Menopause Society: Non hormonal treatments for menopausal symptoms

options.text: Start paroxetine as the non hormonal agent with best evidence
options.rationale: Paroxetine does reduce flushes but is a potent inhibitor of cytochrome P450 2D6, which converts tamoxifen to its active metabolite, so it risks reducing the effectiveness of her cancer treatment. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society: Non hormonal treatments for menopausal symptoms)
source_refs: Australasian Menopause Society: Non hormonal treatments for menopausal symptoms

options.text: Recommend a phytoestrogen preparation available over the counter
options.rationale: Evidence of benefit is weak and inconsistent, and preparations with oestrogenic activity are generally avoided after hormone receptor positive breast cancer. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society: Non hormonal treatments for menopausal symptoms)
source_refs: Australasian Menopause Society: Non hormonal treatments for menopausal symptoms

options.text: Continue lifestyle measures alone and review her again in six months
